Childminder who left more than 20 children alone in her home jailed

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:19:50 GMT

A childminder who admitted leaving children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home has been jailed for two years.

More than 20 unattended children, two under the age of one, were in Amanda Mathewson's house in Dunfermline, Fife, when she was arrested in August 2024.

Her offending only came to light after concerned parents spied on her leaving for a school run without their children.

An internal Care Inspectorate probe found Mathewson, who was been licensed to look after eight children under the age of 16 at any one time, had been tipped off about inspections by an unknown staff member.

Mathewson previously pled guilty to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health.

Sheriff John MacRitchie said Mathewson had committed a "gross abuse of a position of trust" during sentencing at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court.

He read victim impact statements from parents of affected children who described them suffering from "nightmares and anxiety" and developing a "distrust of childcare providers".

Mathewson had been a self-employed childminder for 30 years prior to her arrest.

An unannounced visit by the Care Inspectorate in August 2023 rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good", praising her "warmth, kindness and nurturing approach".

But a year later, one couple became suspicious that all was not as it seemed.

A friend had mentioned their two children, aged one and three, were not with Mathewson when she was on a school run.

BBC Scotland News has spoken to the father of the children. He has not been named to protect their identity.

The couple watched Mathewson in secret on 26 August 2024, parking opposite her home when their two boys were meant to be in her care as she went to collect other children from a local primary school.

They saw Mathewson leave the home with two young girls in a pushchair, then went to the front door - where the father said a child could be heard "screaming" inside.

The couple walked through a side gate to get to the back garden where they found a number of unsupervised children playing.

They were able to enter the property through the back door, finding a child "lying under a table" crying in severe distress.

Upstairs, the father said "a dozen or so young children" were sitting on the floor of a spare bedroom, with another on a double bed, as a TV on top of a chest of drawers loudly played a children's programme.

He said two others were "tightly strapped into a buggy in a way it was not meant to be used".

"It was August. It was a particularly warm summer. It was hot in that room," he said.

"There was no food, no water, no toys, no activities for the children to be engaged in."

The father said he was cradling two of the children in his arms as he walked downstairs when Mathewson returned home.

He described her reaction to seeing him as being "like her soul had left her body".

"I'll never forget it, she was like a child caught in the act of doing something they shouldn't be doing," he said.

"She took her jacket off and she just slumped to the floor. I asked her; 'Amanda, what the hell? How many laws have you broken here?'"

"It's obvious to us now. Her entire life was a lie. She has fabricated pretty much her entire life, her entire personality. It just crumbled in an instant."

Mathewson was arrested and charged a short time later. When police arrived at the home, she had 15 children aged under 12 in her care, as well as 10 children under primary school age and two children under the age of one.

During the subsequent investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was commonplace.

Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten or had anything to drink during her care.

Some also reported their children returning home in dirty nappies.

A court hearing was later told how Mathewson would play loud music and prevented parents from coming into her home in an attempt to hide her offending.

Another parent told BBC Scotland News his daughter was "rummaging in a food waste bin" at nursery after spending mornings at Mathewson's home.

For months after her arrest, he said his daughter would become "distraught" whenever they drove past her house.

He said it became "really difficult" for the family to travel from one side of the town to the other without her becoming distressed.

"I can't imagine what must be going through her mind, the fear of going back there," he said.

"That was heartbreaking and we didn't know what to do or how to help."

He described Mathewson's system of avoiding parents bumping into each other at the same time as being like a "military operation".

"We were let down. We were lied to. Our children were neglected," he said.

"The only question I have is; Why?"

The Care Inspectorate's August 2023 visit was meant to be unannounced, but the regulator has since admitted it is likely Mathewson received "confidential information" about inspections from an employee.

The insider is yet to be identified, despite an internal investigation.

A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said Mathewson "broke the trust" of families.

They said "inspection, complaints and conflict of interest procedures" had been updated in following feedback from affected parents.

Maria Lloyd, independent chairwoman of the Fife child protection committee, said a "learning review" would take place in the wake of the case.

She said it would consider whether improvements to "practice, processes or partnership working" were required.

A Scottish government spokesperson said the Care Inspectorate had carried out an audit of the way complaints against Mathewson were handled.

They added: "We know Scotland's childminding community will be deeply distressed by this case.

"We are working with the independent regulators to strengthen practice, improve processes and enhance transparency."

Law firm Irwin Mitchell Scotland - who are representing a number of families involved - said they have been instructed to explore a civil case against the Care Inspectorate.

Partner Kim Leslie said: "It is beggars belief that a failing of this magnitude could go unnoticed.

"This is a fundamental breach of trust which, by the regulator's own admission, completely compromised the efficacy of regulatory scrutiny.

"The parents want the Care Inspectorate to be held to account."

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:16:34 GMT

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could be the first brothers to play together for England since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago

It may be a surprise to some but Jobe Bellingham's call-up to the England senior side has been a long time coming.

The 21-year-old's career path has been very similar to that of his 23-year-old brother Jude - England's star player at the World Cup and one of Real Madrid's best players. Both were stars of the Birmingham City academy before big-money moves to the German Bundesliga and England call-ups.

Jobe's debut for Birmingham came at the age of 16 years and 107 days - 69 days older than Jude when he made his first appearance for the Blues' senior side.

The central midfielder then moved to Sunderland and helped them win promotion to the Premier League before joining German side Borussia Dortmund at the age of 19 in a deal worth up to £31m.

Jude also moved to Dortmund when he was 17, before developing into one of the world's best players and joining Real Madrid.

Having one of the best midfielders in the world as your older brother comes with challenges and Jobe has consistently been compared to his sibling.

But the former Sunderland midfielder is his own player, wearing 'Jobe' on the back of his shirt instead of his family name. He said it was suggested to him by a former coach because "it shows that I'm going my own way".

England manager Thomas Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live it is "a beautiful story".

"They are both good for each other," he added. "My understanding is they are very close.

"It makes life easier for Jobe to come into camp and know his brother is one of the key players in our team. So, that will hopefully help him, but don't forget he is here on his own merits, and he is not here because of his brother."

Jobe is a different type of player to Jude, sitting deeper in the midfield, but is as physically imposing while still being good on the ball.

He is the current captain of the England Under-21 side, and Tuchel said Young Lions head coach Lee Carsley had been pushing for some time for the younger Bellingham to get senior recognition.

"He's the standout player," said Tuchel. "He's the captain, so the door should always be open for the pathway, always be open for special performances over a long period of time.

"That's what Jobe has done on top of it. He found his way, he found his rhythm with Dortmund. He's had an excellent start to his season, is a regular starter and influential."

This video can not be played

Thomas Tuchel on Jobe Bellingham's England call-up

England host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before travelling to Madrid to take on Spain on 15 November in this next international break.

With Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for the first game, and Bournemouth's Alex Scott out injured after shining on his debut in last month's 7-0 win over Croatia, Tuchel said a natural "opportunity" for Jobe had opened up.

"He deserves to make an impression for us," said the German in his news conference after naming the squad.

"It's an incredible achievement for the family and for the brothers. I saw his excitement straight away and his smile.

"He has an open and calm personality. He's one of five players for the central midfield.

"He's a more defensive player than Jude. So strong on the ball, good physique, a big body, a very physical player and can keep possession.

"It's now up to him, but he's excited and happy and eager to impress, and that's the best foundation to have a good camp for him."

Jude shared a throwback photo of him and Jobe after Friday's squad announcement

If they get on the pitch together, Jude and Jobe won't be the first brothers to represent the Three Lions.

It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville, who both played for Manchester United, last played together for England, and 30 years since they started.

They first played together for England in 1996 against China, becoming the first siblings to do so since Bobby and Jack Charlton 26 years earlier.

Jack and Bobby were both part of England's 1966 World Cup-winning squad.

Bobby was the younger of the two, but made his Three Lions debut first. He went on to win 106 international caps.

Jack, who was not called into the England team until days before his 30th birthday, won 35 caps.

More recently, brothers Nathaniel and Trevoh Chalobah have both played for England, but never alongside each other.

Nathaniel made his solitary appearance as an injury-time substitute in a 3-2 away win against Spain in a 2018 Nations League game.

His younger brother Trevoh, currently a Como defender, made the first of his three international appearances against Senegal in June 2025 and was in England's 2026 World Cup squad.

The Nevilles played 31 times for England

Bobby and Jack Charlton were both in the England squad that lifted the Jules Rimet Trophy at Wembley.

The Chalobah brothers never played together for England, but both featured for the senior side.

1 of 3

Jobe Bellingham has made 14 appearances for Dortmund this season

Jobe has shown remarkable progress since last winter. In the first couple of months, following his move from Sunderland to Borussia Dortmund, he seemed timid, as if he was just trying to avoid making any mistakes. His passes rarely, if ever, caused trouble for opposing defences.

Even Dortmund manager Niko Kovac said at one point that he was surprised how long it might take him to get comfortable in the Bundesliga. But hard work in the gym to build up muscle mass in order to become more explosive and the fact that he received plenty of chances in Dortmund's line-up has helped his development.

In the latter stages of last season, his decision-making was much faster and his intensity seemed higher. Still, Dortmund decided to sign Dutch midfielder Joey Veerman, a specialist at making line-breaking passes, in August.

It meant Jobe's place in the starting XI was far from secure at the beginning of this season.

In recent games, Kovac has employed Bellingham in a more advanced role, as one of the two number 10s behind the striker. In this role, Bellingham drove into the final third with pace and showed intensity during pressing sequences.

His performance in the 2-2 draw against Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga last Saturday was arguably his best since his arrival in Germany.

Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:12:20 GMT

Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.

The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".

Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentary interview with Louis Theroux that there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.

Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".

It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.

Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain.

"They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."

She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief.

"Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened.

"I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."

Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

Ryan continued on the podcast: "This verdict came because women were hurt, and I worry as well about what happens next.

"Because he's obviously spent a long time cultivating this idea that the establishment have invented these claims against him, and he's martyred himself to a growing audience who really still think that it is the courageous survivors who are the villains in this story."

Ryan's comments came on the same day that former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey questioned how and why Brand was able to "get away with it so long?

"Why didn't anybody intervene? Why did those around him enable him? Why didn't any of the senior executives who worked with him call time?" she said on BBC Radio 5 Live's Nick Campbell on Friday.

"I think they were partly mesmerised. I think he seemed to be 'cool' for a while. I think he did have charisma," added Heggessey.

"He brought in a young audience, which a lot of broadcasters crave. So I think all of those reasons... and as people have said, he did hide in plain sight."

Bear Grylls, the adventurer and host of the Discovery Channel's show Man Vs Wild, has spoken about when he helped baptise Brand in the River Thames in 2024.

"Brand's faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism," he said on X, adding that he had attended a few baptisms, including "visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes".

Grylls said he attended as part of a calling of his faith "to love and serve anyone", adding it is "the sick who need healing".

"Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn't want to ever discourage someone's coming to faith," he continued.

But, he said, it was “right that justice has now been served.

"I can't imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day."

Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.

During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.

Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction.

"One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated.

"There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."

In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate.

"The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."

The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.

Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

Man investigated for leaving 17-year-old on Germany's highest mountain

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 12:31:34 GMT

Austrian police are investigating a German man aged 21 on suspicion of endangering public safety, after his 17-year-old female friend was left stranded on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze in sub-zero temperatures.

The teenager called emergency services and was eventually rescued on the mountain at an altitude of about 2,500m (8,200ft).

She was suffering from hypothermia and taken to hospital in nearby Garmisch-Partenkirchen, over the border in Germany, before being discharged.

In Austria, anyone who endangers another person's physical safety can be punished with up to three months in prison.

The pair set off in the early hours of Sunday from the resort of Ehrwald in the Austrian Tyrol with the aim of seeing the sunrise on Zugspitze.

Temperatures that morning had fallen to -12C, a mountain rescuer told German Press Agency DPA.

The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit soon changed.

At one point they separated and the 21-year-old descended alone. The reason they split is unclear, and a police spokesperson declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.

Seven mountain rescuers responded to the call, and a helicopter eventually airlifted the teenager off the mountain. She was then taken to hospital by ambulance.

Although the teenager survived, what happened on Zugspitze on Sunday is reminiscent of a fatal incident on Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, in January 2025.

A 33-year-old woman froze to death on the Grossglockner after her boyfriend left her on the mountain, and he was later found guilty of grossly negligent manslaughter.

The boyfriend had insisted he had left her there while trying to get help, telling the court he had loved his girlfriend and that he was deeply sorry.

The case reverberated throughout the mountaineering community at the time, with prosecutors arguing that as the more experienced climber, he was the responsible guide on the trip and had failed to turn back or call for help in time.

In the latest case in Austria, police have said once they have completed their investigation, a report will be sent to Innsbruck public prosecutors, who will decide if a criminal offence has been committed.

How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 12:16:44 GMT

Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.

He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.

Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.

With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.

He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.

Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.

Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.

The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.

"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."

But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.

"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.

"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."

He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".

The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".

Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".

But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".

In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?

A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."

Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".

"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"

And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".

"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.

At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

We now understand quite how terrible.

Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?

BBC News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 01:22:39 GMT

This video can not be played

What is the polar vortex?

High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.

Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.

It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.

Read more on how the the polar vortex can impact UK weather

Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.

Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.

Sudden stratospheric warming can lead to a weakening of the polar vortex, resulting it in becoming disrupted, even split, high above the Arctic region

If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.

Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."

The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.

Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.

But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.

While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.

These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.

With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".

A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.

Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.

However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."

"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."

One reason is the timing.

The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.

Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.

And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.

While snow is not likely in the coming weeks, a possible continuation of drier than average conditions will be concerning for replenishment of our reservoirs

Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.

Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El Niño, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.

But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.

For Charlton-Perez, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.

With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.

For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

The covid-19 vaccines may have provided health and economic benefits worth up to $64.3 trillion in the first year alone – almost double an earlier estimate. But now, a reanalysis of the data suggests it is actually between $6.43 trillion and $64.3 trillion.

This means that for every $1 spent on the vaccines’ development, between $59.70 and $809 was gained in that year. “It is great to finally see this research published to demonstrate the enormous health and financial benefits gained from covid-19 vaccines, in comparison to the costs that went into their development and delivery,” says Hallie Benjamin at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.

Does each new covid-19 variant pose a significant threat?

The $6.43 trillion figure is based on a cost-effectiveness analysis that is generally used in the health sector and factors in quality of life, while the $64.3 trillion figure is based on a cost-benefit analysis used in the public sector.

Advertisement

Both include data from 173 countries on averted hospitalisations, productivity losses and lives saved. For instance, one of the estimates Benjamin and her colleagues used came from modelling that suggested the vaccines prevented 14 million to 20 million deaths in their first year.

The initial $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion figures were released when the research was in a preprint stage, before it had been peer-reviewed. “We made many changes throughout the peer-review process that strengthened the quality of our findings,” says Benjamin.

The researchers originally used the Value of Statistical Life Years, which considers how many years a person would be likely to live because of the vaccine, a figure that would be lower if someone was older. As part of the peer-review process, they were advised to use the Value of Statistical Life. Team member Mark Jit at New York University says this treats life spans more equally and is aligned with recommendations for valuing mortality-risk reductions.

The cost-benefit analysis figure also increased significantly due to a change from calculating the economic value of avoiding a death, says Jit.

But the returns weren’t equally distributed. The researchers found that the vaccines had the highest returns in richer countries. This was probably because poorer countries accessed them later, so fewer lives were saved and fewer productivity and healthcare costs were averted, says Jit. The results are “a message about the need for being able to distribute the vaccines fairly to the people most in need around the world”, he says.

Getting covid-19 for the first time slightly increased the risk of heart inflammation, blood clots and bleeding disorders among children, whereas being vaccinated against the virus was much safer and sometimes protective

Richard Carpiano at the University of California, Riverside, says we already knew the covid-19 vaccines were a “life-saving success”, but this study reinforces that “protecting the public’s health is protecting the economy”.

This challenges the “black-and-white” thinking during the covid-19 pandemic on the trade-off between protecting public health through lockdowns and protecting the economy, says Carpiano.

He also hopes these understandings will be used for future infectious outbreaks, or pandemics. “We are in a historical period that has been labelled as ‘a new pandemic age’,” says Carpiano. “The probability of another pandemic in the next 10 years is significant, as are the chances of smaller regional disease outbreaks from existing or new pathogens.” This analysis is “fundamental” to informing policy-making decisions, he says.

The earliest firm evidence of the plant’s use as a drug had been chemical traces on wooden braziers in China that implied humans were “smoking” cannabis 2500 years ago as part of funeral rites.

Now, Gino Caspari at the University of Bern in Switzerland and his colleagues have pushed the date back another 300 years with a find at the Tunnug 1 burial mound in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia.

Advertisement

The royal burial mound dates to the time of the Scythians, nomads renowned for their military skills and horseback archery who spread across a huge swathe of Eurasia.

They also found a preserved human hair dating to the same time, and chemical analysis of it detected cannabinol, a compound produced when THC, the psychoactive compound found in cannabis, oxidises, alongside chemical signatures of THC itself, so the person is likely to have felt psychoactive effects.

He says we can’t say how the person consumed the drug – it might have been smoked or the seeds could have just been ingested.

Given its presence in the burial mound, Caspari says the use of cannabis was probably related to a ritual funerary process. That could have been for a religious high, but he suggests there might have been a more sinister use.

“The suggestion that cannabis may have been used to calm individuals selected for ritual sacrifice is intriguing, but remains highly speculative,” says Adam Brumm, an archaeologist at Griffith University in Australia, who recently showed that people were sucking betel nuts to extract a pain-relieving compound up to 25,000 years ago in Indonesia.

Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI

New Scientist November 05, 2026

When I was at school, a new technology launched in the form of a magic box that could answer any question you wanted. It was called Google, and my teachers cautioned that we shouldn’t trust everything it spat out, because anyone could put anything on the internet. Three decades later, history is repeating – with a twist. Schools are now begging Google to allow students to access its search engine, but the tech giant says that is only possible if teachers also accept a new kind of magic box, AI.

Google is far more integrated into education than it was in my day, with its Classroom and Workspace products providing teachers and students with a range of tools from email to lesson planning. More recently, Google has incorporated its Gemini AI chatbot into Classroom, to the chagrin of some US school districts that want to be able to decide whether or not students have access to AI. Sure, said Google, you can switch off AI, but then you lose search. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Google’s Chris Phillips told The New York Times.

Why I have changed my mind about AI and you should too

At first, I thought this must be a misunderstanding about what we call AI. For most people today, AI means a large language model (LLM) of the type that powers Gemini or ChatGPT. But Google’s search engine has long used AI in the historical sense of machine learning, starting in 2015 with a system called RankBrain that helped relate words to concepts in order to produce search results. The AI Overviews you often see at the top of a search today, which launched in 2024, are the only part of the search results produced by Gemini.

Advertisement

Surely, I thought, what’s happening here is that school districts saying “no AI” simply mean no AI Overviews, while Google is quite reasonably saying it isn’t possible to rip out elements of its search engine that have been operating for over a decade in order to comply with a strict “no AI” request. This can easily be solved by making sure everyone is talking about the same thing, right?

Wrong. Google really is presenting schools with an all-or-nothing choice. “If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have search on at all,” Phillips told education news outlet Chalkbeat. This is a product decision, not a technical one. AI Overviews do not appear on every search, and they can be disabled for every search by adding a short code to the URL. Google could surely provide schools with this option, if it wished. When asked to comment, a Google spokesperson sent New Scientist a link to a blog post on AI tutoring with its Gemini product.

We have seen a tech giant use this playbook before. Around the same time that Google was launching its young, upstart search engine in the late 1990s, Microsoft was facing legal action for forcing people to install the Internet Explorer (IE) browser as part of its Windows operating system, in an effort to fight off competitor browsers. At the time, Microsoft claimed that the files for IE were an “integral part” of Windows and could not be removed “without impairing the performance of the operating system”. In 2001, a US court ruled that this integration served to illegally maintain a monopoly, and Microsoft was obliged to make other browsers more accessible. By 2010, Microsoft was forced to offer users a range of browsers, following a European Commission ruling.

Around one-third of AI search tool answers make unsupported claims

There is no suggestion that Google is doing anything illegal in its approach to schools, although the company is currently appealing a US antitrust ruling that found it illegally maintains a monopoly in online search, and commentators have accused it of exploiting that monopoly. “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools”, wrote New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on X. Following the backlash, Google posted on X that for schools, Gemini and search will be off by default and schools can choose to turn on either at their discretion. That doesn’t actually address the issue of having search without AI Overviews, however.

Ultimately, it will probably be for the courts to decide whether Google should be made to offer search without AI, but I am more interested in the question of how and when children should begin to use AI. Google has a 90 per cent market share in search, so it would be naive to think that children aren’t being exposed to AI Overviews, even if they do end up banned in schools. Personally, I know that AI Overviews can be heavily flawed and provide incorrect information, and yet I still find it hard to ignore them at the top of my search results, even while knowing that I should be clicking links to provide websites with revenue if I want them to continue existing.

Research on how LLMs affect learning is still in early days, but the evidence we have is worrying. One study of around 10,000 adults found that people who used an LLM summary rather than a list of links gained a shallower understanding of a topic, seemingly because having the results predigested by an AI required less cognitive effort. Another study of more than 26,000 students in China found that allowing them to use AI drastically improved homework performance, but saw exam results fall – suggesting that the children were letting AI do their homework for them without really learning anything.

Google’s answer to these concerns is its Guided Learning product, which it is adding to search for student accounts. It says the system will pick up when children are looking for help with homework, and walk them through it step by step, rather than simply providing an answer. In tests conducted with around 1800 students in Sierra Leone, Google says this approach provided more than a year of typical learning progress in just eight weeks.

In principle, I am not against the use of AI in schools – it is a modern, useful technology that will surely be part of students’ lives in the future, and they should learn to understand it just as I learned the pros and cons of using Google back in the 90s. The question of how to handle homework assignments in the age of AI, when an essay can be produced in seconds, is thorny and ongoing. One option is to simply scrap homework and require more in-classroom testing, but if Google gets its way and AI ends up being unavoidable there as well, it seems like teachers will have little control. That, to me, is the most objectionable point, as it should not be down to tech giants to set education policy.

Ordering takeaway food, writing emails, reworking presentations: AI assistants are promoted as a way of outsourcing mundane tasks to free up your time for more interesting pursuits. So, what are they actually good for – and what are the risks?

Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedently fast rate.

The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber.

Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole setup to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature. Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute.

Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams.

Because the rotor experiences essentially no friction, and it is magnetic and cold, its behaviour is very sensitive to its environment, which makes it a promising sensor. Wang says this could be useful for builders of quantum computers, which often must be kept extremely cold and isolated in order to work.

Benjamin Stickler at Ulm University in Germany says the levitated spinning magnet could also be used to precisely sense and measure magnetic fields.

But previous studies show that, as cardiorespiratory fitness increases, dementia risk drops and grey matter volume increases. “The more we take care of our cardiometabolic health via activities like physical activity, the more we may prolong the health of our brain,” says Koemel.

But the results don’t mean everyone should suddenly start running up the stairs. “We typically will recommend people gradually increase their physical activity, because radical shifts could increase the risk of certain accidents or injuries,” says Koemel. “A core message is that a little can go a long way here.”

Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, which drain brain waste, may be involved in the onset of Parkinson’s disease. The condition is associated with the build-up of a misfolded protein called alpha-synuclein, which may not be efficiently removed from the brain if the lymphatic vessels are impaired. But the accumulation of alpha-synuclein seems to further damage these vessels, creating a self-reinforcing chain of events where each problem worsens the other.

A dramatic rethink of Parkinson’s offers new hope for treatment

“It is a vicious cycle,” says Justin Rustenhoven at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. This may also help explain why Parkinson’s disease is a progressive condition that worsens over time, he says.

Parkinson’s disease, which affects more than 10 million people worldwide, is characterised by a loss of neurons in brain regions that control movement. This causes symptoms such as tremor and muscle stiffness. The condition is thought to be caused by alpha-synuclein, which occurs naturally in the brain, misfolding and forming clumps that damage neurons.

Advertisement

In 2021, researchers showed that accumulation of alpha-synuclein in Parkinson’s disease may partly result from impaired drainage of brain waste via meningeal lymphatic vessels. These are found in the outermost layer of three membranes, called meninges, surrounding the brain. The vessels receive waste from a network of channels surrounding the brain’s blood vessels, called the glymphatic system, before transporting it to other parts of the body for disposal.

But what causes the lymphatic impairment in Parkinson’s disease was unknown. Rustenhoven and his colleagues wondered whether it may result from alpha-synuclein clogging up the meninges. “No one had really looked at that before,” says Rustenhoven, with most research focusing on changes to the regions that control movement, which are located deep within the brain.

The team analysed post-mortem samples of the meninges from seven people who’d had severe Parkinson’s disease and seven people who hadn’t had the condition. Only the Parkinson’s samples had alpha-synuclein clumps. “For the first time, we showed that these aggregates accumulate at the brain’s borders in people with Parkinson’s,” says Rustenhoven.

Free newsletter

To determine whether such protein accumulation impairs clearance of brain waste, the researchers injected mice with a virus that infected cells called fibroblasts in the meninges. This caused them to continually produce alpha-synuclein at elevated levels, similar to those seen in people with Parkinson’s disease. At such high levels, alpha-synuclein misfolded and formed toxic clumps that spread across cells in lymphatic vessels in the meninges, but not inside the brain.

Two months later, brain imaging revealed that these mice’s meningeal lymphatic vessels drained waste fluid half as rapidly as those of control mice, which were injected with a virus encoding for an inert protein. What’s more, in the former group of mice, immune cells called macrophages had engulfed the alpha-synuclein clumps at the brain’s borders. This caused the macrophages to double in number and produce about triple the amount of TNF-alpha, an inflammatory molecule.

Next, the team exposed sheets of human cells, found in meningeal lymphatic vessels, to either alpha-synuclein or TNF-alpha. Both molecules caused gaps to form between the lymphatic cells, making them leaky, says Rusterhoven.

“The accumulation of alpha-synuclein in the brain borders basically drives an immune response that pokes holes in those lymphatic vessels, making them ineffective at draining,” he says. “We already know from other studies that those lymphatics are important for draining alpha-synuclein, so impaired lymphatic drainage [due to alpha-synuclein] means even more of the protein is going to build up.”

The controversial discovery that our brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is now prompting a rethink of adult brain health, pointing the way to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression

This feedback loop keeps reinforcing itself, which may cause the worsening of brain damage and symptoms associated with Parkinson’s, says Rusterhoven.

The same mechanism probably applies to other neurodegenerative conditions where proteins accumulate, such as Alzheimer’s disease, says Camille Carroll at Newcastle University in the UK. But this understanding also creates new treatment opportunities. It suggests that “therapies that dampen or modulate that immune response could prevent lymphatic dysfunction to treat Parkinson’s”, says Rusterhoven.

The team now plans to carry out similar experiments where mice are studied after they develop Parkinson’s symptoms, not just its associated brain changes. These mice will also be tracked for longer, he says.

“Their mouse model was appropriate for the question they were asking, which was looking specifically at the effects of alpha-synuclein at the brain border on lymphatics,” says Carroll. “But linking their findings to symptoms will be important.”

In ongoing work, the researchers are collecting more brain-border samples from people who died with Parkinson’s disease of varying severity. This will enable them to determine how often alpha-synuclein clogs up the brain’s borders during the condition and at what stage it may start causing lymphatic impairment.

A pill that induces hypoxia in the brain has been linked to improved symptoms of three neurodegenerative conditions when tested in mice

They are also trialling, in mice and human cells, whether drugs that block TNF-alpha can reverse lymphatic damage during Parkinson’s. A prior study looked at people with inflammatory bowel disease, which is linked to a higher risk of Parkinson’s, and found that those who took drugs that block TNF-alpha were 78 per cent less likely to develop Parkinson’s.

An ongoing trial is also giving people with REM (rapid eye movement) sleep behaviour disorder, which often precedes Parkinson’s disease, a drug that blocks TNF-alpha, to determine whether this affects Parkinson’s progression. “This will be very interesting evidence to support our findings,” says Rustenhoven.

Journal of Experimental Medicine DOI: 10.1084/jem.20251245

Hubble Space Telescope is falling to Earth – should NASA save it?

New Scientist November 06, 2026

The Hubble Space Telescope is slowly falling out of the sky, and it could burn up in Earth’s atmosphere as soon as 2032. Researchers are urging NASA to rescue it, arguing that the ageing instrument is still vital for science and will leave a stark capability gap if lost.

Hubble was launched in 1990 and, following an infamous design flaw in one of its mirrors that was only fixed in 1993, has provided a wealth of new science ever since. NASA claims that more than 23,000 peer-reviewed scientific papers have emerged from its images.

Stunning first images show the power of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory

But the space-based telescope requires periodic servicing and raising of its orbit, as atmospheric drag causes it to slowly lose altitude. Hubble has gyroscopes that allow it to shift position to image different parts of the sky, but no propulsion of its own.

Advertisement

The last time that Hubble was lifted to a higher orbit was in 2002, when the space shuttle Columbia visited – one of five shuttle missions to the telescope. Since then, NASA has retired the shuttle fleet and no longer has any spacecraft with the capability to carry out the task. NASA estimates that Hubble has a 10 per cent probability of re-entry by September 2032, and a 50 per cent probability by December 2033.

The space agency has put out a call for ideas from the commercial sector, giving companies until 30 November to submit plans for either raising the orbit of Hubble to at least 600 kilometres or safely de-orbiting it and letting it crash into the ocean. The telescope has parts of sufficient density that they would probably survive atmospheric re-entry.

Free newsletter

Such a move wouldn’t be unprecedented. Earlier this year, a NASA-funded mission carried out by commercial outfit Katalyst Space was launched to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, whose orbit was decaying in a similar fashion to Hubble’s. The mission failed due to a steering problem, but was widely regarded to be possible. Katalyst Space didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Alise Fisher at NASA says the agency is open to ideas from inside or outside the organisation, and isn’t taking anything off the table. “It wouldn’t be appropriate for the agency to speculate about specific potential responses, so we don’t inadvertently limit them, but NASA is looking to explore a range of technologies and approaches, including those the agency may not have considered previously.”

NASA’s call-out explains that a private company would need to supply everything for the mission: the launch vehicle, the spacecraft and, if applicable, the crew. The space agency issued a similar call for ideas in 2022, but did not proceed with any despite reportedly receiving eight submissions. It did investigate a proposal by SpaceX, but the company didn’t respond to New Scientist’s questions on whether it would be submitting a new proposal this time.

Thomas Haworth at Queen Mary University of London is part of a panel of scientists advising NASA on what direction to take with Hubble, which he describes as “the greatest telescope of all time”. He went into discussions with colleagues expecting the focus to be on how NASA could be advised to extract the most science from Hubble before the end of its life, but found that re-boosting its orbit was actually higher on the agenda, he says.

“It’s within the realms of possibility,” says Haworth. “The overall document that we’re coming up with, which still isn’t submitted yet, is going to try and strongly make that recommendation. There is quite a lot of effort to argue for a boost.”

Is an old NASA probe about to redraw the frontier of the solar system?

NASA is likely to make a decision quickly once that recommendation is in, because planning a boost mission will take years, says Haworth. “You need to decide now.”

Stephen Wilkins at the University of Sussex, UK, says Hubble has unique abilities unmatched by any other instrument – including the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope.

Hubble can do high-resolution ultraviolet imaging better than anything currently available. NASA aims to launch the Ultraviolet Explorer in 2030, which will cover the same part of the spectrum but with a tenth of the resolution, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) may launch in the 2040s and match Hubble’s ability. But if Hubble is allowed to burn up in 2032, this could leave a decade or more of lost science, and if the HWO is cancelled, then that could be a virtually permanent setback.

Launching a mission to physically grapple with the telescope, which is 13 metres long and weighs over 12,000 kilograms, will be no easy task. But it could also bring intangible benefits besides lengthening Hubble’s lifespan, says Wilkins.

“While repair is more complex now that we don’t have the space shuttle, attempting to repair Hubble helps maintain key skills that will be essential for future space exploration or exploitation,” he says. “Whether or not repair makes sense ultimately depends on the cost, but maintaining skills should also be considered.”

Why NASA is sending a probe to Europa – and what it’s looking for

Mark Norris at the University of Lancashire, UK, was previously funded by the Hubble budget to scour archived images for ultra-compact dwarf galaxies. “I’d worked out that, in the archive of these galaxies that Hubble had been surveying for other projects, the things I was interested in were must have been in the images by chance,” he says. “It basically built the foundation of my career. I wouldn’t have a permanent job now if it hadn’t been for that insight.”

Hubble was always designed to be serviced, says Norris, so it is fitted with grapple points for robotic arms to grab hold of. But raising its orbit wouldn’t be a permanent solution and it has begun to show its age.

“The instruments are gradually degrading through exposure to the space environment,” he says. “It’s a bit of a miracle it’s still going, but they over-engineer these things and they did service it so many times – they made sure that when the last service was done, everything was left working. It’s still doing really great science.”

NASA administrators will need to make difficult decisions about costs, as ongoing servicing and ground support will be needed on top of any mission to boost Hubble’s orbit.

“If they can save it, it makes sense, but it depends how much [it costs] and what gets axed in order to save it,” says Hayworth. “Say, for example, if they cut LISA [a plan to build a space-based gravitational wave detector]. This is probably personal and biased, but I think the science from that is so exciting that it would be a shame to lose that for the sake of an old instrument.”

A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave for a future moon base

New Scientist November 06, 2026

In video-game terms, the moon is the first level in an unfathomably giant, never-ending realm. It is the place where we, the players, learn the controls and try very hard not to die, in preparation for safely exploring the rest of the solar system. At a convenient 385,000 kilometres from Earth – a stone’s throw in cosmic terms – our planet’s companion is a great testing ground. And the race is on to claim a piece of it for a base.

Unfortunately for us, the moon is also a preposterously dangerous place to be. The volcanic dust there is adhesive, abrasive and corrosive, able to eat through spacesuits and machinery like a swarm of voracious locusts. Its daytime temperature can reach 120°C, while its benighted craters can plunge to -245°C, which is close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature in the universe. There are moonquakes, which (unlike Earth’s own tremors) can last for tens of minutes. And its lack of an atmosphere means that its surface is unprotected from asteroids (which can splatter you) and space radiation (which can give you cancer).

There are so many awful ways to perish on the moon. China knows the risks. So does the US. And yet, these two countries – along with their many friends and enemies – aren’t just keen on sending astronauts to the lunar surface; they are also planning to establish their own nuclear-powered bases, home to rotating astronaut crews.

Advertisement

Asteroid hit the moon and flung rocks 120 kilometres from the crater

I know what you’re thinking: this sounds like the stuff of science fiction, in the sense that you think it will never happen or, if you do, you suspect that it will go horribly, dramatically wrong. But I have been covering these plans for several years now, and I can promise you two things. The first is that, because this new space race is being (partly, perhaps largely) driven by nationalistic zeal, a moon base is much closer to being realised than you might think. The second is that you’re right: if space agencies aren’t exceedingly careful, things could go wrong.

Neither side wants to see a dead astronaut on the lunar surface, which is why these bases must be nothing short of impregnable fortresses. To that end, NASA recently announced that it has selected three new uncrewed scientific missions to the moon, each designed to further the goals of its Artemis programme. The first is a sophisticated seismometer, which will listen out for moonquakes and meteorite impacts. The second will hunt for signs of ice that can be turned into potable water, breathable oxygen and rocket fuel.

So far, so expected. But the third robotic mission really stood out to me, because it is going to investigate a subterranean lava tube.

Yes, you read that right: a tube, burrowed out by actual lava, on the moon.

Lava tubes are extremely cool – and I’m not just saying that because I’m a trained volcanologist. I have walked through several on Earth. They’re serpentine, cavernous things. They often form when a scorching-hot river of molten rock is rushing through a channel. When the river runs out of momentum or magma, the top – exposed to the atmosphere – cools quickly, forming a roof. The rest of the lava drains out elsewhere, leaving an eerie, inky-black hollow behind. Some of them even have nice acoustics, which makes them great alternative gig venues.

The moon is a great big ball of frozen magma. It’s geologically comatose today, but a stegosaurus could have looked up and seen the crimson glow of freshly erupted lava painting the lunar surface. And where there’s an abundance of lava, there are oodles of lava tubes. The problem is that, from the perspective of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter satellite, suspected lava tube sites just look like deep, shadowy pits.

The Marius Hills pit, on the moon’s nearside, is a prime example. It looks like someone punched a hole in the lunar surface, which is why it’s thought to be a natural skylight for a lava tube. Keen to find out for sure, NASA is sending a robotic mission there to scout it out – and not just to settle a few bets between lunar geologists.

Jessica Atkin knows more than anyone else about what it would take to supply food for a moon base. She reveals how to build a lunar farm and what astronauts can expect to dine on

NASA notes that lava tubes offer “natural, ready-made shelters that provide crucial thermal stability and shielding from deadly ionizing radiation and micrometeoroid bombardment”. That’s right: one day, NASA’s astronauts might be living in ancient volcanic vaults to avoid spending too much time on its truly terrible surface.

The mission to the Marius Hills pit – the first plan to explore a lunar lava tube – doesn’t have a launch date just yet. But it does have an excellent name: the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Yes, that one, the warrior dwarf from Middle-earth who loves his axe, despises evil rings of power and frequents all kinds of dangerous caves.

I reached out to Nathaniel Putzig at the Planetary Science Institute, the principal investigator of GIMLI. He swears that the name wasn’t inspired by J. R. R. Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings. He says that he simply wrote down words describing the mission plan and arranged them to make a pleasing sounding acronym.

“At the time, I was only vaguely aware of the Tolkien association, not fully realising that I had happened upon the name for legendary dwarf Gimli, member of the Fellowship of the Ring and the first Lord of the Glittering Caves,” he told me. The name, he said, “won out in the ranked choice voting by team members”. Thank goodness, because it’s literally perfect for this mission.

GIMLI is a joint effort between the Planetary Science Institute, NASA, the Norwegian Space Agency and US tech firm Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. It won’t abseil into the pit itself. Instead, it will land next to it and use its suite of instruments – including a ground-penetrating radar, seismic sensors and a device that measures subtle differences in the moon’s gravitational field – to map out the hidden subsurface, while its cameras take shots of the pit and its walls.

Presuming the skylight does lead to a lava tube, GIMLI won’t just scratch a scientific itch. It will inform NASA’s plans to keep its astronauts from being murdered by the moon.

Car-sized asteroids burn up in Earth’s atmosphere without consequence. But on the moon, they slam, unimpeded, into the ground, and explode like a pile of dynamite. Very rarely – as happened in 2024 – an asteroid the size of a couple of football stadiums crashes into the lunar surface with the force of an atomic bomb. Astronauts are far more likely to be imperilled by pebble-sized asteroids, which sound like less of an issue until you realise that they travel at tens of thousands of kilometres per hour, effectively making them hypersonic space bullets. Fortunately, the roof of a lava tube would handily absorb their impacts.

If the ceiling of frozen lava was thick enough, it would also offer protection from a major solar storm. When the sun is feeling irritable, it can launch a salvo of super-charged particles our way. Earth’s magnetic field and substantial atmosphere deflect and soak up many of them. But the exposed moon takes these bombardments head on. In the event of an especially intense solar outburst, astronauts there could receive a fatal dose and die weeks or even days later of acute radiation sickness. Hiding in a lava tube could save their lives.

Thank goodness, then, that the GIMLI project exists, and can help us answer the many questions we still have. What are the moon’s lava tubes like? Are they roomy? Do they look stable? Could you fit an astronaut habitat in them, or a small nuclear reactor that powers a nearby base? Seeking these havens out is, in NASA’s words, “important groundwork for safe, long‑term living on the moon”.

NASA is targeting the lunar south pole for its upcoming crewed Artemis missions. This is where it wants to establish the first moon base, largely because it is thought to be home to crucial reservoirs of water. Should we expect that base to be at least partly concealed in a lava tube?

“Lava tubes necessarily form in volcanic terrain, and there is little or no evidence of such terrains in the heavily cratered highlands of the south polar region,” says Putzig. So, probably not. But, he adds, “other outposts may well be established elsewhere that lava tubes may be identified”.

Most lava tubes will also require something like rappels, or makeshift elevators, for astronauts to access them. This creates its own hazard: if a clumsy moonwalker trips, falls and gets stuck in a lava tube, or the machinery malfunctions, there’s a chance that they could die down there. Considering all the other ways the moon could take them out, this would be a pretty embarrassing end.

Lava tubes may be a bit of a hard sell: they could be onerous to find, troublesome to access and potentially a bit bleak to live in. I’m willing to bet that, if you’re going to camp on the moon for several months at a time, you would probably prefer to eschew a dark, volcanic labyrinth for a spot on the surface. Even if you’re at risk of being blasted by tiny space rocks, you at least get to see Earth, and the stars cresting the lunar horizon. Even on the moon, the call of the night sky may prove too bewitching a prospect to pass up.

Kylie Wihapi’s sunflowers-topped coffin has been carried into her funeral service to the sounds of Metallica’s Turn the Page and a traditional Māori welcome.

Thousands are expected to attend the farewell for the beloved Porirua deputy mayor after her sudden death a week ago.

Wihapi’s funeral service began at Te Rauparaha Arena in Porirua just after 9am following her tangihanga at Horouta Marae, which began on Thursday.

The 45-year-old married mum suffered a fatal fall in a freak accident at home early on Saturday morning last week, Porirua Mayor Anita Baker earlier told the Herald.

Reverend Pania Houkamau-Ngaheu began the service by telling mourners to speak kindly to each other.

“Turn to each person … tell them how gorgeous they look … touch them on the shoulder. That’s what we want to see here today … to hear today. Love and laughter, some tears, caring and giving.

“The qualities of Kylie. The personality of Kylie.”

Messages of “absolute aroha” had come from around the country.

“She was just a super being, a super daughter, super granddaughter, super sister, super cousin, and yes she was the best wife to a loving and devoted husband, and their son and their fur-babies.”

Those gathered included Wihapi’s “fur-baby”, Houkamau-Ngaheu said.

“He’s down over here with his blankie, and he will be feeling it too. Her absence, just as we all are.”

Baker earlier shared her “thoughts and deepest sympathies” with Wihapi’s whānau, “especially her husband Adam, son Cooper, stepson Arama, her mum and dad Marlene and Rob, her brothers and wider family”.

“My heart breaks for them.”

Wellington Free Ambulance confirmed they were called to Wihapi’s address about 8.30am last Saturday at the request of police but were stood down before attending.

Wihapi was a treasured member of the community, making history as the first person elected in Porirua’s Māori ward and was deputy mayor for the past four years.

Baker said Wihapi brought “wisdom, courage, compassion and an unmistakable energy to everything she did” and said she had lost a trusted adviser and friend.

She said Wihapi’s love for her whānau was at the centre of everything she did.

Wihapi’s husband Adam posted a heartfelt tribute following the sudden loss of his “soulmate”.

“Today is the hardest day of my life. I have lost the love of my life, my best friend, my soulmate, my everything, my wife.

“I loved Kylie with everything and she back to me. She was amazing with Cooper, just the best mother I could have hoped for.

“I`m going to miss you, my darling, you leave a void in mine and Cooper’s heart. I love you so much.”

Civic leaders, workmates and community groups from across the region have been united in disbelief at Wihapi’s shock death.

Wihapi’s son attended Paremata School and she was on the board of trustees for six years. They said it was a privilege to have Wihapi as part of the school whānau.

Other schools from across the city extended their condolences, with Mana College saying, “her positive energy and commitment to our kura and that of Porirua will always be remembered”.

Whitby Collegiate shared memories of Wihapi on the netball court and said she always brought “wonderful energy and enthusiasm” to school events.

“Kylie was a much-loved supporter of our school and a passionate champion of our rangatahi.”

The Kapi Mana Netball Centre said she was an integral part of the local netball community.

“She wasn’t just a valued umpire, but also a great coach of more than one team with Aotea College and Norths Netball, an advocate for our younger athletes, strong community advocate and a friend to many.”

Paremata Plimmerton Rugby Football Club, where Wihapi’s son played, said their hearts were broken for her family.

Councillor Geoff Hayward has been appointed Porirua’s new deputy mayor, with the blessing of the Wihapi whānau.

“I know this feels like indecent haste; it certainly does to me,” Baker said at a meeting on Thursday, before explaining the move was necessary to continue the council’s representation on external bodies and its existing functions.

Hayward told Local Democracy Reporting he was honoured to serve as deputy mayor and would be thinking about Wihapi a lot.

“I can only think of myself as a custodian because Kylie should be doing this job, and I’m sad that she’s not here to be able to do it.”

Traffic management is in place for this morning’s service and Porirua City Council is advising those attending to be aware of pressure in the Arena carpark.

“Please remember that all street parking is free on weekends, as well as the council parking lots on Hagley St. Parking at the railway station and walking to the Arena is another good option.”

Wihapi’s shock death came just months after fellow councillor Mike Duncan died suddenly in June after a daily workout.
