Election-day forecast: Voters urged to track showers and rain radar

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

Aucklanders heading to cast their vote on Saturday may need to dodge thunderstorms. Photo / MetService

Voters heading to cast their ballots today may need to dodge more thunderstorms after lightning strikes sparked three fires across Auckland on Friday.

Three Auckland homes were damaged by fires sparked by lightning strikes as thunderstorms swept across the region on Friday afternoon.

A Severe Thunderstorm Watch is in force, with MetService warning there is a moderate risk of thunderstorms across the northern half of the North Island through Saturday morning.

The watch also covers some central parts of the South Island.

The thunderstorms could bring heavy rain of 10mm to 25mm an hour, with a moderate risk of severe thunderstorms capable of producing localised downpours of 25mm to 40mm an hour or more. MetService warned rainfall of that intensity could cause localised surface flooding and hazardous driving conditions.

The unsettled weather is being driven by a low-pressure system in the Tasman Sea drawing warm, moisture-laden subtropical air over New Zealand.

MetService meteorologist Clare O’Connor told the Herald that conditions were similar to yesterday, although it was impossible to predict exactly where thunderstorms would develop.

“There’s the right mix of warm air and unstable conditions, the right sort of ingredients for thunderstorms,” she said.

Severe Thunderstorm Watches have been updated for today ⚠️⚡️Note: the southern North Island Watch from Whanganui southwards is valid from noon ⏲️Check the details 👉 https://t. co/HZ2TSD5rV7Track those t'storms on radar 👉https://t. co/q7Eu5UKdtF pic. twitter. com/oHjxiwLPU6

O’Connor said it was impossible to predict exactly where any storms would develop.

“There could be thunderstorms around today, but maybe it won’t be the same place as they were today. Maybe passing to the north or south of Auckland rather than right over Auckland like it did yesterday.”

She likened the thunderstorms to making popcorn kernels in a pot.

“Everything is there. You’ve got the heat, you’ve got the energy and everything. But it’s just which one is going to actually go pop first. We don’t know.”

O’Connor said the humid conditions were helping create the instability needed for thunderstorms to form.

The risk of thunderstorms is forecast to extend south across much of the North Island later on Saturday, while showery and unstable conditions are expected across large parts of the country.

Voters heading to polling booths have been advised to keep an eye on forecasts and rain radar updates, with showers expected to be intermittent rather than continuous throughout the day.

“Don’t let the weather put you off,” O’Connor said.

“It will be showers more than just continuous rain all day. So there’ll be breaks in the rain.”

Asked where the best place in the country would be for an election-day barbecue, O’Connor said there were few dry options.

“It’s not going to be the driest, unfortunately,” she said, noting much of the country was likely to see rain.

But if she had to choose...

“Actually, maybe Invercargill.”

Two Kiwi businesswomen talk to Jane Phare about why they persevere in running their sustainable business in Afghanistan, in spite of a relentless barrage of obstacles.

Every time Emma Conyngham becomes overwhelmed by the almost insurmountable hurdles that come with running a business in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, she thinks of the Afghan women she employs in Kabul.

In particular, she thinks of the woman worker who, during a visit by the Kiwi to Kabul in July this year, got down on her knees and pulled at the hem of Conyngham’s skirt.

“Please,” the woman pleaded with her employer, “don’t close the factory. Our families cannot eat without these jobs.”

Conyngham and her business partner, Afghan-born Rahila Sayed, had come close to packing it in this year. The list of problems their company, Waste Free Celebrations, had come up against was daunting. On paper, the costs outweighed the benefits.

The company makes reusable Christmas crackers, seven sizes of fabric gift bags, and wrapping cloths for Hanukkah and Diwali celebrations, designed to do away with mountains of crumpled gift paper and plastic toys that end up in landfill.

It’s a business that attracted the highest award in the 2026 Sustainability & Social Impact Awards, run by awards organisation Clean + Conscious, and a gold award and editor’s choice for its reusable Christmas crackers.

Conyngham admits she didn’t initially start the business with sustainability in mind.

“I’m a gift giver,” she says. That meant hours spent wrapping dozens of presents for her husband Alistair, their five children and a large extended family. Much easier to slip gifts into a fabric bag, pull the ribbon tight and reuse it again next year, she thought. She never imagined that a product she sewed from her Wānaka home to sell at the local markets in 2020 would morph into an export business with a production factory based in Afghanistan.

It was the launch of her own website that would eventually lead to a major shift in her lifestyle. Order numbers soared, catching Conyngham by surprise.

“I couldn’t turn my phone on for two weeks; there were so many notifications [noting a sale] coming through.”

Her sister-in-law, who worked at the Māngere Refugee Resettlement Centre in Auckland, suggested employing some of the Afghan women who needed work. As the orders grew, Conyngham relocated her family to Auckland, but it soon became evident that manufacturing and exporting from New Zealand was too expensive.

Sayed, a widow who arrived in Auckland as a refugee with her children in 2014, suggested relocating to Peshawar in Pakistan, using Afghan refugees there. But when the Pakistani Government started mass deportation of refugees back to Afghanistan in 2023, that plan fell through.

So why not help Afghan women in Kabul, Sayed suggested? Conyngham was familiar with the country, having worked in Afghanistan for the United Nations Development Programme between 2004 and 2007. Although Sayed had grown up in Pakistan, after her family fled Afghanistan when she was 2, she knew the language and the customs.

They set up in 2024, renting a large, old mansion in Kabul to convert into a factory and hiring 34 women who desperately needed work. The women are either widows, or their husbands are disabled or unable to work because of an association with the previous Western-backed Afghan Republic.

What could go wrong? Plenty, as it turns out. Two years on, Conyngham is exhausted with the stress of handling constant, and at times seemingly unsolvable, problems. Surprisingly, the Taliban Government is not one of them, she says.

“All of the issues relating to operating in Afghanistan are because of how other countries perceive Afghanistan, not actually what it’s like to operate there.”

But take your pick of some of the other problems:

Sayed spends eight months of the year overseeing the manufacturing in Kabul while Conyngham bankrolls the operation and spends her days in Auckland frantically working out solutions to near catastrophes.

Being reported as Isis operatives was a heart-stopping moment. She shows the Herald that her hands still shake when she thinks back to that time.

The company sources cotton from mills in Pakistan and, when 5km of ordered fabric was unusable because it was so poorly printed, Conyngham wanted her money back from one supplier. In response, the angry and defensive mill owner reported Conyngham and Sayed to the Taliban as Isis operatives.

In Kabul, the first Sayed knew of the problem was when she tried to enter a code into an online portal for an export shipment and it wouldn’t go through. She phoned the Ministry of Industry and Commerce and was informed of their new status as suspected operatives of a terrorist organisation.

Back in Auckland, Conyngham took screenshots of the exchanges between the Pakistani mill owner and herself.

“I sent them to Rahila and said, ‘show this to the Taliban Government and say if this is who reported us as being Isis operatives, here is the record of our trade dispute showing how angry he is with us and that this is a measure of revenge.’ Within an hour, our account was unlocked.”

Power in the Kabul factory comes on for a couple of hours a day and sometimes not at all. The company has its own solar system, but the panels sometimes get too hot to work efficiently, or they simply run out.

At one stage they were paying local boys to lug large containers of water up the factory’s steep steps because the bore’s electric water pump stopped working. When the containers ran out, they bought bottled water from a local market.

In New Zealand, the basics of life are taken for granted, Conyngham says.

“You know, being able to turn on a computer or turn on your sewing machine or turn on the light or flush the toilet. If there’s no water, you can’t work.

“When the Wi-Fi goes down, communication between myself and Rahila is incredibly difficult. It could be three days before I hear back on a really critical question. We’ve learned just to muddle along.”

Almost every day, she faces another headache that needs to be sorted. When the barcodes printed in Afghanistan failed, Sayed flew from Auckland to Kabul with 20,000 New Zealand-printed barcode stickers. Conyngham joined her in July, armed with a barcode printer to solve the problem in the future.

But it’s the soaring costs that are the most worrying. This year, a shipment that was air freighted from Kabul to the US was intercepted by Customs and Border Protection at JFK Airport in New York.

“They charged us US$13,000 ($23,000) to get the container back.”

That, and this year’s $287,250 air freight bill, puts the Kabul operation at risk.

“That kind of shipping bill is not sustainable.”

All Conyngham can do is hope that the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan reopens in the future.

“If that policy reverses and we can get access to Karachi [the port] again, then we’re back in business. We can ship by sea and our costs come back under control. We’re the ones at the end who take the hit of other men’s wars.”

New Zealander Richard Bennett, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in Afghanistan, has spoken out in the past about the danger of “normalising” the Taliban’s regime of repression and discrimination, particularly against women and girls. But he told the Herald he thinks giving Afghan women employment is a good thing, provided their working conditions and payment are fair.

Although Afghan women cannot work for a non-governmental organisation (NGO), the Government, or in senior roles, the Taliban does not ban employment in the private sector.

Of Waste Free Celebrations, Bennett says it sounds like a business the Taliban would encourage, just as it encourages tourism in the country.

He acknowledges the difficulties businesses in Afghanistan face, including the blockading of goods going over the border into Pakistan.

“It’s impacting the economy, but that’s the intention of Pakistan. They want to put pressure on the Taliban. They don’t want the economy to be successful and this is probably an example.”

The company employs one man, Noori, because certain tasks can only be performed by a man, or there are documents that need a man’s signature.

Because women in Afghanistan are restricted in travelling without a man, Conyngham bought a van so Noori can drive the women to and from their homes – which, in Kabul’s traffic, can be a two-hour trip at either end of the day.

Sayed and Noori can spend hours going between government departments to get documents stamped and signed. Once, it took them eight hours to get two signatures. Sometimes more than a dozen signatures are required to move one shipment.

“So it’s slow, it’s cumbersome, you know, they’re always suspicious, and it’s never-ending,” Conyngham says. “We just don’t know how lucky we’ve got it here [in New Zealand] with how fast and efficient our systems are.”

Several weeks ago they learned that the land the factory is on had been requisitioned by the Government. With Sayed now back in Auckland for a break, Noori is frantically trying to find new premises to rent.

Both Conyngham and Sayed say that compared with how things used to be, Kabul feels safe. When the Herald visits Conyngham’s Whitford home, Sayed is there with one of her six children, 26-year-old Farishta Michan Khel. They chat together in the lilting Pashto language, and Michan Khel translates.

Sayed’s is a story of trauma and tragedy. Her family fled to Pakistan from Afghanistan in the mid-1980s after her father was killed during the Soviet-Afghan war. They settled in a refugee camp in Peshawar when Sayed was 2.

By the age of 13, she was married and gave birth to her first child the following year. She gave birth to five more surviving children after that, and lost many in between. In 2010, her husband, who ran a CD shop in a Peshawar market, was among those killed in a bomb blast. Tradition meant the family needed to take his body back to Afghanistan for burial.

Farishta was 10 and remembers that trip, the only time she’s visited Afghanistan. Her mother describes the three months she spent there as “horrible”. There were bombings, people dying; nowhere felt safe, and everyone was scared.

“Everyone was in sadness,” Sayed says.

Now when she visits, it is different.

“There is peace.”

Conyngham agrees. Compared with when she was an aid worker in the early 2000s, Afghanistan feels safe and peaceful.

“There are so many tourists there now, doing blogs, vlogs and Instagram in Afghanistan, not just in Kabul.”

The Afghan women she employs feel safe and are happy to have work. But, she says, they feel sad they have missed out on (higher) education and so will their daughters. Afghan women cannot attend university or work in professional roles. If they have money, they can pay for private schooling or online education, but they will not be awarded a certificate to prove their qualification.

Conyngham, having worked as a humanitarian aid worker, says changes need to be community-led. She believes change will come, albeit slowly, and she sees signs of change in more liberal Kabul at least.

She can’t influence the way things are for women in Afghanistan, but she does have a sewing business, and she can provide employment, she says. Skilled sewers at the Kabul factory teach newcomers how to sew. They, too, could start their own business one day.

Conyngham knows Sayed’s backstory well and says she is the perfect business partner because nothing fazes her.

“With pretty much no education, to be doing what she’s doing now is extraordinary. I could not be more proud of Rahila, of how far she has come and what she has overcome. She is undefeatable.”

Is the stress and angst worth it? Absolutely, the pair say. It might only be 34 women, but it is employment that has changed their lives, given them hope, they say.

Conyngham: “If it costs me some stress and discomfort ... I can’t take it away from them. Until my hands are completely tied, we are going to keep going.”

Since August 2021, when Kabul fell to the Taliban, New Zealand has contributed $46.7 million in humanitarian and development assistance to Afghanistan. A further $3.8m was provided to support the evacuation and resettlement of 1471 Afghan nationals to New Zealand. Many had worked as interpreters with New Zealand forces and agencies. A further 1149 Afghan refugees have arrived between July 2020 and June 2026.

The Taliban is designated as a terrorist entity under New Zealand law. Afghanistan has a level 4 “do not travel” warning on the Government’s Safe Travel website.

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Tauranga Crown hires former Public Defender Sam Davison for leadership role

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

Sam Davison (right) has been made a director at the Tauranga Crown Solicitor's office, where he joins current Crown Solicitor Anna Pollett (centre) and co-director Richard Jenson.

Former public defender Sam Davison has returned to the Tauranga Crown Solicitor’s office in what he says is something of a “homecoming”.

Davison returned this week to the office where he began his criminal-law career after leading the Tauranga Public Defence Service for the past year.

Crown Solicitor Anna Pollett has yet to announce her plans, but said Davison’s appointment as a Tauranga Crown director was part of the firm’s “growth and succession plan”.

The Crown Solicitor’s warrant for Tauranga expires next year, and Pollett’s co-director, Richard Jenson, appears poised to seek the role should Pollett choose not to apply for a second 10-year warrant.

Jenson helped establish Pollett Legal nearly a decade ago.

Applicants offer their services and those of their firm.

The Crown has been looking to appoint another senior leader for the past few years.

Jenson said they needed to find someone who would be the “right fit” and Davison’s experience and history with the firm meant they had found the “perfect person”.

Pollett said she felt that, “philosophically”, a single 10-year warrant is enough time to hold the office of Crown Solicitor.

“If we’re going to encourage people like [Davison] back into the Crown Solicitors’ network, there needs to be progression or leadership change. So to pass on the baton is a really important factor for me.”

It did not give lawyers with leadership potential much hope without a change at the top.

“That’s where I think we see people moving on, going to the defence bar... or going overseas, because they can’t see a pathway forward within the firm.”

Pollett indicated that, should she decide to step aside, she would stay at the firm, supporting the leadership team and providing continuity.

Davison said the Crown director role was a “good opportunity” to step into leadership and mentor junior and intermediate prosecutors.

“I enjoy the team side of things and, I mean, it’s only day two, but I’ve had a bunch of people through the office with questions about this, that, and the other thing.”

The larger team environment appealed to Davison more than the well-trodden path of going from the Crown to the defence bar to practise as a sole barrister.

The thought of sitting in an office by himself, “sort of twiddling my thumbs and potentially not having someone to talk to, or someone to kind of assist, doesn’t seem as fun for me”.

The Tauranga Crown team has more than doubled since Davison last worked there – from 10, including support staff, to 25.

The caseload has more than doubled.

Pollett said that when she began as Crown Solicitor in 2017-2018, the Crown had 1988 active cases, and disposed of 235.

A disposal is the term used when proceedings finish through a person being found not guilty, a charge being withdrawn, or sentencing.

In 2025-2026, the Tauranga Crown had 4565 active cases, with 276 disposals.

In 2017-2018, the average time to disposal was 9.9 months; now, it’s about 17.5 months.

Jenson said another challenge the Crown faced was the increased complexity of cases and the amount of evidence police could gather.

Contact the Open Justice team

Jenson remained hopeful, despite the challenges.

“The work itself is still tremendously rewarding, and it’s always a great challenge,” he said.

“We have a great team. We work with great people. I think across the sector with defence, with judges... everyone’s doing their best, and they’re all good people aiming to serve the system and serve the community.”

Davison said he hoped to bring with him the relationships he had made working in defence.

“I can bring a different perspective to things, and I suppose an understanding of how things operate from the other side,” he said.

“... I think that makes this job easier when you have good working relationships with people. My hope is that having pretty good relationships with everybody... may sort of help with the relationships moving forward.”

Following his first stint at the Crown, Davison worked in Australia, continuing prosecution work in Victoria with the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Then he did legal aid defence work across the Northern Territory, including in remote Aboriginal communities.

He said his Australian experience gave him an appreciation of the New Zealand justice system’s strengths, but also an understanding of potential improvements.

“I think where there is opportunity for slight tinkering or slightly different ways of looking at things, then that’s something that hopefully I can bring to the table.”

Hannah Bartlett is a Tauranga-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She previously covered court and local government for the Nelson Mail, and before that was a radio reporter at Newstalk ZB.

Tenant awarded nearly $5000 after tribunal finds pensioner housing provider breached obligations

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

Emerge Aotearoa Housing Trust did not do enough for a tenant concerned about a man on home detention living next door, the Tenancy Tribunal has found. Photo / Zoe Blake

A Rotorua pensioner housing tenant has been awarded nearly $5000 after their landlord failed to properly address concerns about a person on home detention moving in next door.

Emerge Aotearoa Housing Trust was ordered to pay the tenant $4942.50 in compensation after the Tenancy Tribunal found it did not do enough to respond to concerns raised over several months.

Emerge took over management of Rotorua Lakes Council’s pensioner housing in March.

About the same time, the man serving a home detention sentence moved in with a relative in a unit closely neighbouring the aggrieved tenant’s.

The man was subject to electronic monitoring with an ankle bracelet, and confined to the property.

The tribunal heard the tenant, whose identity is subject to suppression orders, became increasingly distressed by this arrangement and began raising concerns with Emerge in April.

Tenancy Tribunal adjudicator Mikail Steens found that while the tenant was not accusing the new neighbour of assault, harassment or threatening behaviour, the arrangement had a substantial impact on the tenant’s wellbeing.

The home detainee would use outdoor areas close to the tenant’s home to exercise and spend time with visitors.

As a result, the tenant withdrew from outdoor activities including gardening and exercise, and increasingly isolated themselves indoors, Steens’ decision said.

At times, the tenant left Rotorua altogether and stayed elsewhere.

Evidence presented during the hearing showed the tenant’s concerns continued throughout April, May and June.

The tenant “lived in a constant state of panic and unease” waiting for news, the decision said.

The tribunal found that while Emerge took steps to try to manage the situation – eventually relocating the neighbouring tenant and family member in July – those efforts were insufficient and too late.

“The tenant’s own inherent dignity was overlooked,” Steens said.

The decision acknowledged Emerge staff had been attempting to balance competing needs, but found the provider failed to take reasonable steps to protect the tenant’s right to peacefully enjoy their home.

Steens said the person serving a home detention sentence “should not have been living at the premises to begin with”.

The tribunal ultimately found Emerge had breached the Residential Tenancies Act and awarded compensation for loss of use, quiet enjoyment, distress and alternative accommodation expenses.

Steens rejected a separate claim that Emerge’s actions amounted to harassment, finding staff had investigated the complaints, considered medical information and worked toward relocating the neighbouring household.

He said relocating them was “reasonable” and Emerge had clearly tried to resolve a “difficult” problem.

“The breach was the absence of adequate safeguards at the outset and effective interim measures once the interference [with her quiet enjoyment] became known,” Steens found.

The tenant was granted name suppression due to the sensitive nature of personal and medical evidence presented during the proceedings.

The compensation reflected the tenant’s reduced use of the property and its amenity, costs for accommodation elsewhere and emotional distress.

Although the council was not a party to the case, the dispute occurred in council-owned pensioner housing.

The tribunal accepted the tenant’s evidence that the home detainee had previously used the property as a bail address, and that the council had previously committed to not allowing people serving home detention sentences in pensioner housing.

While the council told Local Democracy Reporting it could not comment on the specifics of the tribunal case at this stage, infrastructure and assets group manager Stavros Michael said it had no policy excluding people serving home detention sentences from its pensioner housing.

Michael said the council was committed to meeting its legal obligations and providing housing services in a fair and lawful manner.

Michael said Emerge was “responsible for day-to-day tenancy and operational matters”, while the council retained “strategic oversight” as the property owner.

He said the council and Emerge worked closely together and discussed tenancy-related matters where appropriate.

“However, in order to protect the privacy of those involved, we are unable to comment on individual tenancy matters.”

He said the council would not make further comment until the appeal process ended and a “final decision” was made.

In an update to councillors in September, council staff said 14 applications related to council pensioner housing remained with the Tenancy Tribunal, 10 of which were adjourned until late October.

Emerge Aotearoa was approached for comment.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

Plans for new McDonald’s in Napier - next to a medical centre

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

The proposed new McDonald's and medical centre (pictured to the back left). Photo / NCC

Plans to build a new McDonald’s and a medical centre right next to each other in Napier have been labelled a “gigantic irony” by a health advocate.

But supporters of the development say people can choose what they eat in moderation, and the project will provide jobs and new amenities.

Te Roropipi is a major development in a large paddock off Wharerangi Rd in Greenmeadows, near Park Island.

When completed, it will feature a new commercial precinct, a large retirement village, and about 140 new homes.

A resource consent application has now been lodged for the commercial precinct, which includes plans for a McDonald’s and medical centre next to each other.

A tenant for the medical centre has yet to be announced.

A Woolworths is also proposed for the precinct, which was announced in February, along with a handful of small shops and a cafe.

TW Property is delivering the commercial precinct while Mana Ahuriri owns the land, which is redress property under its Treaty settlement.

TW Property commercial director Terry May said a McDonald’s and a medical centre were both commercial uses, and there was demand for both.

Napier City Council is currently considering the resource consent application.

May said some would think it was “an outrage” and “terrible”, but people had control of what they ate, which was “a self-management thing”, and McDonald’s was a great tenant.

“Napier, supposedly, is one of the most under-resourced for [medical facilities] in the country.”

He said the supermarket had been the key driver for the commercial precinct, and had certain preferences for the site.

Woolworths had not specifically asked for a McDonald’s.

Mana Ahuriri general manager Parris Greening said the focus of the commercial space was oranga, or wellness.

Mana Ahuriri was opposed to the likes of vape shops that could cause “significant harm”, but did not see McDonald’s in that category.

He said the commercial precinct would also provide employment opportunities, including for rangatahi (youth).

Health Coalition Aotearoa co-chair Boyd Swinburn, who is also a professor at the University of Auckland’s School of Population Health, said there was a clear link between ill health and diet.

“Obviously there is a gigantic irony between a McDonald’s being placed right next to a medical centre.

“If you look at obesity and unhealthy diet, they are far and away the biggest contributors to ill health in this country.

“It’s more than twice the impact of tobacco.”

The plans essentially positioned a fast food outlet “right next to a repair shop of the medical centre”.

He said there was no legal way for the community to object to commercial plans on grounds such as the “health of local kids”.

In his view, that was an area that needed to be revisited.

Napier City Council has yet to decide whether it will notify the resource consent application.

Nearby Tamatea resident Katrina, who did not want her surname published, said locals should get a say on the proposal.

It was a conflict to have a medical centre next to a fast food outlet, and it did not promote healthy eating.

“This is a relatively low socio-economic area with lots of Māori and Pasifika people, and we already have a health crisis in New Zealand, particularly in those demographics.”

She was also concerned about possible future extensions of the restaurant’s opening hours, and believed a third McDonald’s for Napier was excessive.

Taradale ward councillor Nigel Simpson was not opposed to the plans.

“I can see the irony, and the funny side of it, but it is a commercial decision for the commercial interests.

“And at the end of the day, everyone has a personal choice.

“I’d be a hypocrite if I didn’t say I enjoy a burger occasionally.”

McDonald’s said that, if the new store went ahead, it would be the first new one in Napier for almost 30 years.

The Taradale restaurant was the latest to open in 1997. There is also a McDonald’s in the city centre.

The proposed McDonald’s includes a drive-through, but would not be a 24-hour operation.

“McDonald’s is supporting the developer for the Wharerangi Rd site as they work through the council consent process.”

Te Awanga Estate cellar door set to reopen as Skyflower Estate under new owners

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

The site of the former Te Awanga Estate vineyard, cellar door and restaurant will reopen under the name Skyflower Estate. Photo / Jack Riddell

A popular coastal Hawke’s Bay vineyard cellar door and restaurant that closed two years ago is set to reopen under a new name and owners.

Nestled in the foothills hugging the Cape Coast, Te Awanga Estate Winery was a popular summer spot where diners could enjoy local wine and pizza with panoramic views from Cape Kidnappers to Napier.

But in October 2024, the vineyard, cellar door and restaurant were put on the market and have been closed since.

In January, Te Awanga Estate entered voluntary liquidation, while the winery, vineyard and restaurant remained on the market.

In June, the property sold to new owners, who have been media-shy.

Swift Wines owner Lauren Swift had lived near the property in Hāumoana for the past 10 years.

She said the former cellar door was a favourite for its relaxed vibes and location.

Swift Wines had been operating its cellar door at the old Stonecroft site in Gimblett Gravels until the property was sold to Radburnd Cellars in October.

Needing a new location for the cellar door, Swift’s husband, Henry Williams, tracked down the new owners to see if a partnership was feasible.

“We jumped on a call, we met them, we all had really good feelings about each other, and a lot of values and things aligned. So it just kind of happened,” Swift said.

“I see quite a long future with them.”

Swift called the new owners private people, who were living overseas while the property was rejuvenated.

“Their intention is to move back here, and they’ve got some really exciting plans.”

The new cellar door was set to be renamed Skyflower Estate, the owners’ wine brand, offering wines, platters and pizza in an idyllic setting.

Swift said there wasn’t a set opening date, but she was working towards opening by November 23.

“If it all comes off, I’ll be stoked about it, but we’ll see.”

Swift said her team was working their “little butts off” setting up a new menu, wine showcase and giving the restaurant a facelift.

The official opening date will be advertised on Swift Wines’ Facebook page.

Jack Riddell is a multimedia journalist with Hawke’s Bay Today and has worked in radio and media in the UK, Germany and New Zealand.

Horror Florida plane crash a reminder to live life, love family and chase dreams – Editorial

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

A large fireball erupted after the crash in Florida.

Plane crashes regularly make the news, but the tragedy in Florida this week particularly captured attention.

There was the young co-pilot living her dream of flying. The audio transcript detailing her desperate last words as the plane went down is harrowing.

Then there was the tech entrepreneur and his family, including two young children, with their nanny and friends.

They were on the private Learjet 60 headed from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera, the Bahamas.

The plane descended with terrifying speed at up to 22,000 feet per minute. It was described as like a missile. Online footage of the impact is haunting.

It crashed in Palm Beach County, near a mobile home park, early on Monday. All nine on board died. It was a miracle no one on the ground was killed.

The pilot was Jeff Gregory, 55, and co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20.

The passengers were Adam Robinson, 44, founder and chief executive of software companies Retention. com and RB2B, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their children, Emma Robinson, 4, and Charlie Robinson, 2.

Their friends who were also killed were Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and the nanny was Anita Maria Cetina.

The jet was reportedly flying through freezing temperatures when it hit turbulence and ice accumulation. Investigators are focusing on the weather.

It is impossible to imagine the terror those on board would have felt.

But Filgueiras’ distressing words and screams provide insight.

“We’re descending 8000, mayday, mayday, we’re descending 10,000 feet [3048m] per minute,” Filgueiras told air traffic control.

Seconds later: “Declaring emergency seven two two bravo delta, we are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000 feet per minute.

“We’re gonna crash into the ground,” she shouts, then adds: “We are descending 22,000 feet and we are banking 60 degrees.”

Her last words: “We’re out of time.”

The fact that she was able to talk during those horrific seconds says a lot about her strength.

Filgueiras has an incredible story. She loved flying and told her parents at age 12 that she wanted to be a pilot.

She earned her pilot’s licence at 17 while in high school and before she had her driver’s licence. She featured in the media at the time.

Filgueiras worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, and had more than 1300 flight hours.

News reports this week featured photos of a proud-looking Filgueiras in the cockpit or beside a plane.

It was an incredible achievement.

Gregory, the flight captain, was described as a devoted family man and devout Christian with a passion for flying.

There have also been touching passenger tributes.

Images of Robinson and Sharp with their children, all smiling, are heartbreaking.

Robinson was also living his best life. He had spoken about enjoying a life that allowed him to spend time with his children and his wife to be an artist.

“I feel like I’m living the dream,” Robinson told the ProfitLed podcast.

A family member said on social media: “Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives.”

A joint statement from the families of the passengers described Reed and Fehr as “full of joy and adventure” and who “loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation”.

Cetina showed “a legacy of unconditional love and devotion”.

By all accounts, these were good people living full lives.

This tragedy, captured in words, video and images, is a reminder to love family, show gratitude, live fully, follow passions and chase dreams.

It’s another reminder that life is short and can change in a heartbeat.

Letters: Mauao tragedy and the plight of Mount businesses; BMI clarity; phones and driving

New Zealand Herald November 06, 2026

Pilot Bay and Mauao.

Mauao businesses need support

An excellent editorial (Nov 4) describes the plight of businesses near the base of fenced-off Mauao (the Mount).

It goes on to say, “Sure, the fences are still up, but the council has plans to reopen part of Mauao. Let’s hope that eventuates.”

What could be more important than the council shifting heaven and earth to make sure this happens? Support businesses, support healthy activity of climbing hills, make everyone’s summer richer!

On a similar note, after the wonderful Local Board intervention that resulted in the Piha campground reopening, we could also do with prompt attention to plans for reinstatement of the Piha Lookout track.

Plans are currently waiting for Auckland Council approval. The track has been closed ever since the cataclysmic weather event of 2023. Speedy development of this track would definitely make many Aucklanders’ summers richer.

Chris Chrystall, Piha.

BMI facts

A recent article quoted eating disorder organisations criticising routine Before School Checks for including body mass index (BMI) (Oct 28).

They said it was “scary”, “horrendous”, “biased”, “sexist” and “racist” for this simple, validated method for assessing body weight, adjusted for weight and height, to be used.

I am dismayed to see one of the few successful steps NZ has taken to prevent obesity undermined by misinformation.

The model was created, not 200 years ago for a “European male”, but by the WHO (World Health Organisation) from its Multicentre Growth Study (1997-2003).

This is a standardised tool used internationally for under-5s. The charts are specific for age and sex, but not for ethnicity, because WHO found no ethnic differences in BMI in this age group.

Obesity is one of the biggest challenges children and adolescents face. It already affects one in eight New Zealand kids, impacting their physical, psychological and social health.

Childhood obesity is an important and tough problem to address, but not measuring a child’s BMI, not talking to parents about it, not getting professional support for it when necessary, and not monitoring progress at the population level would be a terrible health strategy.

Boyd Swinburn, Professor of Population Nutrition and Global Health, University of Auckland and Health Coalition Aotearoa.

Humanitarian assistance

Before its closure, USAid (United States Agency for International Development) operated and provided development or humanitarian assistance to about 130 countries, distributing about US$40 billion ($71b) in 2023 and US$35b in 2024.

Most of the world’s 77 lowest-income countries received direct USAid assistance.

Following a review by the Trump Administration, under Doge (led by the world’s wealthiest person, Elon Musk) about 83% of USAid programmes were terminated, and the agency officially closed on July 1, 2025, with remaining essential functions transferred to the US Department of State.

Now that the balance of power has shifted in Congress and the Senate, USAid may, hopefully, begin its mission again to make our world slightly more equitable, lifting health and opportunities for many in developing countries.

Rob Buchanan, Kerikeri.

Risks for NZ Rugby

I totally agree with the sports article (Nov 5) that NZ rugby urgently needs to fix its game to make it much more watchable and to stop people switching to league – especially the Warriors. I only ever watch All Blacks tests, and yet I watch all NRL games. The boring part of rugby needs to be fixed ASAP..

Murray Hunter, Titirangi.

Phones in cars

Correspondents Murray Hunter and Jeremy Coleman are absolutely correct when stating that the current deterrents for using a phone while driving are not working.

This also highlights another issue: how many times do you read that the penalty for this or that can be up to, say, $20,000? But you can guarantee that the top figure will never be applied by any judge. In many cases, the penalties are actually there but are watered down. In Australia they also have penalties – $1000 for using a phone in a vehicle – but, more importantly, they actually do enforce it with no excuses, so people know not to try it on.

Time we took note and did the same.

Paul Beck, West Harbour.

Fine print on ‘stationary’

I, too, deplore the highly dangerous use of hand-held phones while driving.

However, readers might not realise that the driver, can be fined $150 for using their phone whilst stationary.

I was driving in Dunedin, heard a ding, waited till I had stopped at the lights, and picked up the phone from the central console to check the notification – a mere glance.

When the lights changed, I drove on, only to be pulled over by three police officers who fined me instantly for using a phone while driving.

Fair enough if I had actually been driving, but I’d been seen waiting, immobile, on the traffic lights camera simply touching my phone.

The cops even confirmed I was stationary, but the charge remained.

.

This apparently applies to waiting at roadworks too. Beware.

Karin Wegener, Kerikeri.

Captain needs a vice

Why does All Blacks coach Dave Rennie not announce a permanent vice-captain? The team may know, but we as supporters don’t know who is in charge if Codie Taylor, the current captain, is unable to carry on. And one would’ve thought it would be a proud role, for presumably a back to have, when Taylor is available as part of the leadership team.

Harvey White, Epsom.

By George, Russell

George Russell’s little tantrum after the Mexican GP by refusing to attend the compulsory media session will be his undoing.

He should have been there to acknowledge Kimi Antonelli’s World Championship success with the team. Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, to their credit, did. What a nice gesture when they hoisted Kimi on their shoulders. Real sportsmanship.

Russell has shown he hasn’t got the huge mental strength to become world champion.

Compare his situation with the mental struggles Liam Lawson has had to endure and all the mechanical failures, and he has still succeeded.

Maybe Lawson would be a fitting replacement for Mercedes.

Jock Mac Vicar, Hauraki.

On Brand

Russell Brand, found guilty of rape and sexual assault, will now have plenty of spare time to reflect on where he went wrong.

Brand projected an image of arrogance and contempt, preying on his coterie of vulnerable women. His conviction sends a chilling message to many men who still share his arrogant male chauvinism.

Larry Mitchell, Rothesay Bay.

Food for thought

Correspondent Keith Burgess asks why New Zealand consumers must pay exorbitant export prices for the agricultural and dairy products produced locally.

If he wants Kiwis to be charged a special local price, there are two ways to achieve this.

There could be a subsidy for local produce that’s earmarked for local consumption, carried by the taxpayer.

Or perhaps the advocates of lower prices for domestic customers think “our” farmers and growers should be forced to sell a portion of their production at lower cost to Kiwi households? Perhaps a fair deal could be agreed on: forgo export profits in good times in return for higher local prices when the export markets inevitably cycle downward.

Anything else results in one group of Kiwis (consumers) demanding another group of Kiwis (producers) sacrifice their livelihoods for no return. Is that fair?

Philip Tetley-Jones, Pt Chevalier.

Short on time? 4 itineraries that turn a long weekend into an epic escape

Sydney Morning Herald November 07, 2026

Rock-art gorges, starlit dining, underground jewels – it’s a rail journey like no other.

Need a break but can only squeeze in a few days away from work or home? These four itineraries are proof that it is possible to pack a lot of punch into a short break or long weekend.

Rock-art gorges, starlit dining, underground jewels – a trip aboard The Ghan offers a front-row seat to Australia’s ever-changing outback.

There is a giddiness at the Darwin train station. It’s 7.30am, and we line up for lanyards, sparkling wine and croissants. Local musician David Spry croons What a Wonderful World. Perky staff in khaki shorts and Akubra hats take photographs of passengers posing beside the red engines of The Ghan that will pull 36 carriages almost 3000 kilometres to Adelaide.

For many Australians, The Ghan is a bucket-list trip, promising the romance of a sleeper train with the grandeur of the outback. I am in a Gold Premium cabin, a step up from Gold – a Baileys nightcap is delivered to my cabin – but more modest than Platinum, with larger cabins and a personal attendant.

Still, there is an egalitarianism to The Ghan, named in tribute to Afghan cameleers who helped explore the centre in the 19th century. Staff are attentive and laidback, including on the off-train excursions, and the locally inspired food – think buffalo curry and honey and macadamia frozen parfait – is delicious.

My cabin is modest but stylish, with timber veneer finishes, cream upholstery and a small but adequate bathroom. But I’m here for the view from the picture window. I soak it in for the nearly four-hour journey to Katherine. Termite mounds as high as two metres rise like alien sculptures. Spindly trees and scrubby grass give way to red dirt.

Food and drinks are included, as are most off-train excursions (you will pay extra, for instance, for a flight over Uluru). In Katherine, I choose a cruise down Nitmiluk Gorge, a 13‑gorge system named by the traditional owners, the Jawoyn, who believe the landmark was carved by the rainbow serpent.

It’s majestic. We meander through the first gorge, looking up at the jagged sandstone all around us. We walk to the second gorge, passing Aboriginal rock art on the way. Our guide points out Jedda’s Rock, the precipice where the heroine falls to her death in the 1955 movie Jedda, the first movie to star Aboriginal actors.

Dinner is served in four-person booths and any social awkwardness soon disappears. My bed is set up while I am dining, and I sleep like a baby, soothed by the rocking of the train. The following day, we are in Alice Springs and I choose the Desert Park excursion. Host Louise leads a show that stars native birds, trained to turn up on cue. A white eastern barn owl, with perfect timing, pops out from a hole in a tree trunk. Its extraordinary hearing means it can pinpoint prey in complete darkness.

Dinner is under the stars at the Alice Springs Telegraph Station, a crucial cog in faster communication through the overland telegraph line. It’s a spectacular venue for linen-clad tables and lashings of food. When we are full and satisfied, we take to the dance floor.

Our final full day off rails is in the town of Coober Pedy, 850 kilometres north of Adelaide. It’s startling, an end-of-the-world moonscape dotted with what look like giant pink anthills. These are opal-mining workings, mostly abandoned, scattered across a stony desert. Coober Pedy is known as the opal capital of the world, but there are no big mining companies here. It’s for chancers who get the “fever”. About half its population of 2000 people live in underground houses dug from the rock to temper the 45-degree summers.

There’s one more night as the train moves towards Adelaide. In the morning, the window offers a different glimpse of Australia – green fields and the outskirts of a city. The Ghan traverses 2979 kilometres, but is over in just three nights and four days – a short escape of comfort and contrast, not to be missed. Gay Alcorn

The writer travelled on The Ghan as a guest of Journey Beyond.

A food safari reveals a lively culinary and cultural scene, and a Maori influence that gives the renewed New Zealand city its unique flavour.

Before starting our kai (food) safari, Ash Jefferys, lead guide from Maori-owned Amiki Tours, has a question: Do I want to join her in a hongi – that traditional greeting where you press noses and share the breath of life? Definitely, yes, but I panic too, breathing in when asked to breathe out. At least I don’t accidentally headbutt her.

Just a short flight from Australia’s eastern seaboard, Christchurch makes a delightful destination for a four-night long weekend. It is renowned as the most English city outside of England, but you can also find the warm embrace of Maori culture here. Nowhere is this dichotomy more apparent in Ōtautahi Christchurch than on the willow-framed Ōtākaro/Avon River, where you can glide past daffodil woodlands on a punt poled by an Edwardian-attired guide but also, on a different stretch of the picture-perfect waterway, make like a fearsome Maori warrior and help paddle a waka (canoe).

Since 2010/11’s devastating earthquakes, Christchurch has renewed and reframed itself, embedding “Maorification” into its low-rise civic rebuild. Stroll around the river precinct and you might spy 14 Maori weaving patterns – representing woven mats of welcome – embedded into the pavement. The one at the Bridge of Remembrance and its commemorative WWI archway, incorporating a jolt of red poppies, is especially poignant.

These subtle artworks mingle with more in-your-face street art such as the country’s tallest mural – the 53-metre-high Narcissa that Jacob Yikes painted along the side of a Cathedral Square hotel. With hundreds of murals enlivening the city, you can cut straight to the more interesting ones via a street-art tour. Reuben Woods, the creative director of local street-art guide Watch This Space, leads me to nooks, carparks and alleys, and says the artworks “aren’t just a response to a post-disaster environment, but allow you to see the other complexities that go on here in rebuilding place”.

“Ōtautahi continues to change and evolve,” he says.

Those changes include a brand-new covered stadium featuring what’s been called New Zealand’s most expensive lawn (a secret mix of three rye grasses); Robbie Williams becomes its first international headliner this month.

For foodies, the big news is this year’s arrival of the New Zealand Michelin Guide. Of Christchurch’s 16 recognised establishments, I squeeze four into my visit. The Athens Yacht Club, near my digs at Hotel Montreal, is all Aegean tableside theatre – think exuberantly flamed haloumi (don’t hold your phone too close to the show), moussaka piled with crispy potato straws, and Greece-meets-Italy “baklamisu” to finish.

My kai safari includes Roca (renowned for its use of fire and smoke, a stand-out dish is the fish crudo with burnt mandarin segments and saffron vinaigrette) and Cellar Door, a wine bar within the same Arts Centre heritage complex as my second stay, The Observatory Hotel. Brunch at riverside Miro includes a life-changing cheese scone with kimchi butter. “Your soul will go to South Korea and back again,” the waiter promises. He’s right, it does.

Kiwis love their scones. The date scones at Sign of the Kiwi – a cosy arts and crafts-style teahouse perched on the Crater Rim Walkway – are justifiably famous. I head out of the city for a half-day guided tramp around Godley Head with Crater Rim Walks. Inclement weather, however, limits our explorations to the World War II coastal defence battery (muralists have been busy here, too) so plans pivot to include defrosting at the teahouse.

More sweet treats – namely lolly cake, an NZ classic – star in my day trip to the seaside town of Akaroa with Adventure by Nature’s Alan Haslip. For morning tea, the bushcraft enthusiast and keen birder finds us a pocket of remnant bushland to relax within. Several stops later (Birdlings Flat’s rocky beach, Little River Gallery), it’s time for an elevated lunch with water views at Caldera Vineyard Estate.

Finally, I can’t leave Christchurch without dining on Tram 411. It plied Melbourne’s streets until 1982 then spent time inside a Sydney pub as a novelty dining space before relocating across the ditch. Unlike the daytime tram rides, there’s no commentary as you trundle around the city centre and pass between New Regent Street’s pastel Spanish Mission facades. That means you can easily shoot the breeze if, like me, you’re seated near friendly fellow diners. As Haslip noted during our outing, “You haven’t met someone until you’ve shared some kai.” Katrina Lobley

The writer was a guest of ChristchurchNZ.

It has hotels and dining options galore, plus colourful reefs within easy reach. Could Fiji’s Denarau Island be the ultimate short-break escape?

It’s early evening in Fiji, and I’m standing barefoot on Denarau Beach as the incoming tide laps at my feet. The setting sun is a golden orb suspended against a blue horizon, its warm glow catching the rim of my wine glass like a tiny flare. Somewhere in the distance, drums beat. Blink. Just like that I’ve been teleported from Sydney’s winter chill to tropical paradise.

I’ve been coming to Fiji regularly for decades, often torn between a fly-and-flop holiday or venturing beyond to explore islands and culture. By staying on Denarau Island, I can do both. First, there’s the ease of it all; a four-hour flight from Australia’s east coast, a modest one- to two-hour time difference (goodbye jet lag my old friend) and a 20-minute drive from Nadi International Airport. Not an island in the Robinson Crusoe sense, Denarau is a purpose-built resort destination connected to the mainland by a narrow strip. Perfect for a short-break getaway.

The next tick goes to Port Denarau Marina, looking sharp after a recent multimillion-dollar berth expansion; it’s a lively hub for dining, shopping and departures to the Yasawa and Mamanuca islands.

Rounding it out are nine accommodation options, including the Sheraton Denarau Villas, Radisson Blu Resort and the Westin Resort and Spa. For foodies, this translates to more than 40 dining options. For our family’s first multi-generational holiday, we’ve chosen the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa, as much for its waterslides and Niu kids’ club as for its adults-only Waitui Beach Club. And, let’s be honest, the promise of French pastries at breakfast.

Come morning, we walk the length of the dark-sand beach, pausing to build sand castles and hunt for hermit crabs. My five-year-old grandson collects sand dollars, while his nine-year-old brother looks for fallen coconuts. I catch my husband’s eye. Fiji is where we honeymooned and, now, sharing time here with our grown family is a gift beyond compare.

Later, we board the thatched-roof Bula Bus for the short ride to the marina, where we stroll past superyachts, stopping for ice-creams along the way. At just $FJD38 ($24) for a five-day pass (kids ride free), the hop-on, hop-off bus is the most fun and relaxed holiday commute you’ll ever take.

With everything close at hand, switching pace is easy, making our brief time away feel twice as long. One day, it’s a morning by the pool followed by an excursion to Nadi Town (15 minutes by taxi) for the fresh produce markets and a fragrant, Indo-Fijian curry. Another, it’s a half-day cruise to South Sea Island where we swim and snorkel through a kaleidoscope of blues, the offshore reef a carnival of fish and coral. For our youngest, the semi-submersible submarine offers a first glimpse at the hidden world below. “Just like in Finding Nemo,” he exclaims. By mid-afternoon, we’re back by the resort pool. No plans. No pressure.

Day four. Spa treatment day. Need I say more? Dinners alternate between themed family buffets to toes-in-the-sand dining at the adults-only Waitui Bar and Grill, to a Bula Bus ride to the marina for seafood and -sundowners. One night it is room service on our balcony under a fairy-floss pink sky.

The thread tying it together is the genuine warmth of the Fijian people, whose wide smiles and “Bula, family!” greeting make you feel instantly at home. It’s a welcome rarely found in the world today. Heading home is a breeze, thanks to Sofitel’s onsite Fiji Airways check-in counter where guests can drop luggage and receive boarding passes before leaving the resort (depending on destination and flight time). This means a sleep-in and more time by the pool.

Can a short, international escape get any better than this? Not even close. Kerry van der Jagt

The former penal colony of Norfolk Island provides a feast for history buffs – and there are plenty more pleasant surprises in store.

If Norfolk Island hasn’t won a Tidy Town award yet, the organisers should get there, pronto. Nearly 1500 kilometres off the coast of Brisbane, the Australian territory is not just beautiful but has the vibe of a place that’s tenderly cared for by its locals.

Their determination to keep trash at bay extends beyond actual rubbish. There’s no McDonald’s. No ugly high-rises or clifftop McMansions. No pokies. No commercial fishing. Cows have right of way and many will be munching grass roadside as you drive by, which you will because holiday rental cottages such as The Ridge, where we stayed, tend to -include a car in the package. Everyone you drive past will raise a barely perceptible index finger from their steering wheel by way of hello – if they don’t, they’re not local. Returning the greeting will help you get into the Norfolk spirit and avoid greasy looks from other motorists.

None of this is what I expected when we booked to visit the island for a long weekend. It’s a doable two-and-a-half hour flight from Sydney (two hours from Brisbane; no direct flights from Melbourne) and while not cheap, with sale fares it’s possible to get there for around $1000 return. (Inexplicably, the flight from Sydney leaves from the international terminal, requiring an earlier than usual domestic flight check-in.)

We went for the history and there’s plenty of it. A British penal colony twice in the 18th and 19th centuries, Norfolk Island was gifted in 1856 by Queen Victoria to the so-called “Pitcairners”, a group who overthrew William Bligh on the British ship HMS Bounty in 1789 and ended up on Pitcairn Island, where many married locals. A good number of Norfolk’s nearly 2200 residents have ancestors among this group, which they’ll proudly tell you about. Some will also speak of their desire to secede from Australia, which took over in 1914 and removed the island’s self-governing autonomy in 2015. That campaign is yet to gain traction – or indeed, much profile at all – on the mainland.

We booked a bus tour for the morning after our arrival, and it was a genius move, giving us a good sense of the lay of an island that measures only eight kilometres long by five kilometres wide.

We visited the deep port where boats deliver the island’s food and grog; a lookout with views down to the historical relics of Kingston, where the first settlers and prisoners once lived; and that World Heritage site itself, where we walked along a row of Georgian homes and through a cemetery with gravestones for the likes of Kezia, who died of typhoid in 1868, aged 24. The island’s most famous resident, writer Colleen McCullough, was buried here too, following her death in 2015, aged 77. You can take a tour of her home elsewhere on the island, should you be a fan of her books.

For more on the history of the place, buy a ticket to Fletcher’s Mutiny Cyclorama, a 360-degree panoramic painting that evocatively tells the story of The Bounty and its mutineers.

St Barnabas was a revelation, too. Built by missionaries, the 19th-century chapel has stunning stained-glass windows designed by William Morris, together with mother-of-pearl inlaid pews. A jewel-like beauty.

Perhaps most pleasantly surprising was the quality of food on the island, from the freshly butchered meat at Slick & Sons to the most excellent coffee and croissants next door at Cafe La Perouse to dinner at The Homestead, a short drive away. Check out the Moreton Bay fig trees on the road out the front of that upmarket restaurant; their exposed roots are big enough to hide a toddler.

Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, arrested in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 20:41:11 GMT

Father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a senior care facility in Polk county early on Friday, and made a brief initial appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday afternoon, the Associated Press reported.

A 14-page federal criminal complaint says that agents seized approximately 78 items and alleges that Markle kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units that he rented for nearly two decades.

An affidavit filed with the ​complaint that led to the arrest stated that two of the images inside the units showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a nude underage girl.

The document, filed in federal court in California, said the recovered material included dozens of slides, photographs, film negatives and books containing the illegal material. It said the FBI was still reviewing the material.

The director of the FBI, Kash ​Patel, said: “Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his ⁠criminal actions. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero ⁠safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

Patel thanked FBI agents in Los Angeles and Tampa, and authorities in Mexico, the Philippines, and Marshall Islands that he said were involved in the investigation.

Some details in the criminal complaint are redacted, such as the name of the federal agent who signed the complaint, who states that they are assigned to the violent crimes against children unit in the LA office of the FBI. The case is presented as United States of America v Thomas Wayne Markle.

“Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the central district of California, said in a statement released by the US department of justice.

“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Essayli told the Associated Press that there was no evidence of victims in the US, based on the seized material, but that the investigation was ongoing. He said his office was aware of public reporting that Markle might have dementia.

Markle is charged with one count of possession of child sexual abuse material, and faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.

Efforts by the AP to reach Markle’s court-appointed lawyer for comment were unsuccessful, the news agency said.

Meghan, the wife of Prince Harry, said last month that she was “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images was found at her father’s former home in the Philippines.

The duchess also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about her father was sent to police in London in 2018.

She had issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his Philippines residence. He was named as a person of interest in the case earlier this week.

According to the justice department statement, FBI agents interviewed a person last month who was aware that Markle was renting the two storage units in California after the bureau became aware of developments in the Philippines.

Markle rented the units since 2008, it said, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Photographs produced by the Daily Mail showed Thomas Markle Sr being taken away in a wheelchair, in handcuffs, wearing a black T-shirt and surrounded by agents wearing jackets marked “FBI”. The UK tabloid asked Markle if he was a pedophile and he replied: “No.” Markle did not answer when the newspaper asked if he had ever collected child sexual abuse material.

A spokesperson for the duchess did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Authorities in the Philippines, where Markle ⁠had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he ​possessed child sexual abuse ​images. British police last month said they ​would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that ​claims had not ‌been passed to ​other authorities when ​they were first received.

He has denied the accusations, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies”.

Markle is a retired television lighting and photography director and he did not attend the 2018 wedding of Harry and Meghan, amid acrimony and estrangement between father and daughter. Meghan has since said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.

The duke and duchess returned to live in Britain in the summer after six years in the US.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport. org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

Macklemore says that nine US arenas turned down his Free Palestine tour

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:46:56 GMT

Rapper called out ‘intimidation, manipulation and suppression’ in a social media post, claiming major arenas refused to host him after the Ed Sheeran controversy

Macklemore says that nine major US arenas have refused to host his Free Palestine fundraising tour, calling out “intimidation, manipulation and suppression” tactics.

In an Instagram post, the rapper says that he hoped to bring the tour to the US, but nine major arenas refused to host the event, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, Los Angeles’s Crypto. com arena and Brooklyn’s Barclays Center.

Last month, Macklemore brought the Free Palestine tour to Dublin, London and Paris in a show praised by the Guardian’s Alexis Petridis as “a triumph”. The shows came in the wake of Ed Sheeran dropping the rapper from his US tour after he made an onstage speech in support of Palestine.

“From the beginning, our plan was to bring this tour home to the US,” Macklemore wrote. “But after weeks of reaching out, nine major American arenas have turned us down.”

Macklemore said that other venues in the New York tri-state area, including UBS arena and Prudential Center turned him down, as well as Los Angeles’s Intuit Dome and Kia Forum, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge arena.

“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year. But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table,” he said.

“The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

In an impassioned post that spanned seven Instagram slides, Macklemore said that he no longer cared about burning bridges with music industry top dogs.

“The intimidation, manipulation and suppression I experienced are part of how those in power keep entertainers quiet,” he said. “It’s their main tactic to keep us in line. Shut up and dribble, or you will be punished.

“But at this point, I’m three years past giving two shits about maintaining any relationships, business or personal, with anyone that isn’t riding for a Free Palestine.”

After making a brief speech in support of “the occupied West Bank” in early September while opening up for Sheeran, Macklemore was dropped from the tour. Sheeran claimed that US venues told him that they would refuse to host the show if the rapper continued as the tour’s supporting act.

“I am not complicit,” Sheeran said. “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Nor does it mean that I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”

Shortly after, all four opening acts as well as Sheeran’s live band quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

On social media, the rapper said: “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.

“I dream of a world where saying Free Palestine is not controversial,” he added. “It is expected. Where artists value their freedom of speech and collective liberation more than their brand deals.

“Look at what just happened in Europe,” he went on, referring to his shows in Dublin, Paris and London. “Three sold-out arenas. Tens of thousands of people from different backgrounds, religions and walks of life standing together. More than forty artists and speakers putting their names and platforms behind Palestinian liberation. For all the attempts to paint this movement as one rooted in hatred, what filled those rooms was love.”

Macklemore went on to say that the political mood of the US was changing in the wake of the Democrats sweeping the midterm elections this week.

“The tides are turning,” he wrote. “Just three nights ago, Abdul El-Sayed won his Senate race on a platform that included ending the genocide in Gaza and stopping U. S. arms sales to Israel. AIPAC spent $42m trying to defeat him. And they still couldn’t win.

“The trouble with buying power is believing you’ve bought the people too. The billionaires depend on our silence and complicity. They forget that we buy their tickets. We fill their arenas. We build their empires. And we have the power to bring them down.”

The rapper closed his statement with a promise that more shows in support of Palestine will follow.

“There will be more shows for Palestine,” he said. “We’ll keep working with other artists and organizers, continuing where we left off in Europe. We’ll probably just take that shit outside where it belonged in the first place.

“Our commitment to raising funds and standing in solidarity with the Palestinian people remains the same.”

As an ending note, he said: “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE.”

Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:23:24 GMT

Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing

Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.

The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.

The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.

The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.

Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.

The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.

Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating. I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”

Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases. Let’s see where this one goes.”

Brand’s trial, which spanned claims of attacks from 1999 to 2009, saw women asked by the defence barrister why they had not screamed during attacks.

Since the end of the trial there has been a debate about rape myths. A No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed calls from the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, for a legal duty that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions, should be examined.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths … we will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”

Siobhan Blake, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) lead for rape and serious sexual offences, said: “The focus must be the actions of the perpetrator and not the behaviour of the victim.

“We know that there is no typical response to sexual assault and myths that victims should scream and fight back are outdated. Some people may freeze or feel unable to speak about it for months or even years, but this is not a barrier to justice.”

Brand now faces years of imprisonment and the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.

He was convicted on Thursday of raping a young fan at his luxury London townhouse in 2009, continuing despite her pleas for him to stop. He had picked her out of a crowd. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar.

Victims are expected to tell of the impact his crimes had on them in court on Monday.

Brand became an international star, acting in Hollywood films, and in latter years an online influencer, but was dogged by whispers and allegations about his danger to women. He was accused of treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

The government says it is committed to reducing violence against women and girls by half.

Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.

“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to come forward.”

Later on the BBC, Burnham was asked about a statement of support for Brand in 2014 as the star faced media criticism, and said: “Well, over a decade ago, and all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do. His crimes are horrific.”

The comedian Katherine Ryan, who warned of a “predator” in the entertainment industry before Brand’s trial, said she felt relief at his conviction.

“They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them,” she said.

“I will never be someone who, like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”

Bear Grylls, who baptised Brand when he converted to Christianity in 2024, said the star’s faith seemed genuine and added: “It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”

Brand was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” – changing from charming to nasty – as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.
