Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:23:24 GMT

The Chilean film-maker, whose films starred Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore and Rachel Weisz, died at his home in Santiago

Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.

He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.

His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.

Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.

His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.

Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.

“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”

He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.

Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.

“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”

His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.

“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:15:49 GMT

Sunday’s hosts need to stop looking for excuses and focus on what they can control to kick off the Nations Championship against battle-hardened Australia

Several things are increasingly guaranteed from an English rugby perspective around this time of year. Bang on cue the injury news and the weather both start to worsen. Cracks in the relationship between the players and their head coach, in this case Steve Borthwick, begin to surface. And as the crowds stream up from Twickenham railway station past the biltong and burger stalls, no one has much idea what to expect.

This year it has been the same old story. Particularly on the injury front. If Tom Curry, Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland had not all been hurt on the Bagshot training pitch, all three would probably be in England’s matchday 23. With Guy Pepper, Benhard van Rensburg, Sam Underhill, Kepu Tuipulotu and Chandler Cunningham-South also out of the running, the squad is not quite as fizzing with energy and dynamism as it might be.

And Borthwick, not for the first time, is back under scrutiny. According to a well-sourced report in the Times, his players sought a clear-the-air meeting in Argentina in July having allegedly grown unhappy with the former England captain’s man management and lack of empathy. It makes Sunday’s opening Nations Championship Test against Australia even more of a must-win game than was already the case.

All this, ironically, in the same week that the Rugby Football Union restated its desire for Borthwick to remain in his post through to the World Cup. Perhaps officials got wind of the impending story. Or, again not for the first time, maybe the chief executive, Bill Sweeney, has once more backed the wrong horse, having jettisoned Eddie Jones barely nine months before the last World Cup.

What a diplomatic mess, albeit a wearily familiar one. It had already been a curious week before these latest allegations surfaced. Sweeney even mentioned a stat suggesting England are the world’s second-best side when they keep 15 players on the field but only eighth or ninth when down to 14 or fewer. No shit, Sherlock. More pertinent, surely, is how England become sufficiently composed under pressure to avoid leaking costly penalties or cards.

Back in Santiago del Estero in July Borthwick opted to blame the “negativity committee” in the media for raising the subject after the game. Given his team had just lost four men to the sin-bin in the second half and barely clung on to win, it felt distinctly odd at the time. Given the newly reported context it now makes more sense.

The truth, then and now, is that something doesn’t feel entirely right about England, whether it be elements of the gameplan, the coaching blend, certain selections, cultural alignment or all of the above. They certainly need to find an urgent cure for the rampaging yellow fever that has cost them 14 yellow cards, plus one red, in 2026 to date. When they are in control of their own destiny, as opposed to scrambling desperately in their own 22, rugby becomes a different game.

This same fixture 12 months ago was, by the end, a prime example. Australia arrived tired and lacking a few key men and the home side, with six British & Irish Lions arriving off the bench, stretched clear to record a comfortable 25-7 win, the highlight being an eye-catching score from – who else? – Henry Pollock.

That result also extended England’s winning run to eight Tests. This year, though, their star has waned significantly, with only two wins – against a below-par Fiji and the Pumas – in their past seven Tests. Which is what has lent an extra frisson to this November even before the RFU’s “nothing to see here” messaging.

What price such corporate froth on Monday morning should Australia get up as they so memorably did in London in 2024? Or if Japan and Jones, having lost only 35-32 to the Wallabies in August, also take a sharp Samurai sword to English pretensions next Saturday? Staging the Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium is all fine and dandy until the party hosts find themselves locked out in the communal hallway while the proper action is going on inside.

The alternative scenario, of course, involves the Wallabies being splattered across the sweet chariot’s windshield, the Brave Blossoms being scrummaged and mauled off the park and the All Blacks being turned over for the second successive autumn. If France, Ireland and Scotland all have a mixed month it is still possible Borthwick’s unhappy campers could make the inaugural Nations Championship final and enter 2027 with rather more in the way of optimism.

Place your chips and roll those dice. The midterm elections in the US have also just underlined how radically things can alter virtually overnight. But if England’s men want to rank among the world’s leading four teams again, let alone the top two, they need to find some kind of positive injection next year, whether in terms of selection, personnel or fresh coaching ideas.

It may not matter on Sunday if England’s front five get an early grip, the outstanding Fraser McReight is countered at the breakdown and the Wallabies are mauled halfway back to Wollongong but there is a bigger picture to be considered as well. Among other things, Borthwick is taking a calculated gamble on senior men such as Jamie George, 36, and Luke Cowan-Dickie, 33, staying fit for another 12 months while Henry Slade is 34 in March.

There remains the nagging worry, too, that the squad’s preparations have been shorter compared with previous years. Whether that has contributed in any way to the training ground injury toll is unclear but Australia’s recent contests against New Zealand, South Africa and Argentina have left them more battle-hardened. Borthwick, furthermore, believes the high-scoring rugby seen in the early rounds of the Prem is not necessarily assisting the national cause and he probably has a point. Then again, having a host of players plying their trade in Japan didn’t hold back Rassie Erasmus’s World Cup-winning Springboks. England, either way, need to stop looking for peripheral excuses and focus on what they can control. Surely there will not be a breathless replay of two years ago when England missed 35 tackles and ended up losing 42-37.

This time, having rejected Shaun Edwards’ offer to assist his side’s defence, Borthwick will be desperate for a 15-man England to keep calm and carry on grafting. If you were to offer him a pressure-relieving three-point win now, he’d bite your hand off somewhere near the elbow.

‘Minimal look, maximal politics’: how the black T-shirt became a political weapon

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:14:46 GMT

The look – worn by Abdul El-Sayed, Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy – radiates authority and no-nonsense masculinity, say fashion experts

For years the black T-shirt was consigned to the clothing category of plain basics. A hidden layer rather than the main event. But modern politics has pushed it to the frontlines as a sartorial shortcut to signal power.

The progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who this week became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history, made a tight black T-shirt his signature look throughout his year-long campaign. Styling it with jeans and friendship bracelets made by his children, El-Sayed described his attire as “minimal look, maximal politics”.

In sharp contrast to the Maga aesthetic of boxy suits, El-Sayed’s T-shirt softens the lines between politics and the public. It’s anti-establishment without being alienating.

“Black radiates authority, seriousness, a certain no-nonsense masculinity,” says Johnny Davis, the luxury director of Esquire magazine.

A black T-shirt has also become a key part of Andy Burnham’s “man of the people” look – so much so that Kemi Badenoch once described the prime minister as a “pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt”.

In July, the former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett swapped his usual smart shirts and suits for a black T-shirt and jeans as he attempted to make a political comeback. Bennett’s wardrobe shift was a deliberate decision by his campaign managers to make him appear “younger, more accessible and energetic”, according to reports.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has turned a black T-shirt into a symbol of patriotism and solidarity.

For Davis, a black T-shirt brings to mind the Hollywood star Jason Statham, Keanu Reeves’s hitman character John Wick, and the Black Flag punk singer Henry Rollins. “It suggests someone who is going to ‘get the job done’, whatever it takes,” he says.

When asked in an interview why he wore a black T-shirt, El-Sayed said it was “the ideal shirt for somebody who has got to be in a bunch of different kinds of spaces and places all day, every day”.

Contrasting El-Sayed’s style with Trump’s, Davis says: “One represents an almost exaggerated version of traditional corporate power dressing; the other is trying to establish a completely different idea of authority. It’s a line in the sand.”

Previously, when politicians including Barack Obama needed to visually convey they meant business, they took their jackets off and rolled up their shirtsleeves.

In May Keir Starmer drew comparisons to John Major when, during a make-or-break speech after a dire set of election results, he appeared on stage without a jacket, the cuffs of his shirt deliberately folded back.

Davis says a black T-shirt feels like the next evolution of that, but this time around “you don’t even need to roll your sleeves up”.

El-Sayed’s T-shirt features a V-neck collar and is tightly fitted, highlighting what the BBC described as his “jacked” physique.

David Hellqvist, a men’s editor and the author of Blue-Collar Modernism, says El-Sayed’s choice of a form-fitting T-shirt is a reflection of his confidence.

“He is very comfortable in his own skin and showing off his body.” Hellqvist says this echoes his political approach. “He doesn’t need to tell people he is going to roll up his sleeves and start fixing problems. They can already see he is doing it.”

So why a black T-shirt rather than white? Hellqvist says black is the colour of “intent and purpose”.

Davis says white has too many James Dean and Marlon Brando associations. “It’s a bit 1950s sex symbol and too try-hard.” The repeated use of a black T-shirt also helped to make El-Sayed feel familiar, whether the viewer was watching him on a TV screen or meeting him at a rally.

Davis compares it to Steve Jobs and his uniform look of a black polo neck and jeans. “It’s personal branding disguised as not caring about clothes, which is quite a trick,” Davis says.

“It suggests you’re too busy doing something important to waste time thinking about what to wear. Once you establish a signature look, you become instantly recognisable.”

ECB forecasting losses of up to £50m in 2027 despite visit of Australia for the Ashes

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:00:49 GMT

Concern among counties due to reliance on ECB funding

Optimism that eventual figure could be reduced to £35m

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) is forecasting losses of tens of millions of pounds next year despite hosting the Ashes, with county executives told last week that the deficit could be as large as £50m.

The anticipated shortfall, after posting a profit of £12.6m in 2025, is due to a combination of the cyclical nature of the governing body’s media revenues, which is largely determined by domestic opposition, and a recent decision by the International Cricket Council (ICC) to withhold a portion of the broadcast payments owed to members that it had been due to distribute in 2027.

The ECB had noted in its 2025 accounts published in May that it was expecting a “significant loss” in 2027 due to the absence of home matches against India, but that figure is now far higher than expected, which is causing concern among the counties.

Ten of the 18 first class counties recorded losses in their most recently published accounts, and the vast majority are reliant on ECB funding to ensure they remain going concerns.

ECB sources have privately acknowledged the scale of the projected losses, but expressed optimism that the eventual figure could be reduced to around £35m, as the amount to be withheld by the ICC has yet to be confirmed and there is still time to add extra commercial and event revenue given the 2027 accounting period runs until 31 January 2028.

The ECB is understood to be working with the ICC to mitigate the impact of the reduced distribution.

The ICC’s decision to withhold broadcast payments next year has come as a surprise and is due to concerns over a projected decline in the value of the world governing body’s next Indian TV deal, with its current contracts expiring next year.

The ICC would ordinarily give its 12 full members a larger back-weighted media payment in the final year of the broadcast cycle as it coincides with the men’s 50-over World Cup, its most lucrative event in the calendar, but it has opted to withhold a portion next year in anticipation of getting a lower broadcast deal in the next cycle to enable it to smooth the drop in payments to members in 2028.

Disney Star paid US$3bn (£2.2bn) for the ICC’s media rights in India between 2023 and 2027, but after a merger with Reliance Industries and Viacom18 in 2024 sought to exit the deal, creating the widespread expectation that it will offer far less in the next cycle as much of the competition has been removed from the market.

The ECB is also hugely reliant on money from Indian TV so has similar concerns about declining revenue, particularly as its current $250m (£185m) six-year rights deal with Sony Pictures expires in 2028, with the expectation that the next contract will be significantly smaller.

Sony’s payments to the ECB are also far higher in years when India tour England, with the £12.6m profit in the 2025 accounts underpinned by that summer’s thrilling five-Test series, and the eight white-ball matches played this summer projected to generate another profit in the ECB’s 2026 accounts. In contrast Channel 9’s deal for exclusive rights to broadcast Australia’s tours to England in 2027 and 2031 is worth only $27.5m (£20.2m) to the ECB.

As a result of this imbalance Ashes summers have always been less lucrative for the ECB despite creating more domestic interest, although the financial losses projected for 2027 are still surprising and buck recent trends.

Beyond the India issue the ECB is overly reliant on media rights income generally, with about 75% of its £310m annual revenue coming from broadcast sales. The domestic rights deal with Sky Sports expires in 2028 and its value has not risen since 2019, another source of concern in an uncertain media landscape.

The impact of the ECB’s unbalanced revenue streams has been compounded by a significant increase in spending in recent years. The ECB raised £520m from the part-sale of the eight Hundred franchises to private investors last year, but the majority of that money is frozen in an escrow account to be distributed to counties wanting to pay off debt or invest in infrastructure projects. The ECB also has cash reserves of around £60m, which it is aiming to increase to £80m.

Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 19:00:49 GMT

The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds

As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.

Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.

The colour of noise tends to animate physicists more than linguists, but researchers at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US found the concept provided fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.

Kathryn O’Nell, the first author on the study, said: “In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.

“It’s particularly cool for conversation, because you can stay somewhere long enough to really get to know each other, to understand the topic, but you’re not stuck there while it gets stale.”

The researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, who answered questions on the chats afterwards. People enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise, they found.

To see whether the effect applied beyond strangers, the researchers ran a similar analysis on conversations between friends about their formative experiences. Again, more pink noise meant more enjoyment.

The effect had real-world consequences, too. When the scientists turned to speed-dating conversations, they found that more pink noise predicted which pairs met up for a second date. Details have been published in Science Advances.

Nailing down what makes a great chat is notoriously tricky, the researchers said. In a bold opening statement to their paper, the authors write: “Good conversation is like pornography – it is difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.”

Colloquially, people talk about being in sync, but the metaphor misses something, said Dr Emily Finn, a neuroscientist and senior author on the paper. “In sync can be incredibly dull,” she said. People can be in sync when they repeat each other’s words and circle a single subject. They might well be immensely bored.

In the study, the scientists took conversations and fed each side into an AI called MPNet. The program scored every turn of the chat on 768 different criteria, covering aspects such as meaning, tone and context. This allowed the scientists to quantify how conversations ebbed and flowed over time.

Conversations exhibit white noise when people fail to follow what has just been said: the chat might jump all over the place, or be dominated by a person who seems oblivious to the other person’s responses. Other conversations can have red noise, which arises when people mirror each other’s language and fall into a conversational rut.

Pink noise lies somewhere in between: a conversational Goldilocks zone that balances stability and flexibility. People will synchronise as they explore a topic, then drift apart as they pull in fresh ideas before converging again to explore those.

The pinkiness of a conversation depends on the people involved, but O’Nell said she suspected the skill could be learned and developed. As part of the study, the team analysed podcasts fronted by two hosts and found that the pinkiness of their conversations increased over the first 50 episodes.

Prof Elizabeth Stokoe, a conversation analyst at the London School of Economics, praised the researchers for moving beyond the idea that “more similarity is better”. But asking whether a conversation is enjoyable risks missing the point, she added.

“There’s a lovely study of a phone call in which a father and his daughter, a young woman with learning disabilities living in residential care, take a long time to say goodbye, and the ending is painful and poignant,” she said. “Reducing conversations to whether they are ‘enjoyable’ can feel bloodless, since many of the conversations that matter most in our lives are like this.”

Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge’s verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail publisher Associated Newspapers.

Harry, Doreen Lawrence, the mother of the murdered black teenager Stephen Lawrence, the singer Elton John and his husband, David Furnish, and the actors Elizabeth Hurley and Sadie Frost faced a legal bill of more than £50m after losing their case claiming that Mail journalists used unlawful methods to source stories.

In an unequivocal ruling in July, Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed their case, stating that the claimants had not proved that any information had been obtained unlawfully.

His 436-page written verdict, following an 11-week trial, said it could not be inferred that a story had been obtained unlawfully if there remained a legitimate and realistic legal way in which it could have been sourced.

In a statement issued on Friday, a spokesperson for Harry and his five fellow claimants said: “We confirm that the claimants have today filed applications with the court of appeal for permission to appeal the judgments of Mr Justice Nicklin in respect of his dismissal of their claims and the indemnity costs order.

“The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed.”

Court staff confirmed on Friday that a bid to appeal against the rulings had been filed at the court of appeal.

Barristers for the claimants had alleged at trial that private investigators, freelance journalists and staff at Associated Newspapers had carried out acts including voicemail interception, landline tapping and obtaining information by deception – also known as “blagging”.

But lawyers for the publisher said Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists provided a “compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles”, including friends and “leaky” social circles, press officers and spokespeople, as well as previous reporting, freelance journalists and stories from other newspapers and news agencies.

Associated’s legal team described the claims as “lurid” and “preposterous”.

After the verdict the former Mail editor Paul Dacre said the case was a “conspiracy” orchestrated by press regulation campaigners to “destroy a paper”.

Harry and Lawrence said the verdict was a “complete and obvious whitewash”. They added: “When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing … then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.”

In August, Nicklin ruled that the claimants had to pay £9,544,355 within seven days as an initial contribution to the publisher’s costs before further hearings to determine the total sum.

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

Police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster: “The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used.

“An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

The Guardian view on the AI backlash: American voters want a say in their future

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:58:05 GMT

The tech sell-off exposes fragile promises, while Democratic victories offer a chance to protect workers and hold firms accountable

This week’s midterms showed that the political bill for the AI boom is falling due. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. On Thursday Wall Street suffered its worst day since the pandemic as $3.2tn was wiped from markets. Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, is hoping to float within the next fortnight for $1.5tn (£1.1tn), but it may not now get even a trillion dollars. The dominant AI chipmaker Nvidia saw its value crash by more than $400bn. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, lost $113bn in two days.

While a few very rich people may be a little less wealthy, the sell-off may not be a bad thing. It brings a needed dose of reality to an industry whose spending plans and valuations depend on heroic expectations of future profits. That is a view held by many influential figures – from Goldman Sachs’ research boss to Nobel laureate Daron Acemoğlu. AI may transform the economy. That does not guarantee investors will earn back the sums being poured into it.

Donald Trump is the other big loser. He rejected concerns about AI and the need to impose stricter rules despite most Americans wanting more safeguards. He called concerns about the potential dangers of AI development a “hoax”. Republicans paid a price for his refusal to listen. Mr Trump argued computing capacity was a national asset that needed to expand rapidly, while dismissing resistance to the infrastructure and the companies building it. The US president was deaf to voter frustration over electricity prices, water demand and disruption. Democrats could campaign against those costs falling on residents while the gains went to tech billionaires and their companies, which donated money to Mr Trump’s favoured causes.

Mr Musk’s SpaceX, a combined space, satellite-connectivity and AI group, warned in its June 2026 prospectus that new regulations could derail its growth plans. He spent $200m in Texas for Republicans as Democrats took aim at AI datacentres in a state where there was rising voter discontent over the industry’s rapid expansion. Mr Musk could not buy this election. Democrats won a US senate seat, the state governorship and wiped out every other statewide Republican office, taking the Texas house with a comfortable margin. Across the US, the blue wave saw wins for Democrats who have been critical of datacentre construction and pledged to slow or pause their rollout.

Democrats say they intend to make AI companies answerable for the environmental and societal costs of their infrastructure buildup as well as the harm their products cause. The new Congress is likely to be much more ready to shield voters from rising prices caused by datacentre expansion, ensure independent safety testing for advanced AI and clarify liability for possible harms. Democrats’ willingness to take public fears about AI seriously is welcome. People need confidence that elected governments can protect their livelihoods and communities.

Whatever happens to tech stocks, the genie of AI won’t be put back into its lamp. This year alone the technology was given as the reason 120,000 Americans lost their jobs. Politicians ought to strengthen workers’ bargaining power and ensure that productivity gains are fairly shared. Just letting the markets decide will only deepen the economic insecurity and political distrust that is corroding democracy.

The Guardian view on Russell Brand: his conviction sends a powerful message

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:57:08 GMT

The brave women who testified against the star have struck a blow against the sexual entitlement that he personified

The conviction of Russell Brand for one rape and three sexual assaults on Thursday would never have happened were it not for the remarkable courage of his victims. There was no guarantee, before the trial, that he would be found guilty; two more rape charges and one of attempted indecent assault ended in acquittal. The women who testified about what Brand did to them between 2004 and 2009 are owed a debt of gratitude by everyone who believes that sexual predators should pay a price for their crimes, even when they are celebrities. On Monday, Brand will receive what the judge said would be a “significant” jail sentence.

The message sent by his rape conviction is particularly powerful. His sexual encounter with “Woman E”, who was 21 at the time, began as a consensual one, before he turned it into an anal rape that left her with psychological and physical injuries. A single case is unlikely to alter a culture of male sexual entitlement, in which it is viewed as acceptable to push women over boundaries that they do not want to cross. But the jury’s acceptance of her version of events – which was supported by multiple witnesses – can still be viewed as a step forward. Far too many women are disbelieved, or not taken seriously, when they make allegations about abuse by partners.

Nearly 10 years after the #MeToo movement, serious problems in the entertainment industries around sexual misconduct and abuse of power – as well as insecure working conditions that make it hard for junior colleagues to speak out – are widely recognised. Brand, who was a highly in-demand media figure from about 2007, picked “Woman E” out of an audience, while one of the sexual assaults he was convicted of took place in Choice FM’s studios, and another of his victims was a Channel 4 colleague. When he initiated a relationship with “Alice” (a pseudonym), she was a 16-year-old schoolgirl and he was on the verge of stardom (his alleged conduct towards her has not led to criminal charges, but was featured in the 2023 Dispatches programme that prompted the police investigation).

Internal reviews led to apologies from the BBC and Channel 4, after the revelations on Dispatches and in the Times and Sunday Times. But it would be naive to claim that the culture that enabled Brand, who was also once a Guardian sports columnist, is no more. His particular shapeshifting, from outrageous Essex boy to anti-establishment commentator to born-again Christian, would be unlikely to fool people a second time. But as the times change, so do the ruses and roles that predators adopt. It is frankly disturbing to be reminded now of just how brazen Brand was about his vicious behaviour (spitting on, choking and humiliating women) in his bestselling memoirs and on the radio. On Thursday, Pan Macmillan announced that it would stop publishing his books – including a British Book Awards biography of the year.

Two further rape complaints are being examined by police. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, has referred himself to the Bar Standards Board after an extraordinary exchange with a reporter that he initiated outside court, after the verdict. But whether or not more charges are brought, and whatever the wider impact of Brand’s disgrace, the women who testified should be proud of their part in exposing him.

Russell Brand has finally faced justice. But other abusers in comedy are still hiding in plain sight

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:35:46 GMT

I love my industry but it contains people who leave a secret trail of pain and devastation totally at odds with their stage and screen personas

Sarah Solemani is an actor, writer and activist who starred in the Bafta-winning comedy Him & Her

I’ve worked in comedy in some capacity for several decades, and I include in that a year in a call centre in north Finchley run by a man who embraced the early stages of hair transplant technology, which was serious LOLS until the company was shut down by HMRC. Acting funny and writing funny has got me far. From winning the best sitcom Bafta for Him & Her, to playing Bridget Jones’s best friend, to writing monologues for Goldie Hawn, who held me like a newborn in her house and insisted we had met in a previous life. I also get to work on new projects with my favourite directors, such as Tom George of This Country, where we make each other laugh from the beginning of the day to the end. Lucky me.

Unluckily, working in comedy has also, for some strange reason, brought me into the close orbit of more than your average number of sexual predators, several of whom are still merrily working. Recently I had to pull a project from a company when I was informed it was common knowledge that a high-level exec was known for allegedly raping a colleague. Another famous comic had to pull a project when I informed them a legend they were working with was also an alleged rapist. That was two rape-related conversations in the same week without a punchline.

If you think there’s dissonance in the pursuits, you’d be right. On one level – the higher level, you might say – we are trying to make work that brings joy and amusement to the deserving masses. Then, in the secret, unfunny world, we are sending clandestine, time-consuming warnings about rapists and trying to covertly deal with the fallout. Are male comedians more likely to be rapists than say, firefighters or coastguards? We don’t have the data on that (but you can bet some poor, out-of-work female comedian is researching it as we speak instead of what she should be doing: WRITING JOKES).

Before he was a conspiracist YouTuber or even a Hollywood star, Russell Brand was a comedian, taking shows up to Edinburgh and building a following on the comedy circuit. For years, it has been common knowledge in comedy circles and beyond that he hurt many, many women. Brand has now been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women. Thanks to the gargantuan bravery of the four women who came forward, he is unlikely to harm again. From my understanding it was those within the comedy community, and one famous female comedian in particular, who helped the survivors bring about justice.

Brand will serve a “significant custodial term” but the British comedy community knows there are more sexual abusers working on sets right now. They may not be tried in their lifetime. But we know. And they know. Female and working-class young talent have also only been made more vulnerable by slashes to comedy budgets and a dearth of TV commissions. I will never forgive myself for introducing one comedy producer to promising new talent, only to find out he had abused them in his flat, offering them London accommodation for their gigs and auditions.

The criminal justice system served the victims of Brand. For the majority of others, it does not: it’s “he said v she said”, and he said wins because the burden of proof is not on him. The informal network of reporting and taking action are crucial to protect women and vulnerable people.

Brand has been brought to justice, but his damage to the culture runs deep. If only he had been the ultimate radical comedian and admitted the harm he had done. If only he had led the way through remorse and rehabilitation, rather than doubling down and putting the women through the pain and humiliation of a criminal trial. If only we had been spared the changing of his shamanic cloaks, and him settling on his current Christian charade, and instead witnessed a man surrendering to true repair and redemption. That would have finally been an act of his worth watching.

Sarah Solemani is an actor, writer and activist

Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.

Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally.

The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.

A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society,” said Martin, adding that European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were “all connected”.

She added: “But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures.”

The Nato alliance continued to monitor the situation and was working closely with allies, according to a senior Nato military official.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries were continuing.

Several European media outlets in Bulgaria, Ireland, the UK and elsewhere reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats warned in an email of further actions against transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said. The Guardian has chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.

Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016. In a Telegram post on Friday the group’s founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement and said the group had not existed since 2021.

Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern.

“It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.

“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

Mark Rowley, the chief of London’s Metropolitan police, urged a measured response, saying past experience with the paramilitary Irish Republican Army offered valuable lessons.

He recalled the phrase “10p terrorism”, when a hoax bomb call made from a coin-operated phone box could disrupt an entire city, forcing authorities to distinguish between genuine and false threats.

The authorities would need to adapt to an evolving threat landscape involving actors around the world, some backed by hostile states, he said.

“We are going to have to adapt to that same methodology to make sure that we don’t overreact to every message we get online,” he told BBC Radio 4.

Hamilton v Leclerc: how can Ferrari solve problem of two number one drivers?

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:08:05 GMT

The Scuderia are hopeful of being in the world championship mix next season but risk puncturing their chances if they can’t corral their men in the cockpits

Going into this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix, all indications are that the status quo at Ferrari will no longer suffice for Lewis Hamilton if the Scuderia’s ambition to return their first drivers’ Formula One championship since 2007 is to be taken seriously.

This year’s drivers’ title is already decided with Kimi Antonelli triumphant at the last round in Mexico and Ferrari are looking towards next season where they are hopeful of genuinely being in the mix against the Italian and Mercedes.

However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce.

In Mexico, with Leclerc attempting to pass Hamilton, the move cost them both, Leclerc with a penalty and Hamilton in going wide and being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win. The outcome denied Ferrari what would have been a likely victory and potentially a one-two. The team principal, Fred Vasseur, condemned the incident as demonstrating a lack of respect for the team and iswas expected to hold a crunch meeting with them both at Interlagos on Friday.

It was not the first time this season the two Ferrari drivers have been uncompromising with one another. At Zandvoort Hamilton was frustrated when, on a different tyre strategy, Leclerc did not pit when first instructed to do so by the team in order to let the British driver past. A race later at Monza, Hamilton went down the inside of Leclerc into the first chicane and was squeezed wide by his teammate into the gravel.

The notable difference after Mexico was Hamilton’s reaction. Previously he has been politic in stating they would deal with incidents behind closed doors – “offline” as he refers to it. After Mexico he publicly criticised Leclerc and before the race in Brazil was more bullish, refusing to be silenced in his criticism and making his position clear.

“Naturally it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken,” he said. “I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more and as long as I’m here that’s how it’s going to be. I’m here to win.”

That he is talking about it publicly indicates the seriousness of the situation. The team have no formal rules of engagement between the two and pointedly neither is considered the top driver in the way that Verstappen is at Red Bull.

Last year with the team struggling it was irrelevant. This year the problem has been brought sharply into focus. With a title at stake in the future it could be the difference between winning and losing but this is far from a straightforward situation. Hamilton came to Ferrari on the back of enjoying de facto No 1 status at Mercedes, pretty much since Nico Rosberg retired after thein 2016 season. Leclerc, who is no less competitive, has enjoyed similar pre-eminence at Ferrari, with whom he has forged a strong relationship since he joined in 2019 and was long the favoured choice as their expected next champion.

The complex demands and the fallout from letting them battle for dominance is far from new, as seen with Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet. Hamilton also knows about it, not least after his acrimonious fight with Rosberg in 2016. The latter was such that Mercedes, having been at pains to allow their drivers to race, had to impose rules of engagement.

Vasseur has been painstaking so far in avoiding that scenario but he was left enormously frustrated after the incident in Mexico and knows how costly it could be.

His is a very delicate balancing act however. McLaren had a similar problem with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in 2024 and 2025, and their efforts to allow their drivers to race without favour but also in managing them to the team’s advantage led to the adoption of their torturously complex “papaya rules”. These were satisfying to neither drivers nor fans, and did not appear particularly edifying to the team themselves. Notably however they did come out of it with the constructors’ title in 2024 and the double in 2025, a result that will not be lost on Ferrari.

It has largely not been a problem for McLaren this season, with Norris enjoying a distinct advantage over his Australian teammate, of which Hamilton and Leclerc are aware. Both are determined to make themselves the focal point of the team; both are aware how important that is if the title is at stake.

This has led to another fundamental problem for Ferrari. By not intervening in the process, they have seen the trust between the pair seemingly stretched to breaking point. Perhaps, it feels, within a whisker of becoming actively counterproductive from which a further, more damaging deterioration threatens.

As Hamilton appears to be now insisting, Ferrari must address the issue but Leclerc cannot be faulted for simply following his instincts as a competitor. Both drivers are committed to the team but both are as equally determined to win, ambitions that match those of the Scuderia, which if they are to be met they must surely now look to manage.

In first practice at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris topped the timesheets in front of the new champion Antonelli in second, with Verstappen third and Hamilton fourth.

In the afternoon Antonelli was on top, from Norris and Verstappen with Mercedes’ George Russell in fourth. Russell is, however, set to take a five-place grid penalty on Sunday for using a new engine in Brazil. Hamilton and Leclerc were in sixth and seventh.

This was “an issue of huge societal importance”, Burnham said in one of the interviews, with Times Radio. “If you leave young people in their 20s without hope, that is a dangerous thing to do,” he said. “People need to have a path. Asked if this could involve cutting some benefits, he replied: “I am prepared to take difficult decisions because I can’t accept the idea that we have a million or more young people in their 20s on benefits. Likening the idea to the proposal to change the triple-lock system of guaranteed pension increases while at the same time bringing in a new system for adult social care, Burnham said the reappraisal of young people’s opportunities would begin in early years.

He said: “Too many young people are not school-ready when they come to school. And the evidence is many don’t catch up. If they’re not ready to learn in reception class, that gap stays all the way through the school system. So it’s part of this. It is about rethinking childhood, in every aspect of it.”

Autism, masking, and building a more inclusive world

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:39:31 GMT

Readers respond to an article by John Harris on the rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years

John Harris’s article addresses all the main issues that are being debated around autism (‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?, 1 November). However, I feel it did not go far enough to broaden our understanding of the challenges experienced by autistic people who do not have a learning disability.

From a young age I sensed that I was experiencing the world differently to other people. I was bullied, and worked hard to fit in. I was fortunate as structurally I had a stable life that mitigated some of the more challenging aspects of my life. Things started to get less manageable when I entered adulthood and left home.

Since the age of 25 I have experienced bouts of depression and ongoing anxiety, often resulting in breakdowns, or what I now understand to be autistic burnouts. Throughout adulthood I have seen numerous medical professionals and repeatedly been directed towards therapies, designed to deal with anxiety and depression, which have had limited success in addressing my life challenges.

Despite having a postgraduate education, I have struggled to hold down many jobs and have had to leave most due to stress. I have ongoing relationship problems. I don’t have children, partly due to reluctance and health issues. I suffer from fatigue and sleep issues.

I was finally diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder at the age of 53. My diagnosis has allowed me to understand my life; what has been harder is getting other people (including health professionals) to understand how challenging it is for me. If there were more stories published that went beyond accounts of obsessional collecting behaviours or discussing whether people make eye contact, perhaps there could be a greater understanding of what autism can look like, informing experts on how to support people appropriately and how to categorise it. Louise King London

Having spent years working adjacent to mental health services, I have come across many people with “classic” autism. I remember when Asperger’s was dropped and “autism spectrum disorders” came into use, I initially mistook the “spectrum” as a continuum we are all on. I know I was wrong, but I wonder if this framework holds a broader social truth – a spectrum with classic autistic people at the far end, Asperger’s a little way along and most people between the middle and the opposite end.

I’m not autistic, but I’m socially uncomfortable. I can confidently present to an audience of hundreds and my grasp of language is good – but I hate using the phone, don’t like meeting people, avoid parties and need my own space a lot. I think that makes me an introvert, but that’s another term that has been adopted as an “identity” rather than a defined classification. As psychiatrists and psychologists taught me, most diagnoses are essentially descriptions; if a description sounds like you, is long-lasting and is a significant problem for your functioning, then you get that label. What this idea misses is that almost everyone finds some aspects of life functionally difficult.

Rather than continuously expanding clinical classifications to grant people validity, perhaps we should focus on creating a society where anyone (or their advocates) can declare what they struggle with, and have our communities and services respond with appropriate flexibility and understanding. Salli Ward Market Harborough, Leicestershire

John Harris quotes Uta Frith calling masking “completely unfalsifiable”, then moves on as if no one had tried to falsify it.

People have. Will Mandy’s group at University College London built the standard masking questionnaire and has spent years publishing its weaknesses, which is what good science looks like. Meng-Chuan Lai and colleagues measured masking by comparing how autistic adults present in a clinical interview with how they perform on social-cognition tests, a gap no one can produce simply by saying they mask.

At Birkbeck, University of London, Jagdeep Wadhwa-Brown is now recording neural activity in autistic adults during social tasks, alongside their own accounts of masking. The study is at an early stage, but it is exactly the kind of test Frith says cannot be done. The neuroscientist Francesca Happé has described watching the mask slip in a tired house guest. That is an observation, not a feeling.

Between us, every week we assess people who present with what is sometimes called “internalised” autism: people who make eye contact, hold down demanding jobs and have spent decades being told, like Abigail Stow (who featured in Harris’s article), that they “can’t possibly be autistic”. The measures need work, and the researchers say so. But “the measure needs work” and “the phenomenon does not exist” are different claims, and only one was put to readers. Dr Louise Legg Counselling psychologist, London Dr Emma Bede Clinical psychologist, London

Israel’s election and self-definition invite questions

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:38:52 GMT

Dr Richard Skues responds to an article by Jonathan Freedland in which he says the opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties

Jonathan Freedland is surely right that the Israeli political parties opposed to Benjamin Netanyahu should make common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens (This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules, 30 October).

He is also right to be pessimistic, recognising that “Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state”.

Yet Freedland also points to the very reason why this is unlikely to change: “it demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state”.

Freedland’s clarity on these matters surely invites a further question: might Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state – in other words, Zionism – lie at the very heart of the discrimination and inequality that have persisted since the state’s founding? Might it not also be fundamental to the perilous situation in which Israel now finds itself, and to the increasingly bleak prospects for its future? This, indeed, is a position held by many Jews who reject Zionism.

Netanyahu’s domination of Israeli politics in recent years is no accident, any more than is the failure of Israeli society more broadly to rein in his excesses. Both have deep historical, cultural and ideological roots, and they go hand-in-hand with the discrimination and inequality that Freedland describes. These are issues that must be confronted seriously by anyone who wishes to see an end to the continuing bloodshed and avert the prospect of Israel’s pariah status and gradual implosion. Dr Richard Skues London

Like the Danes, we need to pay for the society we want

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:37:15 GMT

Karin Blak responds to an article about children’s homes in crisis and what can be learned from the Danish system

As a Dane who went through Danish children’s services, and later worked in Sure Start centres as a family therapist in England, I found your article particularly resonant (English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?, 1 November). Adopting similar care here requires two changes: our attitude to paying tax and our electoral system.

Denmark’s basic national income-tax rate and average municipal income-tax rate together amount to about 37%, almost twice England’s 20% basic rate. Although allowances and other contributions make this an imperfect comparison, we need to acknowledge Danes’ willingness to pay for the quality of services that underpin a stable society. Tax-funded services benefit us at every level of society, including care we hope neither we nor our families will ever need.

But funding alone is not enough. Working in Sure Start centres, I saw the gradual dismantling of a service that should have been the pride of the country. Children’s services need sustained investment, experienced staff and policies that last beyond the next election. When successive governments dismantle or redirect their predecessors’ work, vulnerable children bear the consequences.

Denmark’s proportional electoral system requires parties to work together. I believe proportional representation at Westminster would help us build the broader agreements needed to sustain social provision through changes of government. It would not guarantee good care, but it would help improvements endure.

We need the willingness to pay for the society we want, and a political system that encourages parties to take responsibility for its future together. Children who have already experienced instability and neglect deserve that much. Karin Blak Market Harborough, Leicestershire

John Smedley will always be in vogue

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:36:12 GMT

Tim Heavisides recalls his fondness for the historic fashion firm and his enduring attachment to a black jumper

Re your report (Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market, 1 November), I was fortunate to grow up with a mum who was interested in good quality clothes and fashion, and who, when I was 17, bought me a black rollneck top. Think Roger Moore. Think Illya Kuryakin (The Man from U. N. C. L. E.). Think of me in the lower sixth at a rural grammar school in Wiltshire, who missed going to the Bath blues festival at Shepton Mallet in 1970. I also missed the Isle of Wight ferry once.

I recall going on a school trip to see the film Kanał by the Polish director Andrzej Wajda. There were girls on the coach from the girls’ high school. Shock horror. What should I wear? My black polo top, of course. It would be perfect with my tweed sports jacket. And then Mum uttered those immortal words: “It’s made by John Smedley. You can wear it with anything.”

She was right. She had good taste and she wanted me to have good taste. So thanks, Mum, and thanks John Smedley (and Bill Nighy). Tim Heavisides Church Stretton, Shropshire

Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:12:41 GMT

There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows

“Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.

But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.

New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.

So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.

Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.

The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.

The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.

But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.

In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.

The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.

The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.

This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect, which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.

Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.

This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.

Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.

‘He left the world in ruins’: the author who defied the Taliban and burning tyres to tell Alexander the Great’s epic story

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:11:08 GMT

He is the most powerful ruler ever – and his first biographer was crucified. What drew Edmund Richardson, winner of the £50,000 Baillie Gifford prize, to his short tumultuous life?

He was the most powerful man in the world but he was brought down by one battle too many after a decade at the top. The story of Alexander the Great might be more than 2,000 years old, but it seems timely that a new biography of the ancient ruler won the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction just as President Trump took a battering in the US midterms. “This is a moment,” says its author Edmund Richardson, “where people are finding that there are limits to what unlimited wealth and power can do, and that humanity catches up with you, whether you like it or not. Alexander wants to transform the world – and he leaves it in ruins.”

Wearing a purple velvet jacket, purple scarf and matching socks, with a high forehead and corona of auburn curls, Richardson himself might have stepped out of an earlier age. It is hard to imagine anyone less like history’s favourite mob boss than this softly spoken professor of classics. We are having coffee at the offices of the PR company for the Baillie Gifford prize, the view of the City of London skyline from the floor to ceiling windows a reminder of 21st-century power and economics.

It would, we agree, have made the perfect backdrop for an interview with Patrick Radden Keefe, a previous winner of the £50,000 Baillie Gifford prize and the favourite this year for London Falling, a forensic investigation into the death of a teenager who falls from one of the city’s luxury skyscrapers. “I would never, ever have imagined this,” Richardson says, almost in a whisper. “I am fully expecting someone to tap me on the shoulder and say, ‘I’m so sorry, there’s been a terrible mistake, Mr Radden Keefe is waiting. You can take a coffee as you go.’”

Richardson’s exhilarating, exhaustively researched Alexander: God, King, Man is another triumph for the classics in a year when Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey stormed the box office (Alexander liked to sleep with a copy of Homer under his pillow, apparently). Like many, Richardson first encountered the figure in the pages of Alexander, Mary Renault’s 1969 fictional trilogy, when he was a boy. Critics have described his book as “part novel, part history”.

Richardson doesn’t just make the ruler of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon flesh and blood for a new generation. He also makes bold claims for his subject. “Alexander reshaped reality more profoundly than almost anyone else in history,” he writes. His expansionist campaigns might have been brutal, even by ancient standards, with his empire unravelling before his death, but for Richardson its true legacy is in the “ripple effects” that we still feel today. “It’s in the ways that Babylonian science turns up in Greece, that Greek art turns up on the borders of the Indus, that Egyptian scholarship finds its way into how we understand Homer. It’s in the world becoming far more connected.” He was antiquity’s answer to the internet.

“Alexander’s story is on this impossible scale,” he says. “This is someone who is capable of extraordinary violence and cruelty, extraordinary kindness and love.” Richardson describes the book as a “beautiful monster” to write. From Plutarch to Horrible Histories, there have been countless takes on Alexander’s story: the boy from the Macedon hills, who became king aged 20 in 336BC after his father was assassinated; marched his army into the heart of the Persian empire; had conquered much of the known world by the time he was 30, killing 1% of the population along the way; and who died “brokenhearted” in Babylon aged 32.

“Up until this book,” says Richardson, “my thing has always been writing stuff that no one reads about people no one has heard of. That’s my happy place!” His previous book, Alexandria: The Quest for the Lost City, was a biography of 19th-century archaeologist Charles Masson. But when his editor suggested he write about Alexander himself, he was horrified. “The idea of coming up against Alexander, and all of these thousands of versions of his story written by some of the people I admire the most in the world – absolute terror!”

Richardson, however, wanted to discover the real Alexander, before he became “great”. His search took him on his own decade-long adventure from the storage rooms of the British Museum in London to the catacombs of Egypt and the foothills of the Himalayas. Computer simulation and new discoveries gave him access to evidence and contemporary sources unavailable to earlier historians. But his travels back in time were interrupted by modern-day unrest. “There was a short encounter with a barricade of burning tyres,” he says, referring to a protest he stumbled upon in Cairo, while his visit to Afghanistan was abandoned after the Taliban ransacked his hotel.

“Terrible things tend to happen to people who take up papyrus or laptop to write the Alexander story,” he says. The first, Callisthenes, Aristotle’s great nephew, was crucified, according to some sources. “So for me, there was a sense of the story being something that consumes people. I felt my own fallibility as a writer, as a historian, vividly.” He also had to confront his own mortality.

Around three years ago, Richardson was diagnosed with cancer. He first had a melanoma as a teenager and “they’ve been back a couple of times since”. At this point, he was barely 40. “I was writing this book not knowing if I would be around when it was out in the world,” he says. He wasn’t even sure if he would finish it. His universe narrowed to the fluorescent lights and corridors of hospital. Writing became his way of travelling – “but to the world of ideas. The book, and the people I loved, reminded me that there was a version of myself that was less frightening.”

Although he was given the all clear, this time last year he was back in hospital after he collapsed, probably due to all the stress. When he came round the next day, two patients on his ward were handcuffed to police officers. “And there was me with my laptop and my hieroglyphs,” he laughs. It was a turning point, though. He had been struggling with the ending (“Obviously everyone dies and everything goes wrong”) but he returned to his “tangled” manuscript with “a feeling of trying to find a ray of hope where the light seemed to have gone out”.

Richardson, now 44, grew up in Bristol, the only child of two academics. His father, an American, is a mathematician; his mother, who is part-English and part-Irish, is an art historian. There were “layers upon layers” of books in the house. He went to a Bristol grammar school, where he thought he might follow his father into maths, but he couldn’t resist the ancient world.

“Obsessions are my weakness,” he says. “Even when I was a kid, I would find myself getting lost in stories and falling down rabbit holes.” He made it to Cambridge to study classics, where he was taught by Mary Beard. On a postdoctoral fellowship to Princeton, he met his fiancee, “the love of my life”, the journalist and writer Yepoka Yeebo, who was studying at Columbia. They lived together in New York, before returning to London. “If there is good in what I write, it is her,” he whispers. “She makes me see the world entire, the wonder of things.”

His next subject – although his editor doesn’t know it yet – is the British Egyptologist Flinders Petrie. “I’m going back to books about people no one has ever heard of,” he says. “It’s the story of an archaeologist who, in the deserts of Egypt in 1888, thinks that he’s come up with a plan to defeat death.”

More immediately, he’s off to the BBC next, to talk more about Alexander. “It’s very strange as an academic to find people actually wanting to listen to what you say,” he jokes. “I feel so, so honoured.” Why does he think there is such interest the ancient world today? “It’s not just a story about the distant past,” he says. “We work with fragments, with ghosts, with things that have almost vanished – but that also lets us make these stories our own. There’s no such thing as the definitive book about Alexander. You know that there will be so many books after yours.”

How does he feel about his 10-year battle with Alexander ending in victory? “There have been some difficult times,” he admits. “It’s lovely to come out of that and into light.”

Alexander: God, King, Man by Edmund Richardson is published by Bloomsbury (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply

US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:09:18 GMT

After Thursday’s share price plunge on Wall Street, could the volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections.

This is not the first time stock markets have wobbled in recent months due to concerns over a tech bubble. But could this volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Shares on Wall Street plunged on Thursday, in a rout driven by AI and technology stocks that extended to Asia and Europe on Friday. US markets rebounded after trading reopened in New York, but failed to recover all of the lost ground amid lingering concerns of a relapse in selling pressure.

More than $3.2tn (£2.4tn) was wiped from the value of the US stock market on Thursday – bigger than the annual output of the Canadian economy – after the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell by 5.5% and the blue-chip S&P 500 fell by 4.4%.

After months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies – amid fears of tinderbox conditions in the world economy fuelled by the Iran war and concerns that the tech bubble could burst – the trigger for the sell-off has been attributed to the Democrats’ sweeping US midterm election victory.

Investors are predicting that a Democrat-controlled Congress could lead to tighter control of AI and datacentre construction – slowing development in one of the engines of global economic growth and corporate earnings on the stock market.

Challenging billionaire power and calling out Wall Street and big tech were the rallying cries of many Democrats in the midterm elections. Moratoriums on datacentre construction were effectively on the ballot in several states amid growing public opposition to the building of vast, resource-hungry facilities.

Highlighting the stakes, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO, Elon Musk, set a record for election spending after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans – and moved his personal residence to Texas, the leading state for datacentre construction. After the midterms shares in both his companies fell sharply.

Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for some time, given the astronomical rise in tech company valuations, which some analysts said had become increasingly detached from reality.

One measure of whether a market is overvalued, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (Cape) ratio, had risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued relative to profits.

Highlighting the disconnect, shares in Alphabet, the Google parent company, plunged last week after it reported lower than expected profits, wiping more than $500bn from its value.

Some form of a check on progress was also likely, amid a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries over AI safety. Opinion polls show most Americans are opposed to US datacentre construction, while governments around the world have encouraged citizens to stockpile for multiple eventualities including cyber-attacks.

Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “It is too easy to say that the Democrats will be bad for datacentres.

“Yes, there will be a pause in the buildout and delay in approvals, but if you go off the words of the new Texas governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, they are likely to be more pragmatic and ensure resources are more fairly allocated.”

What happens to the share prices of the US tech giants has enormous consequences for savers worldwide.

The “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – account for more than a third of the S&P 500, meaning that funds that track this index are directly tied to their performance.

AI has been a big growth driver, with the tech boom helping to soften the hit to the world economy from the war in the Middle East.

The prospect of a sustained tech sell-off could prove a big setback, in a blow to countries that have pinned their hopes on the AI revolution creating jobs and generating a productivity boost to overcome years of relative economic stagnation.

In response to the inflation shock from the Iran war, central banks around the world have been raising interest rates. However, an economic slowdown could force a rethink amid the risk of stagflation, when weak growth is accompanied by fast-rising consumer prices.

Financial markets are prone to volatile swings and investors are divided about whether things will get worse from here. Many were, however, worried a big crash was overdue – and when investors begin to lose confidence, it can become self-reinforcing.

Barringer said: “A virtuous circle could quickly turn into a vicious one, and they [investors] must now ride it out until the direction of travel becomes clearer.”

For some, the latest tech rout represents a reset rather than a lasting downturn. Demand for AI and semiconductors will not vanish overnight: new tools will continue to be launched, and datacentres will be built.

Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said the AI investment cycle should remain intact, despite the latest “market indigestion”.

“We do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” he added.
