Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:48:36 GMT

Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come

European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.

Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”

However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose in early trading, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.8% by early afternoon in New York and the Nasdaq by 1.6% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.

That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”

However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.

The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”

Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.

Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.

Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:28:18 GMT

Some relatives of British citizens say they feel left behind, but announcement has brought relief to many care workers

“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.

Williams, 39, was months from qualifying for indefinite leave to remain after 10 years in the UK. But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood’s “earned settlement” plans.

Under pressure from Labour MPs and unions, the home secretary this week offered qualifying care workers a five-year settlement route. But others, among them partners and former partners of British citizens, face continued uncertainty.

Williams, a supermarket worker from London, married a British man in her native Jamaica and joined him in the UK in 2016. Her daughter, now 18, is British. During the Covid crisis, her marriage broke down, leaving them homeless while Williams was on a family life visa.

Migrants with no recourse to public funds can have that restriction lifted in cases of hardship, as Williams did. Housing benefit transformed her life without affecting her settlement prospects at the time.

Last year, Mahmood proposed adding up to 10 years to the settlement qualifying period for benefit claimants. This week she said applicants must have spent five continuous years without relying on benefits.

While Mahmood says family members of British citizens will retain existing settlement pathways, how that protection applies to people whose marriages have broken down or who claimed benefits remains unclear.

“We were never told this would happen, and never would have taken the help if we did, even though my past situation was very grim,” Williams said. “I was due to qualify in a couple of months – now it could be another 10 years.”

Research has found most people on the existing “10-year route”, which Williams is on, are Asian or Black. Williams added: “It’s a racist policy – and it’s like every other year they come up with something that makes you feel further hopeless.”

Ashley, a civil servant from Sheffield who asked to use a pseudonym, arrived from the US in 2017 and moved from student and graduate visas to a spouse visa after marrying a British man in 2025. She expected to qualify in 2027 under the 10-year long-residence route, which the government plans to end. With transitional arrangements unclear, she fears waiting until 2030, by which time she estimates she will have spent £25,000 on visa and healthcare charges.

“I’m one of the privileged immigrants – from a white English-speaking country, I have a PhD. I’m married to a British citizen. And it is still so unbelievably hard,” she said.

Mahmood’s announcement brought relief to many care workers. Under the revised plans, those who entered the route before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year can qualify after five years, rather than the 15 originally proposed. Others face another five-year visa before settlement.

Rasika Samarasinghe, who arrived from Sri Lanka in October 2022 and earns just over £25,000 caring for elderly people, is planning a double celebration. As well as the settlement change, the Home Office has reversed its refusal to let his wife, a teaching assistant, and their three children, aged 12, nine and eight, remain in the UK as his dependants.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

After sending the family “go home” letters, the Home Office told them the refusal should be disregarded. The Guardian understands similar decisions affecting other care workers’ families have also been reversed.

“I felt so shocked and hopeless when the Home Office said my wife and children could no longer stay here,” Samarasinghe said. “The children are delighted they can stay at school with their friends. Now we can plan our future. I feel free now.” His wife is organising a party for their church friends and everyone who supported them.

The government began restricting care workers’ family visas after the Home Office estimated in 2023 that about 120,000 dependants had joined 100,000 care worker applicants.

Care workers have been barred from bringing family since March 2024, and overseas recruitment was banned from July 2025; Samarasinghe’s family arrived before both. A spokesperson for the Home Office said it did not routinely comment on individual cases, but that applications initially rejected could be approved after a review.

Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors welcomed the Home Office’s U-turn, saying: “This is a hugely significant and positive outcome. This family came to the United Kingdom lawfully … We are delighted that this family can now move forward together with renewed hope, security and peace of mind.”

Amenzei Ogiemwonyia, a care worker who campaigned with the Unison union, said: “We organised and refused to be silent, and that’s what the Fairer Visa Campaign was all about: standing up to the rightwing press, lies, propaganda and politics. Some of us are elated – but we still need to read the fine print.”

Campaigners remain concerned. Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol, the chief executive of the Work Rights Centre, called the response, apart from the care-worker concessions, “bitterly disappointing”, and said it was “deeply unfair” that some workers who came expecting a five-year route would now wait 10 years. The Home Office estimates that about 500,000 people will have to wait longer than five years for settlement, which officials say will save billions from the welfare bill.

‘It’s in our blood’: Lebanon, Ukraine and Syria rugby league teams fly the flag despite horrors of war at home

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:12:50 GMT

Players from war-torn countries say they are determined to ‘give people hope’, ‘put the country on the map’ and ‘wear the badge with honour’

By No Helmets Required

There are many reasons for a country to not play rugby league. Being at war does not seem to be one of them. Last Sunday, a few miles apart in Sydney, Syria and Lebanon played international fixtures on contrasting stages. Syria hosted a series of friendlies at the humble home of Bankstown Bulls, before Lebanon played an all-time World Cup classic against France in a frenzied CommBank Stadium. A few days earlier, Ukraine had played a crucial European Championship match in Belgrade.

Lebanon beat France after a wild finish, suggesting they are still among the top eight teams in the world, even if their ranking is far lower due to their inactivity since the last World Cup. The country has been torn apart by the war in the Middle East. “Our last game together was in England in 2022,” said prop Jalal Bazzaz, who played in all three of Lebanon’s matches at the World Cup. “So our aim was just to be good each week. We talked about giving back to where we come from, our roots. It’s in our blood. To put on that jersey, represent my country and put Lebanon on the world stage – it gives people something to smile about, a bit of hope.

“My father came to Australia when he was 11. We grew up in a Lebanese household: the food, the music, you name it. My grandparents could only speak Arabic. My father speaks fluent Arabic. I’ve been around it my whole life. A lot of the boys speak Arabic.” As does Michael Cheika, whose spell as Lebanon head coach ended in extraordinary fashion last Sunday.

Back home, Lebanese sports fans have followed the country’s rare appearance on a world stage. “It’s on TV there,” said Bazzaz. “My mum is in regular contact with people in Lebanon and they loved it. They reckon their whole place is involved. To be able to do that, it’s a blessing, putting Lebanon on the map.”

Lebanon were missing Mitchell Moses, Adam Doueihi and other NRL players through injury, but that provided opportunities for others. Over the past fortnight, the Canterbury Bulldogs player Alex Conti has become a star. The previously uncapped 20-year-old made a name for himself in the group stage, conducting a head to head with France star Arthur Mourgue on Sunday up there with Kalyn Ponga v Reece Walsh in the NRL Grand Final.

Conti was partnered by St George youngster Shadi Hammoud. “I don’t even know what club he plays for,” admitted Chieka after his final game in charge. Hammoud was overcome by the experience: “I wear the Cedar on my chest with honour. I’m representing my family and everyone who moved over to Australia to give us a better life. It’s a little way to repay them for that.”

Having lost their IRL full-member status, Lebanon are unlikely to be at the 2030 World Cup. The domestic scene stopped after the Beirut port explosion in 2020 and is only starting back up now. Despite the ongoing violence, there has been a rugby nines tournament and a referees course at the Lebanese American University in Beirut.

Lebanon will not meet the IRL’s deadline of March 2027 for consideration for the 2030 qualifiers unless the goalposts are moved. Anything is possible given the impact their team and fans had on this World Cup. “It’s quite upsetting,” says Bazzaz. “All these younger guys coming through can’t experience what I’ve experienced the last two World Cups. That’s quite sad, but hopefully we can get back on track.”

Lebanon will continue developing talent in the Heritage RL network, where more than a dozen countries play XIII and nines, among them close neighbours Syria. Many players are eligible for both Syria and Lebanon; UN figures suggest nearly seven million displaced Syrians have fled the country in the 15 years of civil war, with more than a million refugees settling in Lebanon.

Miraculously, Syria are fielding men’s, women’s, boys and girls teams at several age groups in Australia. Four years ago they did not exist. “Our first training session, we had two players there – now we are getting over 100,” says Abdul Nabhan, the president of Syria Rugby League. “Players are coming from all around Sydney and from Central Coast. They see this opportunity to play for Syria and they get here. We have Syrian players in France contacting us, but we’re not in a position to bring them across yet.

“We have kids from 15s up, as well as a girl’s team and women’s. The majority have Syrian grandparents but some have parents too. We have some girls who are close to NRLW and we have boys in New South Wales Cup. Our relationship with Lebanon is great. They’ve been through what we’re going through now.”

Nabhan is working towards getting observer member status with the IRL, which is the first step towards being able to play official internationals. His biggest achievement will be getting rugby league established in war-ravaged Syria itself. The sport has no history in the country but a new competition has been established and universities are signing up to compete. “They’ve signed up to play a local competition, but obviously it’s taking longer because of what’s happening,” says Nabhan.

“It’s not very stable. Rugby union is very big there and we have some players going across to Syria this week to play in the Asia Cup. But, because rugby league is so big in Australia, we are getting there. There’s been a lot of traction the last few months. For us to have done what we’ve done in four years is incredible.”

While watching Syria’s men in action at Bankstown, I chatted to a local man of Syrian heritage whose nephew was playing on the wing. “The whole thing – representing your country, your family, your people – it’s beautiful,” he says. The result was far from beautiful. Syria conceded three tries in the first eight minutes and were beaten 36-6 by the Ozzy Cooks, a team of local Cook Islanders. There was a lot of swearing under the sticks and shouts in Arabic float across the field. Nabhan’s wife, Amanda, is the team’s manager, and their daughter, who has played for Lebanon’s women’s team, is also on the touchline helping out. It’s a family affair.

Running rugby league teams and competitions in war zones is not impossible. Ukraine have played regularly in recent years and were up to 10th in the world rankings before a surprise defeat by the Netherlands in Belgrade last month cost them the Euro B title. They have beaten Greece, Italy, the Netherlands and Czechia since Putin’s tanks rolled over the border.

Ongoing nightmares in Lebanon, Syria and Ukraine ensure that more people will be displaced and many will land in rugby league-playing communities. “My dad came over in the 1980s and people are still coming,” said Bazzaz. “They’ve been through hell and back over there. So we’ll have a lot of more coming through.”

Whirlwhind year from Wolverhampton to Hong Kong for Leger heroine Osborne

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:09:43 GMT

Classic success resulted in contract to ride at high-profile meeting for outstanding female jockey

Saffie Osborne’s year began with a ride on a 150-1 chance in a race worth £7,000 at Wolverhampton on 6 January, when she trailed in last of the seven runners. Its final chapter will open on Sunday in the decidedly glitzier surroundings of Sha Tin racecourse in Hong Kong, where Osborne has 10 rides on an 11-race card, and the 10 months in between have been transformational for the 24-year-old jockey.

A first top-10 finish in the Flat jockeys’ championship was the reward for Osborne’s consistency throughout the May-to-October title race, but the undoubted highlight was her victory on Highwayman victory in the St Leger in September. It was Osborne’s first Group One win, and also the first for a female jockey in a British Classic.

It was a historic success that surely contributed to the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s decision to offer Osborne a six-week pre-Christmas riding contract a couple of weeks later.

Hong Kong’s punters, meanwhile, may be drawn to another key feature of her 2026 season: the consistency with which Osborne’s mounts have outperformed their odds. Her 85 wins from 600 rides since from the start of 2026 returned a level-stakes profit of £31.81, while during the six-month championship race, the profit to a £1 stake was just under £100. In a racing hotbed that is focused entirely on betting, anything even close to that level of success would make Osborne an immediate star.

Hong Kong’s racing industry does not have a breeding industry attached. Instead, its runners are imported from around the world, and 99% are geldings, which are easier to train, show more consistent form and tend to enjoy longer careers than “entire” male horses. Around 97% of its races, meanwhile, are handicaps, with full fields of either 12 or 14 runners (and a couple of reserves to ensure that any late gaps are filled).

Osborne will make her riding debut at Sha Tin, which stages racing every Sunday during the season, but had her first experience of Hong Kong’s famously intense racecourse atmosphere at Happy Valley on Wednesday evening. “It’s really cool to be able to experience it for the first time,” Osborne said this week. “Having watched it on television so much, being able to see it in person was really surreal. It’s an amazing atmosphere and a really unique track, and to be in the middle of such a vibrant city was very cool.”

While Sha Tin is a broad, galloping track with sweeping turns that suits a long-striding horse, Happy Valley is a famously compact venue surrounded by skyscrapers, with tight turns and a high premium on getting a good early position. “Every place you go, races are run slightly differently, and I think it’s just about adapting quickly,” Osborne says. “There’s such different, unique tracks in England and they all have their quirks and different ways of riding them. So you have to learn quickly, and I think that’s something that will stand me in good stead here.”

Such is the popularity of racing in Hong Kong that would-be owners need to join a waiting list, while 88 meetings over the course of last season generated $HK143bn (£13.5bn) in Tote betting turnover and a gross profit – after returning around 86% to the winners – of $HK20bn (£1.9bn).

“I was maybe slightly shocked that I had 10 rides [on Sunday], but very excited,” Osborne said. “I’ve got a lot of homework to do before Sunday, but it’s also really nice to pick up a ride in the feature race [on Silvery Breeze in the £400k Group Three Sa Sa Ladies’ Purse Handicap]. Being so light, I can do bottom weight [of 8st 3lb], and that’s something that’s helped me a lot in the UK and hopefully it can help me here.”

Hollie Doyle and Rossa Ryan will be two familiar faces riding alongside Osborne over the next few weeks, while Richard Kingscote, Harry Bentley and Andrea Atzeni are among former leading riders in Britain that are now based in Hong Kong full-time. Her most formidable rival, though, will be Australia’s Zac Purton, who finished well clear in last year’s standings to claim his ninth championship, ahead of Hugh Bowman, Atzeni and Karis Teetan.

“Obviously, I’d love to ride as many winners as possible, but I know how hard it is to ride winners here,” Osborne says. “I think every place you go, you learn different things, and it furthers your skills as a jockey. And only being 24 and [in] my sixth year riding, you’re still trying to learn as much as possible. [Hong Kong] has such world-class jockeys, so you just pick up things off of them.”

The November Handicap has not had a dual winner in its 150-year history, but both Lord Melbourne and Castle Cove (3.25), the winners in the past two seasons, are back for another crack at Doncaster on Saturday and William Haggas’s gelding is a decent bet at around 9-1 to register a small piece of racing history.

Neither horse has run since last year’s renewal, when Castle Cove was an easy four-and-a-quarter length winner with Lord Melbourne only sixth.

Castle Cove is 8lb higher in the weights this time around but won with a great deal to spare 12 months ago and has a hold-up running style that is well suited to Doncaster’s long home straight.

Aintree 1.15 Paul Nicholls’s string is in excellent form and while Sans Bruit was winless last season, he resumes here after a wind op and 9lb below his last winning mark.

Aintree 1.45 Mydaddypaddy was a fine third in the Supreme Novice Hurdle at Cheltenham and should confirm himself a significant Champion Hurdle contender here.

Doncaster 2.10 There is plenty of pace drawn high to give Coul Angel a tow into the race and he looks ready for this step up to Listed company after two wins in ultra-competitive handicaps.

Aintree 2.25 A luckless run when favourite for the two-and-a-half mile novice at Cheltenham in March in the only blip on No Drama This End’s record and he promises to be as good, if not better, over fences.

‘He’s manipulating its power’: why did Russell Brand convert to Christianity?

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:00:46 GMT

Sincere or self-serving, the disgraced comedian’s case shows how the church became a culture war frontier

The women whom Russell Brand raped and sexually assaulted have for weeks endured the ordeal of a heavily publicised trial. Throughout, Brand held online prayer meetings with followers. Does he feel Christian sympathy for those women?

Only Brand, in the deepest recesses of his conscience, can know.

The answer would be the best indicator of whether the disgraced comic, actor and born-again Christian has worn his newfound faith as a cloak in an effort to deflect and distract from the seriousness of the allegations against him. Or whether his conversion is a profound and sincere one – a spiritual crutch he may need in the coming years.

Whatever the truth, Brand’s case demonstrates how Christianity has become a frontier in the culture wars along which battle lines are now drawn on all kinds of ethical, political and even legal issues.

It is not hard to see why Brand’s embrace of Christ has raised suspicion. His reputation for most of his career has been one of a hell-raiser, and even when spirituality did call, it was the eastern traditions of Buddhism and the Hare Krishna movement that first caught his eye.

Now, latterly dedicated to the teachings of Christ, his very visible displays of devotion have at times seemed farcical.

When Brand was interviewed by Piers Morgan in April, one moment went viral: Brand was asked to quote from a Bible that he was carrying with him – the same he took to the dock in Southwark crown court. When Morgan asked Brand to find relevant passages he had been reading, Brand struggled, helplessly turning pages for more than a minute.

Achieving familiarity with scripture is a lifelong Christian journey. But for sceptics, the moment was compelling proof of a calculated rebrand rather than a spiritual rebirth.

Having spent years as a standup comic, Ravi Holy, the vicar of Trinity Benefice, Folkestone, had long heard rumours of Brand’s predatory behaviour and learned of him mixing in evangelical circles years before the celebrity went public.

Holy said: “There’s that famous verse where Paul says there are people who preach Christ out of true motives, and some out of vain ambition, but it doesn’t matter as long as Christ is preached. I could imagine some saying that about Brand, but I don’t see it like that. I’m interested in the motives of the person.”

Dr Maria Power, an expert in Christian nationalism at the University of Oxford, said: “I can’t really judge whether [Brand] has had a personal conversion, certainly the way he’s gone about it has been very performative: his [2024] baptism in the Thames was very much in the style you would expect from this sort of appropriation of Christianity.

“I’m not saying Russell Brand is part of a Christian nationalist movement, but he’s certainly manipulating its power to try and gain support for himself.”

That Christian nationalism is important context. In the US, a wave of Trump-era populist plutocrats, conspiracy theorists, manosphere influencers and rightwing populists have used Christianity to shore up personal their brands and launder often racist and misogynistic narratives.

Meanwhile, well-intentioned podcasters have given Christian faith a new relevance to people seeking meaning in an uncertain world; a time when Pope Leo XIV and the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, articulate a theology of social justice.

In the UK, the country’s wealthiest Anglican church, Holy Trinity Brompton, known widely as HTB, and its Alpha courses have introduced millions of people to basic Christian tenets.

HTB’s evangelism shaped the spiritual life of Justin Welby before his tenure as archbishop of Canterbury blended liberal and evangelical theological positions.

The Old Etonian adventurer Bear Grylls, who assisted with Brand’s Thames baptism, has praised HTB as “full of love and acceptance”. Paul Marshall, the billionaire owner of the Spectator and co-owner of GB News, has given HTB and the Church Revitalisation Trust (CRT) £13m via his Sequoia Trust.

The image of Christian nationalism in the UK – Tommy Robinson supporters cosplaying as crusaders – is a world away from HTB’s Knightsbridge pews.

Power sees the UK iteration of Christian nationalism as the result of well-funded attempts by wealthy evangelicals and “post-liberal” ideologues to merge Christian social thought with politics – for the sake of “power” rather than a grassroots, working-class movement.

She says Christian nationalism has an 800-year European history, encompassing leaders from King Henry VIII to the Portuguese dictator António de Oliveira Salazar, 19th-century antisemitism and anti-Catholicism, and Ireland’s “near-theocratic” history.

In its current form, she adds, it appeals to a “search for meaning” in an age of insecurity.

Against this backdrop, Brand presents as a dissident martyr to his audience – who see themselves as truth-seekers – while gaining acceptance among some prominent Christians as a celebrity convert.

Among them are those who hope his understanding of Christianity will evolve, just as they hope the adjacent movement of Christian nationalism will give way to an authentic understanding of the gospel that will change society for the better.

Arun Arora, the bishop of Kirkstall, has been outspoken about the threat of Christian nationalists appropriating Christian symbolism to further nativist authoritarianism.

But he warns against “making a window into men’s souls”, adding that he rejoices when people come to faith, “whoever they are”.

“It’s not unusual for people to discover faith during times of personal crisis,” he said. “In that way, celebrities are no different from the rest of us. None of us are beyond redemption.

“I appreciate people will view the outward religiosity of those such as Russell Brand or Stephen Yaxley-Lennon [the real name of Tommy Robinson] with a degree of cynicism, but there is always a possibility for faith to be discovered at times of testing.”

For Nick Spencer, a senior fellow at the Christian thinktank Theos, controversial converts highlight the tension between justice and mercy.

He said: “On the one hand, if Brand says: ‘I was deeply immoral in my attitude to women and sex and I repent as a Christian,’ that’s great. But the court case is not about him being immoral. It’s about him raping people, it’s about him doing something illegal.

“There is this ongoing tension, because you want to affirm a sense of grace, a sense of forgiveness, of repentance and a new life, without ignoring the claims of justice.”

The Rev Holy hopes that if Brand’s conversion is genuine, it makes him “face up to what he put those women through”, publicly apologise and confess.

He added: “I believe in redemption – assuming there’s genuine repentance – but I don’t particularly see that here.

“People, might go: ‘Well, I thought you believed in forgiveness.’ I do, but that doesn’t mean if someone’s committed serious crimes, and then they become a Christian, that you go: ‘Oh well, fair enough.’”

What causes back pain? The surprising triggers, from stress to sitting up straight – and what you can do about it

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:00:45 GMT

Are you one of 600 million people with lower back pain? Osteopaths identify the most common causes – and remedies

Was jet-washing the patio the straw that broke the camel’s – and your – back? That’s a possibility, but experts say the actual causes of back pain may surprise you – and it’s a bigger issue than most may realise. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that lower back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, with cases projected to rise to more than 800 million by 2050, largely as populations grow and age. Here, clinicians reveal some of the unexpected causes, and how to avoid them.

“It’s actually very common to wake up with back pain without having sustained an injury,” says Hannah Whitcombe, an osteopath and naturopath. But in most cases, the hardness or softness of your mattress won’t be to blame.

“People often overlook what they did the day before. An unusually active day can leave muscles and joints feeling sore the following morning, but the opposite can be true too – sitting at a desk or simply being less active,” she says. “So if you wake up with a painful back, don’t just look at the eight hours you spent in bed, think about the previous 16.”

Mindy Cairns, a musculoskeletal physiotherapist and clinical researcher, sees a seasonal pattern. “During summertime patients will say, ‘My back’s been much worse,’ and I respond with, ‘Well, what have you done?’” Some will have spent a fortnight in four different hotels with four different beds. Others, she says, “remember that they washed the patio for five hours the other day and haven’t deduced that this may be the reason for a flare”.

Both extremes – too active or too sedentary – can cause back pain. Antony Bush, a physiotherapist and author of The Back Fix, says office workers can be sitting for 12 hours a day once work, travel and Netflix in the evening are counted, “double what we know gives people back pain”. At the opposite extreme, repetitive loading, relevant for rowers or gymnasts, can be too much for the back. In Bush’s experience, half the cases of back pain have several contributing causes, suggesting it is best to look at the whole picture rather than a single trigger.

If you were told to sit up straight as a child, that advice may not have served you particularly well. Bush argues that a rigidly held but conventionally “good” posture can itself cause back pain, especially if this isn’t your natural resting position. London-based osteopath Anisha Joshi, who counts Rita Ora and Nick Grimshaw among her clients, still warns against a heavy slouch, but says “a very upright, fixed posture” can create tension in certain muscles, most often from sitting in one position for hours without a break.

“Posture is generally most helpful when it’s relaxed and adaptable, rather than forced or held in one ‘correct’ position for hours at a time,” Joshi says. A bent back isn’t necessarily a bad one as long as your movement varies throughout the day.

Bush goes further, arguing that posture myths extend into lifting. He says lifting with a rounded back, rather than the typical straight-back-bent-knees approach, isn’t as dangerous as it’s made out to be. “Contrary to everything you’ve heard, bending with a rounded back and straight legs is best.” Although reviews have found no evidence that one lifting technique prevents back pain, it’s safe to assume that lifting sensibly and building up strength matter more than one “correct” posture.

Pain is in the brain, but that doesn’t mean it’s imagined. In fact, stress – and particularly prolonged stress – can be a physical as well as an emotional trigger for back pain, says Kent-based osteopath Emma Hayward. She explains that stress causes contractions in the connective tissue of the back which, over time, can become fibrosed, or “sticky and tethered”, so the body moves less efficiently, and even minor strains can set off an acute episode. “I very rarely see low back pain in my clinic without the person also having experienced some significant life stressor at the same time. Stress essentially turns up the volume of pain,” she says.

Bush also believes mindset plays a huge part in the management of chronic pain. “We can tell who’s going to get chronic pain better from psychometric testing than we can from MRI,” he says. This informs a more multifactorial assessment of his patients’ physical and mental wellbeing when treating back pain.

An MRI can seem like a route to getting answers, but in most cases findings don’t correlate with the degree of pain felt, Bush says. Disc bulges and joint wear can all show up in people with no pain at all.

Bush describes a study in which two groups with back pain each had an MRI showing disc protrusions, tears and facet wear, which are all normal signs of ageing for their age group. One group was told this was within the normal range. The other received no explanation. “Pain increased in the group of people that went without a pat on the back,” Bush says, adding that their confidence and their psychological and physical measures dropped, too.

Neil O’Connell, a physiotherapist who helped develop the 2016 clinical guideline on lower back pain for the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) agrees that changes seen on scans largely reflect the natural process of ageing. “They’re like wrinkles on the face,” he says, which is why international clinical guidelines say imaging should not be routinely used for back pain.

Bush wants people with back pain to resist an “I’m broken” mindset. “Back pain is a part of the undulating highway of being a human being and you can’t speed up the rate of healing,” he says.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

You can, to an extent, blame your parents for your back pain, says Cairns, and not only through your genes. “If I had a pound for every time one of my patients said, ‘Oh, my mum had back pain, my dad had back pain, my aunt has got back pain,’” she says, though it’s rarely a familial disease. Conditions like osteoporosis or rheumatoid arthritis can run in families, but simple mechanical low back pain is often just “bad luck”, she adds, and it will affect more than 80% of us.

Cairns believes some pain could be attributed to inherited fear: “As a child, if you’ve had a parent say: ‘Oh, my back hurts again. Oh, my back, my back, my back,’ there is a degree to which this is learned behaviour, and you’re fearful every time your back twinges.” This isn’t a dismissal of pain, she stresses, but more that a “twinge” isn’t a sign of damage.

The good news, says osteopath Alison Durant, is that “we are adaptable. By understanding pain and learning to view it differently, you can reduce the nervous system’s protective response and improve function and confidence in movement,” she says. Depending on the person, this could mean addressing protective bracing during painful or avoided movement, working with the breath or discussing how to manage a painful flare-up with a clinician.

Back pain with no obvious cause can be symptomatic of another issue. Patients often come in with back pain that doesn’t look particularly mechanical, says Cairns, which can mean it’s down to an underlying problem such as endometriosis.

Endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the womb lining grows elsewhere in the body, most commonly affects the pelvis and abdomen, where pressure on nerve roots can mimic lower back pain. “Endometriosis is very common, yet can often be misdiagnosed,” says Cairns. “It can also involve the bowel and the ligaments linking the pelvis and spine, restricting movement and contributing to pain.”

In a physical examination, this won’t present like mechanical back pain. “That’s where my clinical suspicion comes in”, Cairns says. If she isn’t 99% certain of a mechanical cause, a referral for further investigation follows. “In collaboration with Endometriosis UK, we are looking at back pain associated with endometriosis through a nationwide survey,” says Cairns, who hopes the work will expand understanding of how the conditions interact.

All the experts agree that the body is more resilient than we expect. “You must make sure you’re not reducing the scope of your existence in the face of pain, but that you’re listening to it and pushing into it a little bit,” says Bush.

Our skeletons are hardy, and built to adapt to the load we place on them. So if the patio needs washing again in two years’ time and your back protests, don’t panic and try to keep moving.

In jailing Joshua Wong, China is telling the world it would crush every hope for democracy on its soil

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:53:05 GMT

My friend was due to be released next January. Under draconian security laws, his sentence has been extended by 10 years

Two years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter.

But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. The judge described Joshua and me as “two ringleaders or masterminds” urging foreign powers to impose sanctions and other hostile actions against the Chinese and Hong Kong governments. The judgment cited previous international advocacy work, media interviews, social media posts and the political activities of Demosistō, the youth-led democratic party we founded.

Much of the cited evidence predates the implementation of the national security law, even though the court insisted it was not being applied retrospectively. Before 2020, meeting with foreign parliamentarians, engaging with and speaking to international institutions, and advocating for measures against human rights abuses were ordinary campaign strategies. These were peaceful means through which we tried to hold those in power accountable. The campaigns raised the profile of Hong Kong’s protests and garnered substantial support; they were so effective that Beijing had to impose the national security law to curb them and impose extensive legal punishments.

There is a stark lack of evidence about Joshua’s actions. Prosecutors said that he conspired with campaigners including myself to ask foreign bodies to impose sanctions on China – relying on his sharing of Facebook posts written by me. But these posts did not directly call for sanctions – they made other appeals, including for digital forensic companies to terminate their cooperation with the Hong Kong police. There’s no evidence that Wong himself advocated for imposing any form of sanctions, or that he had any direct link to advocacy work outside Hong Kong. The court also accepted that no organisation or funding supported his activities after the law came into force.

Still, as flimsy as the evidence is, it’s enough to secure him a decade in jail. The crux of the trial is not legal; it’s political. It is clear that Beijing exercises sweeping control over Hong Kong’s legal and political systems. This can be seen in the tightening of the electoral system by introducing an Iranian-style vetting mechanism, in the jailing of peaceful political dissidents and the emphasis placed on the necessity of “patriots ruling Hong Kong”.

When Chinese leaders categorise Jimmy Lai, Benny Tai and Joshua Wong as the “masterminds” behind the 2019 pro-democracy protests, the legal system must deliver sentences that reflect the trio’s “importance”. That’s why Lai and Tai have been sentenced to 20 years and 10 years respectively, and rank among the most persecuted pro-democracy figures in the region. There are now close to 2,000 political prisoners in Hong Kong.

It’s devastating that Joshua has been behind bars for such a large portion of his adult life. I couldn’t even imagine skipping 16 years before I reached my 40s – during which time many people meet their partner, get married, raise a family and settle into a career. Joshua has been deprived of living fully because of his advocacy for important democratic values. The sentence signals to the world that China is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.

As geopolitical competition intensifies and populism rises, human rights are increasingly treated as an inconvenience to diplomatic and economic interests. Governments speak of stability and pragmatic engagement, while political prisoners slowly disappear from international public attention. The Chinese regime has little reason to change its approach if the repression of Hong Kong carries no meaningful consequences, either to trade or its global standing.

Given that Hong Kong was a British colony until as recently as 1997, the UK, in particular, should not regard the territory as merely another foreign policy issue. The Sino-British joint declaration was intended to safeguard the city’s rights and freedoms. The British government should therefore make the release of Joshua, Jimmy Lai and other political prisoners a priority when dealing with Beijing, rather than responding to each new sentence with another ineffective statement of concern.

For months, I had imagined the day Joshua would finally be free. Now that hope has been pushed away for another decade. We must not forget him, and must take urgent action to demand his immediate release.

Fearing AI disruption, white-collar workers are quitting their jobs

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:00:45 GMT

While there’s no evidence linking AI to mass layoffs, the tech has already ‘changed worker psychology’

When artificial intelligence researcher Mrinank Sharma quit his job at Anthropic earlier this year, the news rippled across the internet. In his resignation letter, posted on X and viewed 15.3m times, Sharma warned of a world “in peril” from the technology he had helped build.

“It is clear to me the time has come to move on,” he wrote. His next move: a poetry degree.

In the months following Sharma’s resignation, AI industry defectors and workers outside of Silicon Valley alike have echoed his sentiments.

Bracing for disruption forecasted by the AI industry, white-collar professionals are voluntarily leaving established careers to pursue professions they feel are more secure or more aligned with their values. Workers across industries – from tech to public relations to consulting – say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs overnight. They worry about AI jeopardizing their cognitive abilities, contributing to climate change, undermining value to customers and compromising security. Some, like Sharma, have left their fields entirely, shifting to vastly different careers.

So far, economic data shows that AI has not wreaked havoc on the workforce. It’s created about 1m US jobs, compared with 200,000 layoffs attributed to AI, according to the Economist. But as AI executives continue to warn of disruption, 71% of Americans believe the technology will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, according to the Pew Research Center. As workers fear for the future, though, they’re making major decisions about the present.

Some white-collar workers have begun to look beyond the dreams they were sold as AI reshapes jobs.

After spending nearly a decade in public relations, 30-year-old Vanessa Hsia decided to seek a master’s degree in comparative literature.

“I felt very burnt out and concerned with the direction of the industry: chasing quantity over quality, relying on AI rather than critical thinking, prioritizing short-term wins over long-term strategy,” Hsia posted on LinkedIn. “I have no idea where this path will lead, but I’m taking my own advice: the world is on fire, might as well do what you want.”

Hsia and her former colleagues in PR feared AI would eventually replace them, she said, noting that specific tasks like pitching reporters over email were already being automated.

“I’ve been sold this dream that if I work really hard in my career, I’ll climb the ladder, that I will be respected in my field and paid a fair wage,” she said. “But then you have this technology that exacerbates the fact that, actually, no, that’s not guaranteed.”

The safe, tidy way of life defined by a bachelor’s degree, desk job and career ladder is in its death throes, accelerated by the encroaching tidal wave of AI, Hsia contends. It’s an opinion echoed by other white-collar workers.

“The career that I’ve had for 10 years is kind of fundamentally gone,” said a software engineer at a big tech company, who requested anonymity for fear of retribution. The engineer and his peers believe their roles will soon cease to exist as AI automates coding. “We all thought we would be software engineers for another decade or two,” he said, adding that he’s considering leaving the industry. “Now it’s completely changed.”

For some workers, AI has accelerated feelings of instability and purposelessness they already had in their careers. Hanna Horvath spent most of her twenties as a content marketer and editor. But earlier this year, the 29-year-old left her editing job at personal finance platform Bankrate to freelance in copy writing and social media marketing, serve as a financial planner and publish a Substack newsletter.

Even before the introduction of AI, Horvath felt like her day-to-day work had drifted away from what she was hired to do, becoming “meaningless”. And after witnessing multiple layoffs at her company, she no longer felt assured by the promised stability of a nine-to-five job.

Once her company mandated AI use, Horvath felt even worse. “AI doesn’t have to replace your job to fundamentally change your relationship to your job,” she said. “So many of us were just becoming project managers instead of actually editing content or writing content.”

On LinkedIn, Horvath wrote that though the larger conversation about AI has been about job displacement, the tech “has already changed worker psychology”, referring to people’s fears and loss of purpose. Now, with varied streams of income, Horvath said she feels more financially secure and less vulnerable to AI replacement.

Some white-collar workers are effecting complete professional 180s: from tech to law enforcement and advertising to acting.

Chris, who asked to go by a pseudonym for fear of retribution, left his software engineering job to join the police department of a major east coast city last year. AI had taken “a lot of the thinking” and fun out of coding, and he feared being displaced, he said.

“There’s no job security in corporate anymore,” said Chris, who spent more than a decade doing white-collar work. “You’re expendable, you’re an asset.”

Chris counts himself lucky to have left software engineering as his employer started to push AI on his team. Now, as a police officer, “there’s a satisfaction I never got in engineering … In a lot of ways I am happier,” he said, referring to working directly with his community.

Similarly, Kara, who asked to go by a pseudonym to speak candidly about her former career, said leaving her job as an advertising producer to focus on acting while moonlighting as a barista made her “feel spiritually lighter”.

Kara had experienced increasing burnout, much of which she attributes to being instructed to use AI despite her concerns over legality and creative use. She said her team was encouraged to use AI-enabled production tools like Runway, which generates AI videos and images, and ElevenLabs, an AI voice generator, to supplement its creative work. As the producer, she was charged with handling legal clearance at a time when AI-generated video and audio based on a human’s likeness is still a gray area.

Her employer “compelled” the team to incorporate generative AI, then “in the same conversation, warned about the legal dangers”, she said. The result was constant stress.

Kara also worries about AI generating art after training on the work of human artists. Between her creative opposition and the stress of overseeing AI’s legal use, the job “became untenable”, she said. She’s been transitioning to what she calls her “survival job” as a barista “quite happily”, she added.

For years, the architects of AI have insisted that their technology poses immense economic threats. In May 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicted AI would lead to the displacement of half of all entry-level white-collar jobs by the end of the decade. That carnage has yet to materialize.

This year, Amodei doubled down on his stance in an essay on his website.

“AI is increasingly matching the general cognitive profile of humans, which means it will also be good at the new jobs that would ordinarily be created in response to the old ones being automated,” reads his essay, which calls AI a “general labor substitute for humans”.

Workers’ fears likely stem from company leaders’ warnings and the layoffs they’re seeing, even though data doesn’t show AI is causing job loss, said Brendan Moore, a University of Notre Dame economics professor who’s studied worker sentiment on AI and job insecurity.

“Between the proclamations from tech CEOs saying there are going to be mass layoffs, to many large technology and telecommunications companies that are citing AI as reasons for layoffs … people are saying: ‘Oh, this is due to AI,’” Moore said, adding some companies likely would’ve downsized regardless.

Workers still drive the economy, so if large numbers of them change course, wages, prices and economic growth could be affected, Moore said. Following the “great resignation”, when workers quit en masse during the Covid-19 pandemic, wages and consumer inflation rose. If the fear of AI provokes mass resignations, similar economic disruption could materialize.

“Just the fear of job loss alone, even if mass job loss never comes, can affect the economy,” Moore said.

Though AI leaders have walked back their dire economic predictions in recent months, it may be too late to reverse negative worker sentiment, which has garnered the attention of lawmakers.

Earlier this year, the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill to impose a federal moratorium on the construction of new AI datacenters until safeguards were in place for workers facing job loss. AI leaders “do not want to just replace specific jobs. They want to replace workers,” he wrote in an op-ed for Fox News, calling AI a “nightmare” for the working class.

At the same time, some tech executives are calling out their industry’s failure to articulate a positive vision for the future.

“It is surprising that the discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom,” Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, wrote in an August essay. “I do not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future.”

For workers, the issue is much simpler: AI is destabilizing their professional lives now – so they are taking matters into their own hands.

“Uncertainty is making people anxious,” said Horvath, the financial planner. But “you can’t have nihilism, because at the end of the day, it only hurts you”.

I have flung myself headfirst into Sarah J Maas’s romantasy universe and I find myself a changed woman

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:00:44 GMT

Some dismiss books like A Court of Thorns and Roses as mere genre fiction. But reading for pleasure has its own magical power

Fitness influencers love to inform us that “summer bodies are built in winter”, and boy oh boy have I spent the last three colder months in the southern hemisphere in a deep phase of preparation. I had a meticulous spreadsheet. I tracked everything with military precision. I committed to my grindset and sacrificed for my goals.

However, my end result wasn’t a six-pack of abs and a back strong enough to carry a dinner convo with the most punishing of acquaintances. It was to consume the entire back catalogue of Sarah J Maas – 16 books in total (including the novellas) – in anticipation of the long-awaited sixth book in the A Court of Thorns and Roses series.

I have flung myself headfirst into the Maasverse and like many readers I find myself … a changed woman.

Unless you have been living under a rock, or are Nobel prize for literature recipient Anne Carson (who mostly reads books written in 500BC), it has been impossible to miss the chokehold that the romantasy genre has had over (mostly) millennial women for the last several years. Characterised by blending elements of fantasy and romance together and catapulted into our hearts and nethers by its wild popularity on BookTok, romantasy is all over our bestseller lists and our social media.

Sarah J Maas is expected to crack 100m copies sold after this week’s release of A Court of Splintered Harmony and is arguably romantasy’s biggest superstar. Unfortunately, this feels exceptionally radical in 2026, with global literacy rates at an all-time low. (The vice-president of the US failed to pronounce “English proficiency” at a recent press conference, and Alix Earle, an influencer, proclaimed two weeks ago she has “never read a book … maybe Dr Seuss”.)

The flipside of the coin is the category of readers I affectionately call “The Man Bookers”. Their tastes are academic, bordering on performative; they do not read for pleasure, but for knowledge and masochism. They’ll have as many opinions on the Booker prize and the state of contemporary literature as tote bags full of physical media; their bookshelves are stacked with volumes from Fitzcarraldo Editions, the New York Review of Books and Dalkey Archive.

I adore Man Bookers in all their pretentiousness. My boyfriend falls into this category and politely informed me this morning – in an extremely performative male final boss move – that he has read “approximately eight single sentence novels” which is a shocking thing to hear at any time, let alone when one is half asleep and still in bed.

These literary consumers are generally the No 1 haters of romantasy lovers. They see us as basic and are quick to sneer and chide us for chugging down “faerie porn” on our Kindles.

To this I say: what the hell is wrong with you? Genre fiction is exceptionally important! Why is it globally acceptable to be a massive fan of Tolkien or George RR Martin or Frank Herbert, and yet Sarah J Maas is met with derision?

Obviously we all don’t have to like everything (as you will no doubt remind me in the comments) but when a subgenre dominated by female authors and consumers is judged for the same things male authors are celebrated for (rabid fanbase, elaborate world-building, scantily clad magical females), I cannot help but cry misogyny.

Speaking of, it only takes one look at the news to see why it’s no wonder women are turning to fictional faeries for entertainment. On TikTok and Reddit there is an entire theory (with many videos) on the supposed ACOTAR-to-divorce pipeline. Quite simply, the theory goes, women are reading these books, observing the complicated yet ultimately healthy relationships depicted in them, and leaving their shitty husbands. Shocking to realise that being treated with kindness and adoration is a fantasy in 2026!

My friend Rosie Dent – a prominent Maasverse expert and BookTok sensation – says, “Reading romantasy is actually an act of rebellion in this puritanical hellscape.” Rosie is among multiple BookTokers who have entire treatises on this series; her musings are articulate, insightful and thorough and probably researched enough to warrant a PhD. I messaged her throughout my strict reread and was grateful for her deep knowledge of the lore.

I have never been a part of an adult fandom before and this one is spectacular. I’m currently in a romantasy book club with some of New Zealand’s most successful and intelligent comedians. Surprise! The smartest and funniest women you know are reading smut!

And so, as I finally dive into A Court Of Splintered Harmony (after months of hard work), I can’t help but notice I’m a bit more excited, a bit more alive and a bit more connected than when I started. The power of fiction! I’m now reading nonstop. Every day. And definitely enjoying my literary wares more than my significant other (it’s not a competition but it’s true).

As my favourite fit man Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson says: “Success isn’t always about greatness. It’s about consistency.” And to that I say – consistent reading for pleasure? Not a fantasy any longer.

Johanna Cosgrove is an award-winning actor, writer and comedian

‘I’m not shaving my legs just to not orgasm’: 14 single women on their relationship to sex

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:00:44 GMT

Women of all ages across the globe open up about their sexual experiences amid a time of supposed societal sexual upheaval

The recently released film Wicker is full of sex. So much sex that some theaters released a 4D version where audiences can feel their seats creak in sync with the passionate lovemaking of the protagonist, a fisher played by Olivia Colman, and her husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård.

Also, this husband is made of wicker.

The film comes at a time of supposed sexual upheaval. Headlines wail about younger generations having less sex, and gallons and gallons of digital ink have been spilled over the concept of heteropessimism – the idea that women who engage in romantic relationships with men are doomed to unfulfilling sex. In this context, it makes sense that women would be drawn to the idea that the only way to find a satisfying sexual and romantic partner is to have them built out of twigs.

But is it really so bleak out there? The answer seems to be yes – and no. We asked single women to share their relationship to sex, and women of all ages across the globe opened up about their experiences.

Answers have been edited and condensed for clarity.

I’m 86, I live alone with my dog, and I enjoy the freedom of no attachment to a man. Before this, I was married twice, and selectively sexually active with men until my mid-60s. Sex was important but disappointing, because I was rarely with a man who knew how to satisfy a woman. I’ve consistently needed a light touch, and come easily, but the men I was with were mostly too rough and thoughtless! I’ve usually chosen older men; I hear that newer generations of men are getting better at it.

Now I can take care of myself as easily as I want with a small, comforting vibrator and I’m really happy with that. – Anonymous, 86, California

I refuse to live without sex. I like men, and have discovered since becoming single again at 48 that older men are still interested in sex, and the interesting ones prefer women closer to their age.

I had about 10 difficult years raising a severely autistic child. Sex was one of the only ways I could do something for myself. It was an absolute priority in my life, something that helped me hang on to my sanity and my humanity. Now that I’m no longer a full-time caregiver, sex is more about connecting with my partner, but for years I was a very selfish lover. Men don’t seem to mind being given instructions and being pursued. In fact, they seem to love it. – Beverly, 56, New York

Sex is super important to me. It’s a need, something I engage in for my health and wellbeing, not just connection. I need to feel regular physical contact, or if that isn’t available, I use a vibrator. There is nothing like an orgasm to help get you through the challenges of life. There is no shame in loving sex!

Over the last couple of years, my body has experienced trauma because I’m BRCA1 [a breast cancer gene]: I’ve had three operations including a double mastectomy and the removal of my ovaries and fallopian tubes. I was seeing someone through that experience, and it was so important to know that I could still enjoy sex with my new implants and lack of estrogen. It was daunting and I’m still getting used to it. You need to adapt as you age, but honestly, I’m having better sex than when I was younger. – Tamara, 55, UK

As a teenager, I developed a fear of becoming aroused to the point where I was uncomfortable sitting on uneven surfaces or anything that might cause genital sensation. I was raised in a very sexually conservative household, but as a teenager I realized I was a lesbian and struggled a lot with that before deciding in my late 20s that I was going to be less afraid. I started my first romantic relationship a couple of months ago, and despite being very attracted to my partner, I am still trying to get over my fear of sex. – Anonymous, 30, US

I’ve always had a high sex drive, and perimenopause hasn’t changed that. In my previous relationships, it was often higher than my partner’s. Sex to me is about release and imagination. It’s fun. But the thought of involving a male partner (sadly I’m heterosexual) who won’t take the time to have good sex, doesn’t call you back, wants you to play a certain “feminine” role or present your body in a particular way means that masturbation is far more fulfilling. I’ve always had better and more frequent orgasms with self-pleasure rather than with the majority of my previous partners. It’s a wonderful gift that the human body has given us. – Anonymous, 51, UK

I am a straight woman and I was attracted to men, but I have always found sex to be wildly overrated. It’s fun at first, and great for getting pregnant (I had two kids, both planned), but basically not all it’s cracked up to be.

Now that I’m widowed, I enjoy having control over all aspects of my life. I can pursue things that really interest me instead of having to consider the needs of my husband. I loved him, but I really am enjoying widowhood. I have no interest in a romantic relationship.

There are many things for me which are more pleasurable than sex, which makes me feel odd. But I can get as big a thrill out of a good book, a great meal or even a well-played classical work as I ever did out of sex. – Anonymous, 66, Spain

I had relatively boring sex until I turned 50. As a young woman, it was because I was not comfortable with my body so I found it hard to relax and enjoy myself or feel desirable. Later, my long-term relationship was not a happy one. We had functional sex. I could orgasm once I heard it was “OK” to stimulate myself while having intercourse (revelation!) but our physical connection was a bit like augmented masturbation for me.

When we separated, I developed an unexpected connection with a guy which was so amazing. This was my sexual awakening. I thought: This is what I have been missing out on?! It was incredible for a range of reasons: I was more at ease with my body; he absolutely desired me and did not hesitate to show and tell me, so any doubts I had were wiped away; we also had an extremely intense emotional and intellectual connection.

Since then, I’ve had some relationships with good sex, but nothing quite like that. Now I’m able to relax about my body and just enjoy myself. Currently, I’m single and not having sex with anyone, which is frustrating because I want it in my life! – Anonymous, 60, Australia

I am very uninterested in sex and relationships now. My experiences with men have been deeply painful, and I am tired and just want to be left alone! I started having sex at 15 years old and always had a partner until my last relationship ended when I was 24. I never learned how to have sex that was for me; it was always about performing for the man. Part of this performance involved keeping my body small and stereotypically attractive – during the years I was sexually active, I spent so much time staying thin, hairless and blonde.

I have such a protective mindset now around my body, life and home. I hope if I continue to do the internal work around body image, building myself up and creating a life for myself that I genuinely want, then I might one day be in the position to re-engage with sex from a healthier standpoint. – Anonymous, 26, Australia

I have a pretty healthy relationship with sex. I enjoy it shamelessly. Inside the bedroom, I can be who I want with who I want. I can be a top or a bottom with men, women, non-binary people, etc. It’s been a wonderful way to relieve stress, learn about myself and what I like, and give pleasure to someone else, which I deeply enjoy. I have a “friend with benefits” I see once a week, and I also started leaning more towards ethical non-monogamy. It allows me more freedom to have a variety of different sexual experiences without the guilt of hurting someone’s feelings.

My current friend with benefits has shown me exactly how I want to be touched – with intention, reverence and respect. It’s given me the courage to speak up for what I want and like, and what I don’t like. This is something I had always struggled with, especially with men because a lot of them don’t listen or only consider themselves. – Katie, 34, Canada

I was a bit of a wild child in my 20s and had a lot of sex. In my 40s, I had a partner who opened my world to the joys of desire, longing and attentiveness. But our relationship grew out of infidelity and never quite recovered. Since then, it’s been a desert. I went four years (four!) without dating, and the landscape here is awful. Perimenopause has also put a damper on things.

Some say they can live without sex … not me! Desire and passion must be part of the equation. I’m still looking, but I’ve worked to not flame out, so to speak. And pleasuring myself has always been a part of my sexuality. – Anonymous, 52, Oregon

Having grown up religious, I was a late bloomer. Once I decided to start having sex, I was excited to explore the sexual side I knew I had. However, I was diagnosed with herpes just days into my second ever sexual relationship. I was given little information or support by the NHS, and no option for medication as I don’t have regular flare-ups. But once you have it, you have it for life and you have to disclose it to each new partner.

The disease itself has absolutely no impact on my life, but the stigma is huge and horrible. Disclosure means I’ve been rejected out of hand, often by people I saw a future with. Early in my 20s, it stopped me from having spontaneous or casual sex, all things I wanted to try. Just last week, I was rejected after six great dates by a man who said: “I can’t afford to catch it from you in case we break up. Then I’ll be out there on my own with herpes. I like sex, but like most of my friends, I’m not having a lot of it. I’ve been single since January, and I don’t really enjoy casual hook-ups, so sex has been out of the picture for a while. I miss it, but I don’t want to have sex just for the sake of it. Casual sex can feel so emotionally empty and unsatisfying. And I’m not tidying my bedroom and shaving my legs just to not have an orgasm. – Jenna, 25, Scotland

I love sex. It was something I was made to feel ashamed for many years, that as a woman I enjoyed fucking.

To me, sex is completely separate from love. I feel able to place sex with the rest of my hobbies. I have people I enjoy skateboarding with, and people I enjoy having sex with. Sex with someone you love can be a lot better (as many activities are when in love), yet I have had absolutely universe-melting orgasms with people I have no great affection for. – Anonymous, 37, UK

The first times I had sex at 16 and 17, I had vaginismus so sex was difficult and I was very scared. I did casual sex and one-night stands and it’s not my vibe at all. If you have casual sex often, you realize men don’t care about a woman’s pleasure. I can confidently say my female friends have similar experiences. – Guillermina, 24, Argentina

Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:03:38 GMT

Far-right politician addresses Conservative Political Action Conference and makes unsubstantiated claims about election fraud

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.

Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”

Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.

Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.

“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.

Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.

Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”
