‘I’m never going to be bloody Robert De Niro!’: Rob Brydon, the most chipper man on TV

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:00:43 GMT

The nicest man in acting is back with new comedy, Bill’s Included. He talks about rejecting Hollywood, refusing to play a villain – and why he just can’t make fun of Steve Coogan

‘I’m a nice person, you know,” says Rob Brydon, as I met him in a basement green room of the BBC, where probably nobody with such a mellow ego has ever sat. “I am a people-pleaser. That’s who I am.” It’s an unnecessary clarification – at 61, he’s been nice on TV, as himself and in character, for most of our adult lives.

We’re here to talk about his new six-parter, Bill’s Included, but his character in it, the eponymous Bill, is such a distillation of pure Rob Brydon that it’s (accidentally, he says) a celebration of his entire career. As the show opens, Bill has just been left by his wife, who’s run off with the gardener. At no point does he ever fire the guy – “I like him!” – but otherwise, his life is completely upended. The utterly plausible cocktail of his civic mindedness and howling loneliness drives him to take in four lodgers, local university students.

The opening moments, before he gets his young super-woke crew, are so powerfully reminiscent of Marion and Geoff that it’s like being whacked around the head and given a hot chocolate at the same time by the year 2000. The hugely funny and poignant series was Brydon’s breakthrough sitcom, the first he wrote himself (with Hugo Blick), based on a character he’d created at college – Keith, a taxi driver, speaking straight to a dashboard camera about a marriage that, the viewer realises, has been toast for ages. “I’m so thick,” Brydon says now. “It’s only when watching Bill’s Included that I went: ‘Oh, it’s got a bit of a Marion and Geoff vibe.’ Honestly, I swear to you, that hadn’t occurred to me. You don’t think about your own stuff. That’s 26 years ago!”

Steve Coogan was one of the executives on Marion and Geoff, and has been badgering Brydon to do more character comedy ever since. “I fobbed him off for years, then we made a taster of this landlord-and-students idea a few years ago, but it wasn’t right. I was too creepy.” Surely not … “I was, I was creepy, and I didn’t realise it! It was just me as a middle-aged guy, going: ‘Come in, have a sit down,’” – he does an impression of his most mellifluous and ingratiating Welsh timbre, and he’s right, it’s incredibly creepy – before snapping back to his regular voice.

Brydon and Coogan’s creative entanglement has been fruitful: 24 Hour Party People, about Factory Records in Manchester in the late 80s/early 90s – Brydon had a small part as a caustic naysayer who doesn’t like the music, Coogan played the legend Tony Wilson, head of the label. Then, Cock and Bull Story, in which they both brought the atmosphere, playing themselves, sort-of, as two egotistical actors scrapping with each other, failing to make a film about a book, Tristram Shandy, failing to become a novel. The genius of that film is all in the control: they caper about but pull it back from slapstick; it’s knowing but not arch. Seeing Brydon and Coogan mess about on set gave director Michael Winterbottom the idea for The Trip, whose Northern Lights series – its fifth – is coming soon.

When the pair first met in 1997ish, it was at a Holiday Inn in Reading. Brydon was in an improv group with the solidly magnificent Julia Davis, along with Ruth Jones, who he was also at school with, and they’d all been to the Hexagon to see Coogan, who “was already at his first peak. He was in the West End with The Man Who Thinks He’s It, he’d won a million Baftas already, he was doing what I wanted to do at the time, which is character comedy,” Brydon remembers.

“He’d started out in voiceovers, he was the same age as me, so I could see all these parallels between us.” I can’t help but remark that people, if they meet a peer they really admire, sometimes don’t like that person very much. “What, envy and stuff like that?” says Brydon, taken aback. “I can imagine that sort of person, but I can’t imagine me being like that. Envy, brute rage, competitiveness? I’m none of those things. I just look at him and think: ‘Great. Isn’t he good?’ One of the hardest things in The Trip is when Michael wants me to ridicule his career. He’s got a brilliant career!”

Brydon’s career isn’t exactly a Harrison Ford-level wilderness-to-stardom tale; he had work in improv, doing voiceovers and radio panel shows before Human Remains in 2000, when he was 35. But that blistering two-hander with Julia Davis, in which they play a variety of miserable couples, landed the same year as Marion and Geoff, and Brydon’s forte was unarguable: character comedy in which he is defiantly uncool, self-deluding and in a variety of luckless scenarios. He can effortlessly carry a show, but is just as memorable in an ensemble. His tightly wound Uncle Bryn is the performance people can’t let drop, “more or less every day, someone will come up to me and tell me how much they love Gavin & Stacey. There’s a real affection for it.”

Bill’s Included is his first show since Gavin & Stacey’s epic finale, and the camera’s on him almost constantly. His relationship with the four students, Christian (Dylan Brady), Hettie (Ada Player), James (Harry Baxendale) and Zahra (Yasmin Al-Khudhairi) starts off as a broad clash of the generations. They’re noisy, he’s fussy, and whenever they use their buzzwords – checking their privilege, trauma bonding, finding a safe space – Bill says naive, delighted things, such as: “These are the kinds of nuggets I’m going to get from you, like truffles.”

“I think that’s quite an authentic thing, someone of his age, his personality, would feel,” says Brydon. Quite fast, it becomes affectionate. “He starts off calling them the students, and by episode three, he’s saying: ‘I’ve got to go and do a thing for the kids.’ They’re not my kids! But I like to be needed.” It may sound low-stakes, but his heart is so painfully close to the surface, and the peril of some Dr Marten-ed youngster stamping on it by accident sets up intense emotional jeopardy.

Often the laughs feel ripped out of you, sheer exuberant relief that no one got hurt – like the feeling of being at a circus, except instead of tigers, you’re being entertained by suburban manners and wounded middle-aged pride. “I am what I am,” he says at that “suburban” word. “My world is not the world of the agent provocateur, activist, disruptor. That’s not me. I’m riding the horse in the direction that it’s travelling. That’s a phrase, isn’t it?” I’ve never heard it – maybe it’s Welsh, I suggest? “It’s probably from a self-help book, isn’t it?”

To stick with the phrase, few could have predicted that the horse he’s riding – whether on The Trip, Gavin & Stacey or Would I Lie to You? – would travel for so long. These are, or were, all decades-long shows, yet when Brydon describes The Trip taking shape, it sounds like that episode of Seinfeld where Jerry and George go to see some TV bigwigs to pitch a show about nothing. “Michael [Winterbottom] said: ‘Six half-hours, no script really, and different restaurants.’ I said to him: ‘You’d be lucky if you get one good half-hour.’ I was very wrong.”

From the first episode, The Inn at Whitewell, in 2010, it is plain that the idea is dynamite, but very weird dynamite. Between the squabbling, the self-aggrandisement and the impressions, you can understand why it’s funny, but the depth of feeling catches you unawares. Even by series four, you still can’t figure out why it’s as moving as it is. “How [Winterbottom] makes those shows, he doesn’t cut to comic rhythms, he has storytelling rhythms, so when we saw the cuts of the first series, it was quite jarring. He’s quite pure, Michael. He isn’t manipulative of his audience, whereas a comedian, all you’re doing is manipulating your audience.” Even after 16 years, Brydon still hasn’t turned into a food snob. “We had whale and stuff, in Scandinavia. It’s a bit like chicken.”

If you think The Trip’s been going a long time, Would I Lie to You? is now in its 19th series. “A lot of people say they watch it before going to bed. It puts them in a nice frame of mind. If you watch that show, you think the world is an agreeable place, where people get on with each other.” His nice-guy shtick is surely parodic, I decide, though he says, no, he can do villainy if he wants to, it just doesn’t do it for him. “There was a while when I thought: ‘If I host a show like Would I Lie to You?, I’ll never be taken seriously as an actor.’ But then I thought: ‘Look, I’m never going to be bloody Robert De Niro anyway, so let’s just do it.’ I think the fragmented media landscape is a gift to someone like me. There were people in Barbie – I had a tiny part in that – who didn’t even know I was an actor.”

If he sounds philosophical, almost Buddhist-ly – without front, or certainly without professional puffed-up-ness – that’s because “people always look at careers in a vacuum, and they’re not, because my life is not my career. My life is my home, my family, my friends. I’ve got five children! Katie’s 31 and George is 15. So I’ve never been in that place where I could go to Atlanta and make the X Men versus the B Men.” He’d take a second season of Bill’s Included, for sure; he’d love that. But, he says, “I don’t think your career is your greatest source of happiness. Maybe it’s from being divorced – this is my second marriage – and I’ve worked out where I’m happiest. And it’s being in the garden, with friends and in nature.”

Bill’s Included starts on 20 November on BBC One at 9.30pm.

This article was amended on 6 November 2026. Rob Brydon’s character in Marion and Geoff was called Keith, not Geoff as an earlier version said.

‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:00:42 GMT

Operation Black Vote chair says Tory leader’s claim that Britain should not apologise has caused ‘hurt and disbelief’

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.

David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.

In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.

Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.

Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.

But he said Badenoch’s comments highlighted wider concerns about the UK’s political climate, adding: “At Operation Black Vote, we are hearing profound anger, hurt and disbelief.”

He added: “For us, this is not an abstract historical debate. It concerns our families, our heritage and our humanity. Political leaders should not underestimate the depth of feeling within black communities or their democratic power.”

Weaver said that in seeking an apology, Commonwealth nations wanted recognition of continuing colonial legacies that hampered development, and that Badenoch’s comments were “profoundly insulting”.

This week marked the second anniversary of Badenoch becoming the first black woman to lead a major British political party. OBV, a national, non-partisan civil rights group founded in 1996, welcomed her historic achievement in becoming Tory leader in 2024.

Meanwhile, although black voters were more likely than any other voters to have backed Labour in the 2024 general election, Weaver said OBV had found they felt “despondent” with the party and “taken for granted”, in particular over its handling of the consequences of the Windrush scandal.

Weaver added: “All parties should understand that to not apologise for slavery, the worst crime against humanity, is an insult. An apology should not have to be begged for. It should be an expression of genuine remorse and moral responsibility, not a carefully managed political statement designed to demonstrate toughness or avoid obligation.

after newsletter promotion

“Reparative justice is not just about money. Ending an injustice does not erase responsibility for perpetrating it. We must ask why acknowledging this particular historical injustice remains so difficult and whether deeper racial attitudes continue to shape the debate.”

Badenoch, who has advocated a “colour-blind” approach to race, has long argued that people from ethnic minorities should be free to express differing views on race without being accused of betraying their communities.

But while attempting to frame herself as a unifier, Badenoch has given roles to the hard-right politician Rupert Lowe, Katie Lam – the MP who said a “large number” of legal migrants “need to go home” – and the former neo-Nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, while outlining plans to scrap the public sector equality duty and leave the European court of human rights.

Weaver said: “She’s the leader of the Conservative party. That’s a big deal. She’s got a high popularity rating and can be very effective. But many black voters tell us there’s a lot of mistrust for her lack of empathy – and because she will sometimes say things her white counterparts could not say and get away with it. So she becomes the front for unacceptable views on race.

“The current state of public discourse – and the silence when it comes to challenging it – contributes to a sense among black communities that they are being treated with contempt across the political spectrum.

“This is not just about Badenoch. Just because you’re black doesn’t mean you have to hold a particular point of view. But your heritage, whether you are white or black, does not place your views beyond challenge. An apology for slavery is about humanity and decency and seeing people’s worth. Andy Burnham must do the right thing – and soon.”

Downing Street and the Conservative party were approached for comment. Commonwealth leaders have said the UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year.

After the midterms, the global right is reeling. But the danger of Trumpism will never be gone

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:46:27 GMT

Yes, the Republicans suffered humiliating defeat. But the fact that a Trump presidency was even possible means something like it could happen again

He’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad.

Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats in the popular vote for the House of Representatives was greater even than the 11.2% swing recorded in the Watergate midterms of November 1974, following the resignation in disgrace of Richard Nixon. Trump had worked hard for many months to undermine these elections, either by gerrymandering districts in his favour or preparing the ground for a later claim the vote was rigged, but to no avail: the democratic system proved too resilient, and the American public too determined to have their say. And have it they did, in a voice loud and clear.

Beyond the US, the temptation will be strong to see this as the moment the wheels came off the authoritarian, nationalist populist bandwagon that has rolled through so much of our politics this past decade. Viktor Orbán’s fall in April was pivotal, but the humiliation of Trump was always going to matter more. Thanks to the sheer might of the US, Trump has for a decade been the engine of the illiberal international. And now it is sputtering.

All that is cause for delight. But the risk is that those who have fought nationalist populism will take Tuesday’s success as their cue to relax. That would be to repeat the mistake made by Trump himself – and too many others – in November 2024, when he interpreted his win over Kamala Harris not as the cry of a public fed up with rising grocery bills and petrol prices, but as a permanent “vibe shift” in the culture and a mandate to turn the US into an autocracy, take a chainsaw to US government agencies, have masked men abduct and shoot American citizens on the streets, launch a doomed and disastrous war, and fill the US capital with monuments to his own vanity, all while lining his pockets and those of his inner circle.

The equivalent error this time, whether it’s made inside or outside the US, would be to read these midterm results as the end of the Trump threat and as proof that normal service will resume shortly. The danger of Trumpism, sadly, will never be gone. Because if something can happen once, it can happen again. Trump was possible – which means another Trump is possible.

That is the lesson the US’s traditional allies, in Britain, the EU or elsewhere, need to internalise. Even if Capitol Hill will soon be in saner hands, even if Trump’s eventual successor is a good internationalist who believes in a rules-based order, the reliability of the US as an ally can never again be taken for granted. After Trump, the US’s status as a guarantor of western security is anything but guaranteed, contingent instead on this or that election result. Which means that the rest of the west must still plan for its own protection and defence.

Sure, nationalist populism is now badly damaged, marked as the cause of losers. What’s more, Trump may well have demonstrated that nationalist movements whose sole currency is grievance will ultimately always fail – thereby deterring voters in France and Germany tempted to vote for Marine Le Pen or the AfD.

after newsletter promotion

But, again, it’s hard to rely on that. Did Trump fail because politicians of his ilk always will? Or was it because he made stupid and, crucially, avoidable decisions, such as attacking Iran – which not only broke his core pledge, so cherished by Maga voters, to end wars rather than start them, but also drove up the very inflation he was elected to curb? Either way, it’s hard to speak of inevitable failure when describing a man who, despite all the havoc he wreaked the first time around – including the violent insurrection of 6 January 2021 – was elected to a fresh term less than four years later. He disgraced himself, but was rewarded with victory.

Besides, it’s too soon to speak of Trump in the past tense. True, he’s lost the doormat House and the rubber-stamp Senate that enabled him to act without restraint. But a weakened Trump is not necessarily a tamed Trump. I think of the seasoned Washington hand who told me Trump in defeat could become “a cornered animal”. When it comes to the world stage, he still has the power to act – foreign policy is largely the preserve of the president – and a double motive to do so. First, he will want a legacy to offset this week’s historic drubbing and, second and even more elementally, he craves the attention. The notion of ceding the spotlight to Democrats, or in fact anyone, will appal him.

Maybe he will bow to the demands lodged by JD Vance - in a statement on X that saw the vice president all but break from his boss – and move to end the war with Iran, even if that means capitulation. Or he might double down and push for the toppling of the Tehran regime that he likely believes would give him the place in history he deserves.

Until 20 January 2029 those decisions will be Trump’s. He still has the power to shape world events, even if that power has diminished. Take as just one example, the US relationship with Israel. That country had elections of its own last week that, though far from delivering the repudiation of Benjamin Netanyahu many Israelis sought, did wipe out his parliamentary majority. Coalition horsetrading is now under way, and the US midterms are already playing a part. Israeli opposition leaders argue that what Netanyahu long claimed as an asset – his closeness to Trump – is, after Tuesday, a liability, rendering Israel’s prime minister “toxic” among the Democrats who will soon wield power on Capitol Hill. If that argument prevails, the blue tsunami will have claimed not only Kansas and Texas, but the man once dubbed the Republican senator from Jerusalem.

On the morning of election day, Trump announced the termination of military aid to Israel, perhaps in a last-ditch attempt to win over Tucker Carlson Republicans who are hostile to the country. He could continue on that path, especially if he seeks to punish Netanyahu for his role in the joint US-Israeli war on Tehran that broke his presidency or, alternatively, he could defy Vance and hug the Israeli PM close.

The point is, these fateful choices still rest with Trump. Democrats will soon have the power to investigate allegations of corruption and hold him to account. America’s allies in Europe and elsewhere will soon find in Washington people who talk like partners, rather than enemies. Both prospects come as a great relief. But that does not alter two key facts: Trump happened – and he’s still there.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Digested week: The harrowing backstory to the John Lewis Christmas ad

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:12:03 GMT

Plus, the king’s regret-without-liability statement on slavery, and getting mogged by Collins dictionary

All eyes on America as a nation decides, but this week Brits faced an equally large question: namely, how do we feel about this year’s John Lewis Christmas ad? It’s a confusing one. On the one hand, high off her flinty brilliance in six seasons of Slow Horses, Kristin Scott Thomas is a welcome addition to any production and I could watch her waft around a big house without the pretext of either John Lewis or Christmas.

On the other hand, it’s all a bit odd. The advert’s much discussed storyline in which Scott Thomas’s daughter and son-in-law come to the door with their owl-eyed children doesn’t exactly emanate Christmas spirit, even as the “before” in a before-and-after story.

Why does the grandma appear to have no relationship with her grandkids? Has there been a massive fight in the family? If there has, is it about new inheritance tax rules and how they might push Christmas gift-giving more in the direction of money – deed transfer, not 20 quid in an envelope – over presents? Has the Scott Thomas character raised the possibility that she doesn’t trust her family to look out for her if she puts her house in their name, and have they shot back, huffily: “That’s ridiculous, mother, we’d always do right by you, do you really want us to give 40% of your estate to HMRC when there’s a perfectly sensible way around it?” And has she replied, coldly: “Why would I care, I won’t be here.” To which have they replied, in a howl of protest: “We think you’re being very selfish.”

Has she said to them: “Look, I’m already contributing substantially to the school fees after the 20% VAT hike, what more do you want from me?” To which have they replied: “Fine, we’ll pull the kids out of private and send them to state school, but we’ll need money for therapists, so can you please put the house in our name?” To which has she replied, in a deadly escalation: “Vote Reform then if you feel so strongly about inheritance tax,” to which have they replied, absolutely screaming at this point: “How very dare you, we’re on the left!”

To which has she snorted: “Well, I know for a fact that he – pointing to her son-in-law – voted for David Cameron at least once,” to which has her daughter exploded: “Ohmigod, says the woman who voted for Brexit!” At this point has her son-in-law walked quietly over to the wall and mimed beating his head against it? Does she even want them there for Christmas? Is that why the kids are so sullen? Is this who we are as a people now and has it fallen to John Lewis to tell us?

A rigorous workout for our nerves, as we look towards the US midterms and try to avoid tempting fate by saying words like “landslide”, “got this”, or “win” ahead of time. For reasons of self-preservation, my assumption is that Donald Trump’s poor approval ratings will somehow resolve themselves at the 11th hour and hand us a fudge of a result, allowing him to stagger on.

This anticipatory hedge is bolstered by British TV news hacks who, almost to a person, manage to find the most lunatic anomalies in any voter set to share with the viewers back home. A Texan of Mexican origin who has lost family members to brutal deportation raids by ICE but still intends to vote for Trump? Tick. A well-to-do family appalled by Elon Musk’s efforts to buy the election and stick a huge datacentre next to their house, but for whom the top voting priority is the question of gender identity and will be voting for Trump, too? Yup. A sense of Americans-say-the-funniest-things animating most foreign reporting? That, too.

King Charles visits the Caribbean and issues a regret-without-liability statement around Britain’s role in the slave trade, but it’s his hissy fit at not having an umbrella that catches my eye. This petulant side to the king is one we haven’t seen in full glory since his meltdown, four years ago, over a leaky fountain pen at a signing ceremony, and I couldn’t enjoy it more.

Then, Charles popped out of his chair, paced the room irritably and snapped, “I can’t bear this bloody thing! Every stinking time!” while Camilla staunched the flow of ink and calmly got on with her own signing. In this week’s incident, the king, caught in a sudden downpour at an outside ceremony in Antigua, gesticulates wildly and with a furious stream of what we might assume to be invective, looks sharply around for someone to hand him an umbrella. Camilla, meanwhile, grips her own umbrella and beetles off, stage right, leaving her other half to compose himself and remind the rest of us of the endearing normalcy of royalty – or how our social order enables and forgives adult tantrums, depending on one’s view.

New threshold crossed! For the first time the word of the year from one of the big dictionaries is a word I haven’t encountered. I don’t know what this means but it’s probably not good. Either that, or “mogging” isn’t quite as widely used as Collins suggests. Apparently it’s a term taken from bodybuilding and applied to people one-upping each other on the internet, as in, per the dictionary’s explanation, “your friend’s sourdough mogs the loaf you spent all weekend proving”.

I mean – and I know this is what happens when you age out of exposure to new idioms – it sounds totally made up to me, like something from an old episode of Brass Eye, specifically the one about deprived youths loading pensioners into shopping trolleys and “git-surfing” them round the estate.

Almost a week on from Martha Stewart’s disastrous choice of Halloween costume and it’s worth a revisit to remind us just how enjoyably poor her decision-making was. After dressing as a homeless person with a sign around her neck reading “I am hungry. Please help!” the 85-year-old had to apologise, although you could tell she wasn’t happy about it and later came up with the claim that she had only worn it because someone spilled chocolate on her “other” costume. Hilariously unconvincing from Martha, and I couldn’t love her more.

Nigel Farage’s exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:00:51 GMT

The clear-out at the newspaper seems driven less by politics than by a shift towards AI – and journalism will pay the price

Nigel Farage has been writing columns for the Daily Telegraph since 2016, most of which have promoted the previously Brexit and now Reform UK party he leads, or accused his rivals of going soft on immigration. For this privilege the paper’s cash-strapped bosses paid him around £4,000 a month, adding up to nearly half a million pounds over the past decade.

News broke this week that Farage’s services are no longer required by the Telegraph’s new German owners, Axel Springer, though sources close to Farage say that he resigned. The paper is also reported to be negotiating the exit of Allison Pearson, who has been complimentary of far-right activist Tommy Robinson’s “rough-diamond charisma”, which together have prompted rumours that Springer has called a halt to the paper’s rightwards shift, calling it back to the basics of its Conservative party bible past.

All the attention so far has focused on the departure of these controversial columnists: subscribers have threatened to leave in posts on X, with mutterings about Springer’s pro-EU stance and the existence of its internal LGBTQ+ network.

Yet, while there are signs of a tonal shift away from some of the more outre Telegraph rantings, most of the outrage misses the main cause of the change. “This wasn’t politics,” one insider told me. “It was just money.”

The Telegraph is just the latest example of the trend for media organisations: while still attracting trophy prices such as the £575m Springer paid to acquire the newspaper in June, many no longer have the money to pay for journalists. As new Telegraph Media Group chief executive Carolin Hulshoff Pol told staff in announcing the cuts, the Telegraph’s print sales continue to decline, its search traffic is under pressure and AI is changing everything.

In total, more than 100 people are said to be facing the axe before Christmas, almost 20% of editorial and commercial staffing. The company has not confirmed numbers but sports and culture, two departments considered the mainstay of Telegraph coverage, are expected to be harder hit than comment.

Some journalists have already announced their departure. A post by Liam Halligan, who has written a well-regarded economics column for 27 years, prompted sympathy as well as some outrage on X about the possible left turn. Few mentioned the fact that Springer boss Mathias Döpfner is said to be a fan of the platform’s owner, Elon Musk, and encouraged him to back Germany’s far-right AfD party (as reported by the Telegraph itself).

Others to leave include the head of long reads, Lisa Markwell, a former editor of the Independent on Sunday, who no one would accuse of swivel-eyed bigotry.

The perceived toning down of anti-migrant, pro-extremist content in recent weeks is more likely to be a reflection of the current zeitgeist, with both Reform and the Maga right having seen better days. Besides, as one senior Telegraph journalist told me: “As for singling out Brexiteers, they’re all Brexiteers here (bar one or two notable exceptions).”

Before the Springer takeover, during the three-year ownership limbo after Lloyds Bank seized assets from their former owners, the Barclay family, staff had been expecting cuts under a new owner. Other prospective owners, which included RedBird IMI and the owners of the Daily Mail, were all expected to cut costs, especially when the price rose to a level that defied economic reality. This is partly because the independent directors brought in to sell the business were apparently more focused on decorating rather than selling off the top floor.

Media owners in this prolonged time of crisis, facing a business model savaged by the internet and a collapse in trust, have tended to cut jobs slowly, over time. But Springer, obviously in a hurry, having waited 22 years since its first offer for the Telegraph, was not prepared to wait any longer.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Yet Döpfner had cheered a depressed newsroom in June, when he spoke of using the Telegraph to push into the US market as a centre-right, pro-free speech challenger to the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times. His words seemed to echo those of another media mogul with global ambitions: Rupert Murdoch. Amid a legal battle about the future of the Murdoch family trust, Murdoch said that his papers would be the “protector of the conservative voice in the English-speaking world”.

Yet Springer’s expansion plan, we now learn, is based on greater use of AI. Though details of how this technology will be used are yet to be revealed, there is talk of it being utilised to streamline the content produced across all Springer’s outlets, which includes Politico and Business Insider. The lack of a human editor, if not touch, seemed to be evident in an official email jointly signed by Hulshoff Pol and Chris Evans, the paper’s editor; if anything screams “written by ChatGPT”, it’s announcing job cuts with ambitions to turn your company “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.

It is hard to feel sympathy for Nigel Farage, who appears to have no trouble getting people to pay him ridiculous sums of money for various jobs. The same cannot be said for more than 100 journalists who face the possibility of Christmas with no job at all.

Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

The club cricketer dubbed “Clicky Ponting” in response to accusations of cheating during the English summer has been handed a two-year ban from the sport. His team, Saltburn CC’s 2nd XI, have also been relegated.

Brian Devine earned online notoriety back in July after footage from Division Two of the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League went viral. In the clip, Devine was seen clicking his fingers in the field and successfully tricking the umpire into believing a Norton CC batter had edged a catch behind.

As well as a new nickname – a nod to former Australia captain Ricky Ponting – it saw Devine provisionally suspended by his club for the remainder of the 2026 season while an investigation was undertaken by the league. Further examples of the practice subsequently emerged and were circulated widely online.

After a series of player interviews, written statements, and a review of the footage by a three-person disciplinary panel, both Devine and Saltburn CC accepted misconduct charges. The following sanctions were announced on Friday:

Devine is now banned from all cricket under the auspices of the England and Wales Cricket Board until the end of the 2028 season. The ban covers “playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams”.

After an appeal against their sanction, Saltburn CC have been fined £300 and their 2nd XI has been relegated to Division Three of the NYSDCL. The 2nd XI will also start the 2027 season with 60-point deduction, while previously relegated Middlesbrough CC have retained their place in Division Two.

In a statement, the NYSDCL looked to draw a line under the matter and acknowledge the impact it had on a volunteer-run club that found itself the subject of widespread condemnation and global headlines.

“The League recognises the strain this has placed on many people, especially those who were abused online and in person,” the statement read. “We ask everyone to respect that the formal process is now complete.”

This is an age of anti-vaccine unreason – and even NHS staff are not immune

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 09:00:48 GMT

When fewer than half of health service workers have taken up the flu vaccine, there is little hope for the rest of us

Good news. Edward Jenner’s rustic thatched hut in his Gloucestershire garden where he conducted his first smallpox vaccination in 1796 has just been saved by English Heritage. Here Jenner gave free vaccinations every week to local people. Here he became the single human being to save more lives than any other person who has ever lived.

This triumph of the age of enlightenment, at a time when a third of children died before adulthood, is too easily forgotten. But enlightenment itself has been in retreat, with Robert F Kennedy Jr, Donald Trump’s health secretary, leading the vanguard of unreason, dismantling vaccination programmes and stirring vaccine conspiracy and paranoia around the world. His infectious messaging has contributed to falling vaccination rates in rich as well as poor countries. Here’s hoping this week is the end of that Trumpian rolling back of reason.

What would Jenner think now as the winter flu season approaches? Last year fewer than half of frontline NHS staff in England were vaccinated, with only one in 10 trusts reaching the (very low) NHS target of 60% protected against flu. Healthcare workers have a high risk of catching flu, spreading it to vulnerable people and to their own families, and taking sick days when they are most needed. These people are trained in science, steeped in evidence of the extraordinary value of vaccines, and yet many are reluctant. Doctors were the staff group that scored the highest, but still only half of them got vaccinated – half! – instead of influencing the public towards protection.

Overall, healthcare workers in GP practices were the most likely to take up the vaccine, with 53.5% covered: they have most access, and are likely to be prodded by colleagues. But even so, that’s disgracefully low for people with signs on their noticeboards urging patients to get the jab (free for NHS and care staff, under-16s, over-65s and vulnerable people). Official figures show an astonishing difference between the best and worst NHS trusts, from the highest at 77.2% to the lowest at 0.6%.

Why so few? The reasons, finds the National Institute for Health and Care Research, are complex. The easiest to solve are practical obstacles – for example, badly timed clinics not matching work on the wards, instead of anytime drop-in sessions. But deeper reasons suggest staff lack the motivation or are suspicious of employers, with some “feeling like the organisation does not care”, finds the NIHC.

Some don’t think flu is serious, others that vaccines don’t work, or that protective equipment and hand gels will do. Some don’t trust vaccine safety information, while others fear secret side-effects and distrust pharmaceutical companies.

Ethnic minority staff are more likely to be vaccine hesitant out of general mistrust of institutions they feel are not on their side. But, as compilers of the latest NHS guidance stress to me, the variation in rates of vaccination is miles wider than the smaller disparities in ethnic makeup or social differences in staff: that can’t account for that yawning 77.2% to 0.6% gap.

Something happened during the pandemic that stopped NHS staff getting vaccinated. Despite the heroic risks they took then, Covid has left a strong residue of mistrust, alongside a poisonous stream of anti-vaccine misinformation on social media. Meanwhile, the anti-science right keeps stirring suspicion of anything the state recommends. Before Covid, 74% of NHS staff took the flu vaccine, but now the official target has fallen to just 60%, though the NHS constitution commits to a 100% offer of the jab to eligible groups.

The mystery is why NHS staff, most of whom are dedicated to their patients, don’t do the right thing of their own accord. As a matter of patient safety, vaccination should be a compulsory condition of NHS service (excluding those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons). Anyone working with children needs a DBS check, drivers need licences, doctors and nurses need qualifications. Compulsion was ordered in late 2021 as some staff refused the Covid vaccine mid-pandemic, but it was rescinded almost immediately when surveys suggested 80,000 people might lose their roles. No one dared test if that would really happen, when losing so many staff would do more damage to patients than the risk of infection.

What would work? The NHS coordinator I spoke to said that trusts with high staff vaccinations encourage close colleagues to act as persuaders and explainers, convincing all but a few adamants. You wonder about the working culture of hospitals with very low rates and disaffected staff.

The NHS has 1.55 million staff, reaching deep into every community. They should be vaccine advocates at a time when fewer children under five are getting their full routine jabs – down again this year, failing the World Health Organization’s 95% threshold for herd immunity.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The next flu pandemic is a matter of “when, not if”, says the WHO. For national herd immunity, we need compulsory vaccination as a civic duty, along with compulsory voting and paying your taxes. Flu vaccines last winter prevented about 100,000 hospitalisations, but in a bad flu wave an average of 2,660 patients a week will occupy a hospital bed. But fearful politicians think that this is a price worth paying rather than face down libertarian anti-vaxxers.

What would Jenner think of today’s NHS staff? This smallpox saviour faced fierce opposition but his work was later championed by the pro-science Prince Albert, who erected a statue in his memory in Trafalgar Square, amid demonstrations by anti-vaxxers and the military who regarded those plinths as theirs. Within a year of Albert’s death in 1861, they shunted Jenner off to a remote spot in Kensington Gardens and erected on his plinth Maj Gen Sir Henry Havelock, who died of dysentery at the siege of Lucknow while putting down an Indian rebellion.

Time, I think, for a national vaccination day, in keeping with our current life-sciences success. Jenner should be brought back from exile in a triumphal carriage to his plinth and Sir Henry – well, anyone who wants him can have him.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Dear Andy Burnham: the full story of enslavement has to move beyond comforting stories

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 07:00:46 GMT

The prime minister’s focus on white abolitionists and working-class solidarity diminishes the true scale of Manchester’s reliance on the slavery economy

In May 1767, a notice was placed in the Manchester Mercury for “Any Gentleman, or Lady, wanting to purchase a Black Boy, 12 years of age” to inquire on Market Street, at the site of today’s Uniqlo clothes shop.

After 15 years of painstaking work through the scattered fragments that recorded and pointed to Manchester’s enslaving history, I still don’t think I have come to terms with my moment of discovery, a few months ago, of those few words captured in black and white. The sale of a human being, a child, on our busiest shopping street.

The reality of Manchester’s relationship with enslavement is something that we as a city are yet to fully appreciate and are only slowly beginning to unravel.

Andy Burnham’s article published in the Guardian on Friday is the most positive response yet by a UK prime minister to calls for full recognition and reparation for Britain’s role in transatlantic enslavement. It offers hope and new space for dialogue and development.

From the point of view of Britain’s collective memory and understanding, however, the statement leaves space for greater depth of engagement and reflection to inform a national and local understanding of the true scale and reality of this history.

While clearly acknowledging that “Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people”, the region’s former mayor chose to lead and close his piece by referring to Thomas Clarkson’s 1787 anti-slavery speech at Manchester Cathedral and the letter of solidarity from a group of Mancunians, collectively described as “workingmen”, during the Lancashire Cotton Famine.

On the surface, these seem natural touch points that a leader might use to draw inspiration from progressive moments in our history. However, understanding our local or national relationship with enslavement by focusing on a few short windows of solidarity and success in more than three centuries of brutalisation, dehumanisation and systemic profiting and reliance is like trying to tell the entire story of the Norman conquest through looking at a single panel on the Bayeux tapestry. In the dark. With just the light off your mobile phone.

Many readers, perhaps, will think this is splitting hairs. But consider for a moment the difference between these statements: “We were the first country to end the slave trade” v “It took us 250 years to end the slave trade.”

Or, from a Mancunian context: “Starving cotton workers stood in solidarity with enslaved people during the civil war” v “The whole economy and development of industrial Manchester relied on enslavement and public solidarity with the enslaved came about once the cotton had already been already embargoed for years.”

The 1863 Lincoln letter that Burnham refers to came 56 years after Britain had ended its own transatlantic slave trade and 25 years after slavery was ended in Britain’s colonies – a period during which Manchester’s economic reliance on enslavement actually grew.

In 2007 UK government and lottery funding was deployed in a nationwide programme to commemorate the bicentenary of the abolition of the British slave trade. This was the most widespread collective effort to date to conduct local projects around these themes and resulted in hundreds of exhibits and events.

One of the biggest reflections from communities and historians after that programme was the concern that in many areas it resembled a national “Wilberfest” – with a disproportionate focus and celebration of white abolitionists’ successes. We naturally want to tell ourselves a positive story about our national history, and by far the most comfortable aspect of it is abolition and the eventual success of those campaigns.

And as for Mancunians, we are rightly proud of our progressive history and working-class identity. The Cotton Famine story – that thousands of out-of-work operatives met on New Year’s Eve 1862 and voted to support the union blockade of vital cotton supplies to Lancashire on humanitarian, anti-slavery grounds – in particular, appeals to our best version of ourselves with its “workingmen” aspect. This is echoed in our memorial landscape, where the only public marker of the fundamental reliance of the emergence of the world’s first industrial city on enslavement is the statue of a white man: Abraham Lincoln.

That meeting and letter from Lincoln thanking these working men is a fact. But less than four years earlier, on the eve of civil war, the activist Sarah Parker Remond bravely declared from the stage of the city’s Athenaeum that she was “convinced that, as a rule, the heart of Old England beat truly to the anti-slavery cause, but in Manchester and Liverpool she had found something that approximated more to the pro-slavery spirit of America”.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

In the Guardian’s Cotton Capital series, published after it acknowledged its founders’ links to transatlantic enslavement, we showed how Manchester as a city, its institutions, and its textile production grew in symbiosis with the expansion of the Cotton Kingdom of the US South from 1790 to 1860 – at which point 80% of its raw cotton came from enslaved labour in America.

These facts were not lost on Frederick Douglass, who five weeks before his 1846 arrival in town succinctly and perfectly analysed the colonial-capitalist system, which the Manchester Men stood at the head of shaping and financing: “I will give you an invariable rule by which to ascertain the price of human flesh in the United States. When cotton gets up in the market in England, the price of human flesh gets up in the United States”. Seventeen more years of unprecedented slavery-based economic growth ensued before the Lincoln letter was drafted.

All of this, of course, came after the abolition of British slavery in the 1830s. New research into local anti-slavery debates for the forthcoming landmark exhibition at the city’s Science and Industry Museum exhibition (in partnership with the Guardian and the Scott Trust Legacies of Enslavement programme) has shown that calls for the abolition of British slavery surged into Manchester’s political debate directly in response to the uprising of up to 15,000 enslaved people in Demerara in 1823, only to drop off again until becoming a key election issue in 1832 after the Christmas Uprising of about 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica, which finally forced the British establishment into decisive action.

Burnham fails to mention in his piece that the British people were very much “made to pay for the wrongs of slavery” at that point. The eventual 1838 emancipation from British slavery was bought through a government loan of £20m in reparations to the enslavers, who re-invested much of it into British and imperial economic development. The formerly enslaved people received neither financial compensation nor land.

As the exhibition’s consultant historian, I would like to invite the prime minister to join us in Manchester next year, where we will be attempting to give a much broader and holistic context to re-ground our collective memory of our shared history. He would be welcome to invite the culture secretary and the heads of the Heritage Fund and Arts Council. He can even bring all the G20 leaders and the king, too, if he’d like.

As the UK builds towards the bicentenaries of abolition in 2033 and emancipation and compensation in 2038, we need to see commitments of serious investment into descendant-led programmes and multi-year community engagement and research to tell the fullest story possible.

By no means should we knock down or decry those aspirational moments that challenge us to live up to the highest ideals of solidarity and shared humanity. But Burnham’s call to “confront our complicated history” does not involve telling yourself the best, most comforting version of that story.

That erases the true scale of our reliance on the slavery system, the injustice of state compensation paid to enslavers, and the vital agency of Black abolitionists in forcing debates through mass uprisings, radical intellectual analysis, and public provocations and testimony. It also means we cannot fully understand or come to terms with the reality of our local and national history and achieve true repair and restitution.

Matthew Stallard is a writer and historian of industrialisation, colonisation and enslavement

Hegseth Faces Scrutiny From Both Parties in Aftermath of Midterms

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A looming impeachment push could put President Trump’s polarizing defense secretary in a standoff with Democrats and Republicans.

By Helene CooperGreg Jaffe and Eric Schmitt

Reporting from Washington

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth disclosed war plans in a chat on a commercial app that accidentally included a journalist, faced allegations of war crimes in the Caribbean and frustrations over his purge of top generals, and survived it all.

But now his fate is one of the biggest questions in the aftermath of the midterms. Even his own bosses acknowledge that the war against Iran, championed by the self-proclaimed “secretary of war,” was a major contributor to the Republican blood bath in the elections.

Mr. Hegseth was already battling hostile bipartisan forces in Congress, including an impeachment effort introduced by a Republican — Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

Congress still has not passed the Pentagon’s $1.5 trillion overall budget request, with lawmakers in both parties pointing to the combative defense secretary as among the reasons it has not moved forward.

A part of this defense funding measure, the National Defense Authorization Act, would fund salaries for troops, weapons production and everything in between. But it also remained stalled after months as lawmakers complained that the Pentagon had not consulted or communicated with them on a host of issues, including the war in Iran.

And President Trump’s efforts to push through another aspect of the funding, some $350 billion in military spending using a special budget bill that could not be filibustered, had not advanced either.

This was before the Democratic victories on Tuesday night.

Mr. Trump has stuck with his defense secretary, who has made amplifying the president on culture-war issues the center of his tenure at the Pentagon.

Mr. Trump told Fox News on election night that he did not intend to make any changes to his cabinet, and on Wednesday, when asked specifically about Mr. Hegseth, he told reporters, “I think he’s doing a very good job.”

Pentagon officials also say Mr. Hegseth is not going anywhere.

After Republican losses in the 2006 midterms, the first cabinet member to fall in President George W. Bush’s administration was Defense Secretary Donald H. Rumsfeld, a magnet for criticism for his management of the war in Iraq.

Mr. Bush had said he was keeping Mr. Rumsfeld, just days before he announced that his defense secretary was leaving.

“Donald Rumsfeld was gone the day after the Bush administration was repudiated by the American people in the 2006 midterm election,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat expected to be the next speaker of the House, said in an interview. “Why is Pete Hegseth still around?”

Mr. Hegseth posted a defiant video on social media Thursday. “We don’t back down, and that especially applies now,” he said. In the video, he bragged about tearing down Democratic “sacred cows,” like diversity, equity and inclusion, and repeated his oft-proclaimed aversion to transgender troops in the military.

“We will continue to drive President Trump’s agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100 percent committed to leading the department until the end of President Trump’s term in office,” Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, said in a statement.

Mr. Hegseth has been among the loudest champions of the eight-month-old war against Iran, which early on he declared the U. S. military was carrying out with “brutal efficiency.”

But in the aftermath of the election, the narrative has solidified that the G. O. P. thumping this week was largely because of the war, which led to higher prices at gas stations and grocery stores across the country. The conflict has also depleted the U. S. military’s global stockpiles of weapons.

Vice President JD Vance said in a social media post on Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war,” a statement that several Pentagon officials viewed as a direct shot across the bow at Mr. Hegseth.

Lawmakers and aides believe that the impeachment charges brought by Mr. Massie have a solid chance of passing the House with the support of several Republicans. G. O. P. leaders could delay an impeachment trial, and it would be exceedingly difficult to get two-thirds of the Senate to vote to convict him.

But the House vote alone was likely to constitute a bipartisan vote of no confidence in Mr. Hegseth by Congress at a critical time, as the administration was laboring to win approval of a Pentagon spending package and a substantial increase in the military budget.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Massie doubled down on his vow to press for impeachment. “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” he wrote on social media.

Mr. Massie has accused Mr. Hegseth of using his office to conduct political retaliation against his critics, including Senator Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, and of failing to get congressional authorization before the war in Iran.

In private conversations since Tuesday, Mr. Trump has laid much of the blame for his party’s midterm losses on his political team, according to two people who have spoken with him, and who described private conversations on the condition of anonymity. So far he has not appeared to blame Mr. Hegseth or Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U. S. Central Command, despite polls showing that the Iran war soured the public on the Trump administration.

People close to the president say he has indicated he wants to stand by his defense secretary, though some allies caution that the situation could change given how many Republican lawmakers have been complaining about Mr. Hegseth to the White House.

On Friday, Representative James R. Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told NewsNation that the decision was up to Mr. Trump. But, he added, “I can tell you with a high level of confidence that there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth.”

Some of Mr. Hegseth’s allies have quietly been talking about a way out: Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, who was elected governor on Tuesday, needs to pick her successor. To Mr. Hegseth’s allies, the seat would let the defense secretary leave the Pentagon on his own terms instead of being forced out.

But that would mean putting a divisive figure in another red-state Senate seat that Republicans would have to defend in 2028; several Republican congressional aides and Republican political operatives in Tennessee said such a move was unlikely.

If he stays, Mr. Hegseth will face headwinds on Capitol Hill.

Senator Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said it was critical to stop Mr. Hegseth’s purge at the Pentagon.

“We can certainly stop it bleeding, and that probably means the departure of Hegseth one way or the other,” Mr. Reed, who is expected to be the committee’s next chairman, said in an interview.

He said Mr. Hegseth had created a “toxic” climate, adding: “He’s weakened the mutual respect and trust that you must have for a military organization.”

Inside the Pentagon, some senior officers were already rethinking their retirement plans, said senior defense officials, who discussed sensitive personnel matters on the condition of anonymity. In the past year, Mr. Hegseth has blocked the promotions of more than 50 officers selected for general or admiral rank, often without a stated reason.

The officers had been chosen by boards made up of more senior military leaders. The nominations are good for 18 months, even though Mr. Hegseth declined to send them to the White House and Congress for final approval.

Many of those officers had planned to submit their retirement papers in the coming weeks, if not sooner. On Wednesday, senior military leaders had begun telling some of them to wait. Mr. Hegseth’s interventions are highly unusual and unpopular with military leaders and Congress.

A new secretary of defense could reverse Mr. Hegseth’s decisions on the officers, clearing their path for promotion and allowing them to continue their military careers.

If Mr. Hegseth survives the looming impeachment effort, he will also face scrutiny over other issues, congressional officials said.

They said Democrats would mount a robust oversight campaign on military spending that could include riders that force the Pentagon to comply with various congressional directives.

Democrats plan to hold hearings on the boat strikes, which have killed dozens of people in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific who the administration says were drug traffickers since the strikes began last year. They also intend to demand more information about the U. S. bases across the Middle East that were damaged in the war.

Representative Adam Smith, the Washington State Democrat who is poised to reclaim the chairmanship of the House Armed Services Committee, outlined his priorities in a letter to Democratic colleagues on Wednesday. He called for establishing an oversight subcommittee that would investigate “the illegal war against Iran, unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America, and the deployment of the military to U. S. cities.”

But some analysts warn that Democrats will have to walk a fine line between demanding accountability and appearing as if they are targeting American troops.

“The new Congress has a choice — it can opt for made-for-social-media-outrage show-trial hearings,” said Peter Feaver, a political science professor at Duke University. “Or it can try to repair the low-information environment surrounding defense policy with substance-focused oversight and engagement.”

Annie Karni, Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman contributed reporting.

Helene Cooper is a Pentagon correspondent for The Times. She was previously an editor, diplomatic correspondent and White House correspondent.

Greg Jaffe covers the Pentagon and the U. S. military for The Times.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Cornell Faculty Passes Vote of No Confidence in Administration

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

The vote is largely symbolic but serves as a sharp rebuke of campus leadership’s handling of a rape allegation that put the university in the national spotlight.

By Sharon Otterman and Alan Blinder

The Cornell faculty senate passed a resolution of no confidence in Cornell’s central administration on Friday, urging change in how the university should handle the persistent and troubling issue of sexual assault on its campus.

While largely symbolic, faculty members said that they believed the vote would serve as a rallying cry for those who wanted a new approach and new leadership to resolve a crisis that was sparked seven weeks ago, when a former student filed a lawsuit alleging she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024.

“This is just the start of what we’re hoping will be a wave of change,” said Ariana Kim, an associate professor of music who was one of the resolution’s co-sponsors, in an interview. She said she hoped that new leaders could step into positions of authority that “have a better pulse on what life and needs look like for our students.”

The final vote was 56 percent in favor, 37 percent against and 7 percent abstaining or not voting.

Cornell’s powerful board of trustees, which appointed Michael I. Kotlikoff as the permanent president after years of his service as provost, has ultimate control over the university’s leadership. It has shown no public sign of fraying in its support for him.

“The Board of Trustees remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus,” Anne Smalling, chair of the board of trustees, said in a statement.

“This confidence is rooted not only in the administration’s actions to date and plans moving forward, but also in its track record of navigating complex problems, as it did in restoring federal funding, preserving free speech, and leading the university through Covid,” she said.

The no-confidence resolution was proposed by more than a dozen of the university’s faculty senators in early October. Unlike similar resolutions at other universities, the resolution does not name specific university leaders, or call out exactly what mistakes were made.

Instead, its one sentence simply states that the faculty senate, an elected group of about 130 faculty members, “has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”

Supporters of the resolution have argued that its sweeping language was designed to indicate that the ongoing problem of campus sexual assault must be treated as a systemic issue. Passing the measure, they said, is meant to send a signal to students, alumni and the wider world that they know Cornell needs to do a better job in responding to allegations such as those made by the former undergraduate, known as Jane Doe.

Beginning in 2024, Cornell’s Title IX office conducted a lengthy investigation into her allegations and issued punishments to the seven men that she accused. Two were expelled; two others were suspended; and three more were given lighter punishments, including writing reflection papers. But critics have argued that those punishments were not enough and that Cornell’s police should have done a better job convincing the local district attorney to bring the case before a grand jury.

The men have denied wrongdoing, and none of them have been charged with a crime.

More recently, critics have faulted Cornell’s central administration for taking too long to respond publicly to the lawsuit after it was first reported on by the Cornell Daily Sun on Sept. 18, leaving toxic rumors and discourse to build online.

Mr. Kotlikoff waited more than two weeks to make a public statement about the case. Mr. Kotlikoff did not pledge to suspend fraternity parties on campus until the public relations crisis over the case intensified and nearly two more weeks passed.

“Instead of taking some kind of systemic approach as leaders, the Cornell central administration has had a reactive and piecemeal approach, which has eroded the trust of students, faculty and staff,” said Rita Lieberwitz, a faculty co-sponsor of the resolution, who spoke in favor of it in late October. “They don’t seem to have the desire, either, to really lead systemic change.”

While faculty no-confidence votes remain rare, they have picked up in the last decade, driven by increasing tensions on college campuses, including over how presidents handled Covid-19 policies, protests over the bombing of Gaza and sexual misconduct, said Willis Jones, a higher education professor at Southern Methodist University.

University faculty do not have the power to remove administrators. But even the calling of such a vote can sting, putting frictions on public view and unsettling boards eager to protect their schools’ reputations. And because the academic world has historically embraced the notion of shared governance — dividing campus power among boards, administrators and faculty members — the votes can upend fragile alliances and traditions.

“While no-confidence votes don’t mean presidents automatically lose their jobs or will be reprimanded by their boards, they deliver a publicly damaging message that can ultimately lead to their demise,” Michael T. Nietzel and Charles M. Ambrose wrote in a book published this year, “No Confidence: When College Faculty Turn Against Their Presidents.”

Some presidents, of course, have stayed in their jobs for years after losing no-confidence votes. Eli Capilouto, for instance, remains atop the University of Kentucky more than two years after such a vote, and Laura Rosenbury still leads Barnard College, though the faculty voted no confidence in her in October 2024.

But Lawrence H. Summers resigned as Harvard’s president in 2006, less than a year after a no-confidence ballot. And Minouche Shafik stepped down from Columbia University’s presidency about three months after losing a similar vote in 2024.

Surveys and studies have found that roughly half of campus leaders who lose no-confidence votes leave within a year, though it is not always clear how much the votes factored into those moves.

“The full impact of many no-confidence votes cannot be known until there’s been sufficient time to allow a full assessment of the sequelae,” Dr. Nietzel and Dr. Ambrose wrote. “Often, what is said and what unfolds in the immediate aftermath of a vote is very different from the final disposition of the matter.”

Last week, faculty senators voted 76 to 48 against delaying the vote until after an investigation into the Jane Doe abuse allegations, commissioned by the Cornell board, is completed. It will be led by Sally Yates, a former U. S. deputy attorney general.

Benjamin Leynse and Vimal Patel contributed reporting.

Sharon Otterman is a Times reporter covering higher education, public health and other issues facing New York City.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

Dizzying Week for Investors as Politics, A. I. and the Economy Collide

The New York Times November 06, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

With a lot of information to process in a short time, many market watchers said the moves were extreme — in both directions.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Joe Rennison

Investors faced a whipsaw week in which stocks jumped after Democrats swept the midterm elections, then fell on renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence industry, and ended on Friday somewhere in between.

The S&P 500 index was set for its fourth-straight weekly loss, of around 2 percent, a modest result that masked wrenching swings from day to day. The index had gained as much as 1.8 percent and fallen as far as 3 percent for the week, the biggest range of movement in a single week since April.

Many investors and analysts said the market moves were extreme — both up and down. By Friday, some equilibrium appeared to emerge: The S&P 500 rose roughly 0.5 percent, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq, which was at the forefront of a rout the day before, gained even more.

Investors have had a lot of information to process, seemingly all at once. Pre-election jitters gave way to a landslide victory for Democrats on a scale not seen in decades. The relief at a clear result quickly gave way to worries of tougher A. I. regulation, compounded by underwhelming earnings reports by some key industry players. And finally, on Friday, stronger-than-expected data on the U. S. labor market showed the economy remained solid.

“We are telling our advisers to buy the dips,” said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group. “The economy is not doing badly.”

Others also saw opportunity in the upheaval, expecting stocks to bounce higher. “As painful as it sounds, I think this is a dip-buying opportunity, not the start of a large decline in A. I.,” said Tom Lee, co-founder and head of research at Fundstrat.

Broadly, investors and analysts said they expected the market to rally into the end of the year, with bouts of volatility along the way, as plans for how newly elected Democrats will oversee the A. I. build-out take shape. The current Republican-led Congress and White House have adopted a largely hands-off approach to the A. I. industry over the past two years.

“While we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results, we do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” said Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management.

Investors were already on edge before this event-filled week, with periodic sell-offs reflecting concerns about the A. I. industry’s performance, despite bumper profit reports from many of the companies at the forefront of the technology.

A rush to build data centers had led companies to borrow enormous sums in debt markets, with no promise that returns would later justify the expenditure. And with companies all trying to grow at the same time, supply chain bottlenecks had put real-world constraints on those aggressive business plans.

Then there were the midterms, with the potential for a contested result and legal challenges, and the outlook for other important market factors, like the war with Iran and the path of interest rates, hanging in the balance.

As the voting result became clear, stocks rose on Wednesday in what traders call a “relief rally,” fanned by a surge of buying from investors who had been waiting on the sidelines until the campaign was over.

A day later, that exuberance began to fade. Two chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, had reported earnings that fell short of expectations, dragging down others in the industry, including heavyweights like Nvidia, which exert a heavy influence on market indexes.

Analysts assessing the financial impact of the Democrats’ electoral sweep pointed to a fundamental, though still modest, reassessment of the growth prospects for A. I. businesses. The shift in power at statehouses around the country led many to suggest that stricter regulation of data centers could slow plans in places like Texas, where the world’s largest tech companies are rapidly building out computing capacity.

The S&P 500 opened slightly lower on Thursday, but the sell-off quickly gathered speed, extending into more panicked trading that fed off investors’ long-held concerns about the assumptions underlying the lofty valuations of some A. I. companies. The S&P 500 ended the day with its largest decline in nearly two years. The fallout reverberated around the world.

Markets across Asia, which were closed during the worst of the selling on Wall Street, had a chaotic open to trading on Friday. The severity set off a 20-minute trading halt at the tech-heavy KOSPI, which plunged 6 percent by the end of the session, pulled down by the memory-chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 sank about 6 percent, dropping the index into a bear market, defined as a 20 percent fall from its recent peak.

But as trading got underway in Europe the tide began to turn, with some semiconductor companies in the region posting gains.

The latest U. S. jobs report, released before U. S. markets opened on Friday, also eased investors’ worries. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than analysts were expecting, and the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1 percent.

When Wall Street began trading, markets stabilized. The Nasdaq rose more than 1 percent, driven by a rebound in chipmakers. Nvidia gained 3 percent, reversing some of the previous day’s loss.

For Mohit Kumar, a strategist at Jefferies, the recent turmoil was not a sign of the unwinding of the A. I. trade, even if it is subject to tougher oversight in the years ahead. “One could argue,” he wrote in a research note, “that having more guardrails makes A. I. investment more sustainable in the medium term.”

Reporting was contributed by Aruni Soni from New York, Sui-Lee Wee from Bangkok, and Jason Karaian and Eshe Nelson from London.

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.
