Strong Hiring Reinforces a Sturdy Job Market

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Unemployment fell in October, extending years of stability for a U. S. work force threatened by inflation and artificial intelligence.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. The average is calculated as a three-month moving average.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

By Sydney Ember

Businesses added workers at a vigorous clip in October, continuing a string of healthy hiring that underscored the job market’s stability even as inflation and concerns about investments in artificial intelligence pressure other aspects of the economy.

The report affirmed that the labor market remained solid and even showed some glimmers of momentum that could begin to relieve persistent anxiety among workers about their ability to find work. Employers added 165,000 on a seasonally adjusted basis last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday, and the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1 percent.

Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000, bringing the average increase per month over the past three months to 137,000. The labor force participation rate ticked up for the third month in a row.

“Workers are still nervous about the current state of the job market,” said Daniel Zhao, the chief economist at Glassdoor, a career site. “But at the very least, today’s report is a step in the right direction towards building up that worker confidence again.”

A big question hanging over the labor market, and the economy more broadly, is the impact of A. I. on jobs. Investors’ concerns about the trajectory of investments in the technology sent stocks plummeting on Thursday.

So far, A. I. does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses despite some headline-grabbing announcements. The job gains last month were relatively widespread, with a range of sectors adding positions. Even some white-collar industries thought to be heavily exposed to technological disruption added jobs. Professional and business services, which includes accountants, lawyers and other office work, gained 70,000 positions last month. The financial activities sector tacked on 7,000 jobs.

Note: Data is seasonally adjusted. Charts represent cumulative percent change since January 1, 2022.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

But there are some indications that the rise of A. I. is one factor depressing hiring, particularly for entry-level positions. One reason may be companies are choosing to invest in the technology rather than adding workers. Employers may also be holding off on hiring as they assess A. I.’s capabilities.

“We have seen this slowdown at times in the pace of hiring because firms’ current work force can be more productive,” said Courtney Shupert, an economist at MacroPolicy Perspectives, a forecasting firm. “And so that just changes the urgency with which you need to hire additional workers.”

Even people who do have jobs have been losing leverage, as wage growth has slowed and inflation has eroded their spending power. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent compared with the same time last year, well below the rate of price increases.

The glacial wage growth is likely to keep the Federal Reserve’s focus squarely focused on tamping down inflation. The central bank held rates steady at its meeting last month and will convene again to consider rates in December.

On the flip side, A. I. is fueling a surge in demand for workers in construction, manufacturing and other industries tied to the data center build out. Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs in October. Nonresidential specialty trade contractors added 8,000 jobs.

NSH USA, an industrial equipment manufacturer based in Albany, N. Y., which refurbishes wheels used on trains and subway cars, is benefiting from the A. I. boom. Some of the company’s machines are used by manufacturers of diesel generators, for instance, which are in hot demand to provide backup power to data centers.

But finding enough skilled labor has become more challenging now that electricians, welders and workers with similar technical experience are in such high demand, said David Davis, the company’s president and chief operating officer.

“It’s definitely been more difficult as of late,” he said. “You see that in the salaries and the wages for the skilled technicians; it’s gone up dramatically.”

NSH has added about two dozen workers to its payroll in the past year and a half, and now has about 150 workers in the United States, most of them in the Albany area. The company has 10 open positions listed, and would hire more workers if it could find them, Mr. Davis said.

Note: Data is not seasonally adjusted. Inflation data is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index. Wages are year-over-year changes in average hourly earnings. October 2025 is missing from the inflation data because of the government shutdown.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By Keith Collins and Jacqueline Gu

In addition to the October jobs report, there have been some other tentative signs that the labor market may be perking up. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may feel more confident in their ability to get new jobs. Job openings also rose.

Yet the remarkable stretch of labor market stability and low unemployment has not felt favorable for many Americans, especially those without jobs. The average duration of unemployment rose to 27 weeks in October, the highest level since the end of 2021.

The job market has been especially depressed for certain groups. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates, for instance, stood at about 5.2 percent in the third quarter of the year, according to an analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, well above the overall unemployment rate.

After jumping in September, the unemployment rate for Black workers fell back a bit to 6.6 percent, that level far exceeds the unemployment rate for white workers.

“I still don’t think we can pull out the champagne and start the party,” said Liz Wilke, the chief economist at LinkedIn. “If you are looking for a job in this economy, I don’t think it’s easy.”

Hal Beresford, 43, has been applying for work since he was laid off from his job as a senior finance manager at a large consumer goods company last November. He has secured interviews, but has not had success landing a new position, despite having master’s degrees in public policy and business administration.

Unable to pay his mortgage, he recently sold his townhouse in Cincinnati and is living in a friend’s basement in Pasadena, Calif. When he is not job hunting, he fills his time building algorithms for prediction markets using A. I. He is thinking about becoming a math tutor.

“I applied for a bunch of jobs and I had a ton of interviews — none of them went through,” Mr. Beresford said.

The overall labor market sluggishness, alongside frustration with rising prices, is one reason that many Americans are downbeat about the economy, a sentiment that powered the blue wave in this week’s midterm elections.

“The dynamism has been dampened quite a bit,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. “People don’t necessarily feel good about that.”

Ben Casselman contributed reporting.

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

How Farmers’ Frustration With Trump’s Policies Helped Democrats

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Anger over tariffs and higher costs because of the war in Iran led many Republican farmers and ranchers to vote blue — or stay home.

By Kevin Draper

While voters of all stripes rebuked President Trump’s tariff policies and the war with Iran on Tuesday, those issues were top of mind in farming and ranching communities across the country, catapulting Democrats into top positions in Iowa, Kansas and Texas.

That’s because farmers “have kind of been like the canary in the coal mine,” said Lesly McNitt, the vice president of public policy at the National Corn Growers Association. Over the past two years, farmers and ranchers immediately felt the effects of some of the Trump administration’s decisions and executive orders, she said.

Months before tariffs drove up the prices of imported consumer goods, China stopped buying American soybeans in retaliation, depriving farmers of expected income. Weeks before gas prices soared, the war in Iran caused a spike in fertilizer prices, raising farm costs.

Democrats now face the challenge of finding long-term ways to support farmers and ranchers, negating the uncertainty of recent years.

The biggest piece of legislation that Democrats can tackle is the five-year farm bill, which has passed in the House and is awaiting consideration in the Senate, where it will need 60 votes to end debate and move to a full vote. That could happen before the Democratic-majority House and Senate are seated in January, but legislators are more likely to approve a one-year extension instead, and the new Congress will have to take up the bill again next year.

Corn-heavy states will also look to Congress to allow the year-round sale of 15 percent ethanol fuel blends. Dairy groups have been clamoring to reform visa programs for temporary agricultural workers.

“We want steadiness with what is going on,” said Kyle Hemmert, a Republican rancher in western Kansas. “That is where Republicans have failed so bad for Kansas and the nation. That’s why they got their butt whipped.”

While farmers welcomed the $12 billion farm bailout disbursed early this year, several groups said the funding was a Band-Aid that didn’t address deeper problems in the industry. The additional $15 billion in promises that the Trump administration made to farmers and ranchers — including $8 billion in aid tied to high diesel prices in the weeks leading up to Election Day — did little to sway Republicans.

And neither did Mr. Trump. At his final rally before the election, in central Kansas, the president bragged that farmers had told him he was the “best president in the history of presidents for the farmers and ranchers” before admonishing ranchers — not for the first time — to produce cattle faster.

(The gestation period for a heifer is about nine months, and it takes about two years to raise a calf before it can be slaughtered for beef.)

It was not a winning closing message: Kansans elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the U. S. Senate for the first time since 1932.

The biggest loss of Republican support came in Seward, Ford and Finney Counties, rural areas in southwest Kansas that are home to around 25 percent of all beef production in the country. The region is heavily Latino, and was the target of federal immigration raids in September that the cattle industry roundly denounced.

In 2024, Mr. Trump won 66 percent of the vote in Finney County. On Tuesday, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican seeking a second term, won just 47 percent of it. Democrats did not even run a candidate from the area for the Kansas House of Representatives in 2022, and their candidate lost by more than 30 points in 2024.

This year the party won. The seat was one of up to 20 that Democrats may have flipped in the Kansas Statehouse after votes are counted and certified.

Martin Rosas, president of the United Food and Commercial Workers union local that represents Kansas meatpacking plant workers, said that after the raids he had received a concerned call from the state’s senior Republican senator, Jerry Moran. He did not receive one from Mr. Marshall.

“Everyone you talk to is very conscious that the Republican Party is not a friend of the working people,” Mr. Rosas said. Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, spoke to those workers after the raids and told them that immigration policy was decided on the federal level, and that the way to change it was to get out and vote, he said.

The economy of southwest Kansas, from dairies and feedlots to farming and trucking, relies on meatpacking plants operating at full capacity. “We hear a lot from farmers in southwest Kansas that are not happy,” Mr. Rosas said. “The gas prices, fertilizer and war in Iran have triggered their anxiety, and the party of Trump no longer identifies their needs.”

Mr. Hemmert, the Kansas rancher, said he didn’t like Mr. Marshall but had voted for him anyway. He considered voting for Mr. Hamilton but disagreed with his reluctant support of legal abortion, illustrating the challenge Democrats will have to hold on to rural voters in the long run in ways that go beyond agricultural issues.

In Iowa, even though Republicans won in many rural areas, there was a swing toward Democrats. In the second-biggest farming state, Democrats won the governorship, a Senate seat and three of four House seats. All were held by Republicans.

The Iowa Farmers Union doesn’t typically endorse candidates for national office. But it decided to do so this summer, after two years of what its president, Aaron Lehman, called “policy blunders” by the Trump administration.

The Farmers Union asked for, and expected, Iowa’s all-Republican congressional delegation to push back against tariffs, the war in Iran and cheap imported beef, he said.

The state’s farmers were “really disappointed that they did not see an Iowa voice standing up in reaction to these proposed policies from the administration,” Mr. Lehman said.

Some farm organizations endorse candidates closer to Election Day, concerned more with supporting the front-runner than trying to influence the outcome. But the Iowa Farmers Union endorsed a Democratic slate in September, hoping it would change the minds of some people who traditionally vote Republican.

“We expected that we would feel some blowback,” Mr. Lehman said. “And in fact, the opposite happened. We were hearing from folks saying, ‘I’m glad someone is standing up and saying this.’”

Sid Miller, the departing Republican agriculture commissioner in Texas, did not mince words about how his party fared on Tuesday. “It was a zombie apocalypse,” he said. “It was our Waterloo or our Little Bighorn. We got annihilated.”

Mr. Miller was not on the ballot Tuesday after he lost in the primary when Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, backed his opponent. That candidate lost on Tuesday to the Democratic nominee, Clayton Tucker. Mr. Abbott also lost.

Voter opposition to data centers was the biggest factor in Republicans losses in Texas, Mr. Miller said. He said farmers and ranchers opposed data centers because they were largely built near their land and the transmission lines ran along their farms. Ranchers were also hurt when the president’s plan to import more beef lowered the price they received for their cattle, and farmers had to pay more for fertilizer and diesel.

The thought process of many of these voters, he said, was “I’m a Trump supporter through and through, and they’re killing us, so I’m not voting for them or I’m not going to vote at all.”

But perhaps the biggest surprise has come from the U. S. Senate race in Mississippi, where Scott Colom, the Democrat, was leading the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 1,813 votes. Votes were still being counted.

Mr. Colom worked to frame Ms. Hyde-Smith, a rancher, as out of touch and unsympathetic to soaring costs, calling her “Cindy High Prices.” Eight months after Ms. Hyde-Smith told a local news anchor that “there are plenty of other proteins to choose from,” Mr. Colom dropped a campaign ad that went quickly went viral.

“Pick another protein?” says a man flipping burgers on a backyard grill in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.” (Except for chicken, shoppers aren’t picking other proteins.)

If the unofficial results hold, Mississippi voters, just like those in Kansas, Iowa and Texas, will have picked another party.

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.

Kevin Draper is a business correspondent covering the agriculture industry. He can be reached at kevin. draper@nytimes. com or kevin. draper@protonmail. com.

The Markets Are on a Yo-Yo. You Don’t Have to Be.

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

your money

Feeling a bit wobbly? Here are four things to consider that might provide some peace of mind.

By Ron Lieber

Ron Lieber is in Year 19 and counting of urging calm when things seem crazy.

Market go down. Market go up.

We’ve seen this kind of two-day volatility before, dozens or maybe hundreds of times for the gray-haired among us. But this go-round does feel a bit different in the wake of a political earthquake.

And that’s fine. Markets are indeed about the feels — what humans or the trading robots they have programmed believe will happen to companies next. And big surprises that augur unpredictable change fire circuits in the brain.

So by all means, do something. But that something isn’t necessarily buying or selling stocks. Instead, remind yourself that you are a person of above-average reserve and emotional intelligence as you consider the following points.

It’s nearly impossible to consistently predict how individual stocks or the overall market will perform in the short or medium term. That’s why so many people invest in index funds, dropping bits of money in at regular intervals and leaving it there for decades.

For those who don’t invest that way, ask yourself this: Is this the moment to see whether you are some kind of market seer? Did you predict that President Trump would win in 2016? Win again in 2024? Does the “gridlock is good for the markets” thesis going around this week make sense to you — or actually defy logic? And do any of us have any earthly idea how Mr. Trump might behave now, if we ever did?

It’s hard to forecast markets. It’s difficult to game out politics. Put the two together, and it’s an advertisement for ceasing any guesswork, holding all stocks and keeping them for the long term, come what may.

How much money did you earn in the past 12 months? And how much money did your portfolio throw off?

If you’re not retired or otherwise out of the work force, that first number is probably higher than the second one. That makes your income at least as important as your investments in any short-term personal risk assessment.

There are times when the warning signs on employability are as plain as day. This week, News Corp’s chief executive, Robert Thomson, gleefully discussed how artificial intelligence offers “so many more choices in reading voices” for HarperCollins’s audiobooks. Audiobook narrators — and I’ve been one twice at Harper — should keep an eye on this, even as the publisher’s chief executive has said it remains committed to live human beings.

Listen for how other executives talk in public, and ask questions in your own industry that might yield indications of your own personal risk and the advisability of a career pivot.

And if your income is at risk, there is no shame in wanting to sell some stock to put your portfolio on more stable footing or contribute to an emergency fund.

Let big events in the world — a change in power in Washington, the imposition of tariffs, a war, zillions of dollars flowing to artificial intelligence — be a trigger to look at the big events on your own short- to medium-term calendar.

My younger daughter just started middle school. There’s a pretty good chance she’ll go to college in seven years.

As someone who needed a lot of financial aid, I can’t bear the thought of her savings’ being at risk. Earlier this year, with A. I. driving so much of the stock market and having seen excellent returns over a decade, my wife and I dialed back the equities portion of our 529 account by 20 percentage points.

This is not a recommendation, and it wasn’t an attempt to time the market. It was deeply personal — a measured attempt to reduce anxiety now with the sober knowledge that there could be a large cost in dollars if stocks have many more great years.

On Thursday night, after a bad day in the stock market, Mr. Trump logged on to social media and blamed “Dumocrats” for having brought losses to Americans’ 401(k)s. This is pretty rich from a guy whose tariff adventures have sent markets on many single-day benders in his second term.

But to even discuss his market commentary risks a kind of counterproductive short-termism. Your price is not yesterday’s closing price or today’s or the day after Election Day in 2028.

Your price is Day 1 of the kid’s going to college, or the moment seven years from now when you want your down payment fund to hit the magic number you’ve set, or the day before your retirement or the day after you die and an outsize bequest stuns the development director of some deserving institution.

As ever, there is no guarantee that the stock market will get you there or that the labor market will allow you to save regularly. But if you tune out short-term noise, you’ll probably feel better on the path to that day.

Ron Lieber has been the Your Money columnist since 2008. His beat is beating the system.

Trump Chief of Staff Accused of Blocking Healthy-Food Policies to Attract Donations

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

In a no-holds-barred interview with Joe Rogan, Calley Means, a former top health adviser, accused Susie Wiles of repeatedly bowing to lobbying pressures and fixating on campaign contributions.

By Christina Jewett and Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Calley Means, who resigned as a top federal health official two weeks ago after clashing with the White House, on Friday accused President Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, of bowing to “unrelenting” pressure from industry lobbyists while prioritizing political fund-raising over Americans’ health.

In a two-hour interview with the podcaster Joe Rogan, Mr. Means said that Ms. Wiles withheld support from his efforts to make children’s diets healthier, citing the need for sugar industry money. He said her team demanded more approvals of flavored e-cigarettes, a top priority for major tobacco companies that donated at least $20 million to the G. O. P. in 2026. And he said they gave in to heavy lobbying from the kratom industry to relax proposed restrictions on products often referred to as “gas station heroin.”

“Susie said to me many times: ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms,’” Mr. Means said.

In recent days, Ms. Wiles has become a target of criticism and finger-pointing in an escalating blame game after Republicans’ stunning losses in the midterm elections. In a post on Truth Social on Friday afternoon, Mr. Trump announced that Ms. Wiles would leave her post on Monday and Stephen Miller, a top White House adviser, would replace her.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Ms. Wiles and the White House were not immediately available to comment. The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services have responded to past allegations of lobbying influence on the administration’s health care policies by saying the administration consistently acted in the best interest of the American people.

Mr. Means, a close ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. who helped build the Make America Healthy Again movement, avoided criticizing Mr. Kennedy or Mr. Trump. He directed his ire almost entirely at Ms. Wiles, a former lobbyist and political consultant, who he asserted had “spent her career taking money,” including from the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries and from the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, a former client.

Mr. Means framed Ms. Wiles and her top deputies as welcoming lobbyists into the White House while sidelining Mr. Kennedy and infantilizing Mr. Trump. Mr. Means made a larger argument about the corrosive role of corporate money in politics, but also suggested that the president should “exorcise” Ms. Wiles and her aides “from the White House.”

Ms. Wiles’s policy interests also aligned with those benefiting her family, Mr. Means said, claiming that any corporation that hired her daughter, Katie Wiles, a lobbyist for Continental Strategy, “was getting a high priority.”

“So if you’re a special interest and you want to get something done, the secret’s out,” Mr. Means said. “You pay Susie’s daughter, and it was openly discussed when they had a client.”

Mr. Means’s tirade against Ms. Wiles, while depicting Mr. Kennedy as a “hero,” comes as Democrats are beginning to consider their new powers to investigate what they view as the most destructive actions of the Trump administration. Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who will lead the influential Senate Finance Committee, has already announced an investigation into Mr. Kennedy’s role in “corruption favoring” of the tobacco and kratom industries.

In the podcast interview, Mr. Means said the administration fumbled a series of issues that had been crucial to the MAHA coalition that had helped propel Mr. Trump to the presidency.

The missteps included an executive order aimed at supporting the production of glyphosate, the herbicide tied to cancer that many MAHA supporters want to see restricted. The order was issued in February, as the Supreme Court was about to hear oral arguments in a case that would determine whether Bayer, the maker of glyphosate, could receive immunity from lawsuits alleging the weedkiller caused cancer.

Mr. Means asserted that military leaders did not believe the order was necessary to protect national security, as the White House said. He described how one of Ms. Wiles’s deputies dropped the executive order on a table and said it was nonnegotiable.

“I read it, I said, ‘This is a political disaster,’” Mr. Means recalled. The aide was insistent. “Please inform Bobby. And this is not up for discussion.” He pointedly told Mr. Means that the health secretary should not call the president, adding, “Susie then called Bobby’s office and said, ‘We’re not discussing this.’”

The executive order was announced the next day, infuriating MAHA leaders.

Mr. Means also claimed that Dr. Heidi Overton, then a White House health official whom Mr. Trump has since nominated to lead the Food and Drug Administration, had helped Justice Department officials create legal arguments urging the Supreme Court to review the glyphosate case and supporting Bayer’s position.

The Supreme Court sided with Bayer in a decision that gave the company broad liability protection and infuriated many in the MAHA movement.

Mr. Means joined the White House after working on Mr. Kennedy’s campaign and helping to broker the partnership between the secretary and Mr. Trump; he later went to work directly for Mr. Kennedy. He is primarily interested in the secretary’s food agenda and has not been involved in more controversial policy-making on vaccines.

But in the interview, he accused Ms. Wiles of pressuring Mr. Kennedy to downplay vaccine safety while relying on the work of a pollster, Tony Fabrizio, who receives funding from the pharmaceutical industry.

Mr. Means also described how some of his efforts to draft policies to make the food supply healthier were thwarted, such as one aimed at pushing the food industry to address whether the amount of sugar in children’s diets was appropriate.

“And that’s where Susie told me we can’t do that,” Mr. Means said. “‘I need the sugar industry money.’”

Mr. Means also said that Dr. Marty Makary, the former F. D. A. commissioner, was “pounded” in numerous meetings to approve flavored e-cigarettes, which James Blair, a former deputy of Ms. Wiles, framed as “a core midterm issue.”

Dr. Makary left the agency in May over the disputes on the matter. Mr. Means said that Dr. Overton did what Dr. Makary would not: “She wrote up a policy to relax standards on fruit-flavored vapes.”

Mr. Means said that his “last straw” came after months of delays on his effort to arrive at a definition of ultraprocessed foods, which could eventually lead to regulation. He said that he and Mr. Kennedy went to Ms. Wiles, who denied any special interest influence on the matter.

“Lied to us to our face,” he said, recounting that he later heard her say we need to “do something” about MAHA.

Mr. Means said he believed Democrats were also guilty of ceding to similar influences and said the solution could come from a presidential candidate running on the issue of amending the Constitution to take money out of politics.

“Americans need to understand that if they are getting whipped up and excited about policy promises through our existing structure, they are being duped and gaslighted and lied to,” he said. “We need to have systemic reform.”

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

Secrecy, debt and soaring fuel costs all contributed to the Odyssey’s downfall. Here’s an inside look at how the “endless cruise” unraveled.

The Odyssey, docked last week in Cambodia. Its main lender has since taken control of the ship. Credit... Soveit Yarn/Reuters

Supported by

By Ceylan Yeğinsu

He was either going to come out a genius or a fool.

That’s what Benjamin Schatz, a Harvard-educated lawyer, says he told his friends two years ago when he invested more than $500,000 to buy cabins and equity in Villa Vie Residences, a start-up offering a multiyear residential cruise.

Last week, its cruise ship, called the Odyssey, ground to a sudden halt in Cambodia when the ship’s operators announced that they could no longer afford fuel. Given hours to disembark, the Odyssey’s 200 passengers, some of whom had sold their homes and used their retirement savings to live on the ship, found themselves stranded in Southeast Asia. On Wednesday, Villa Vie’s main lender took control of the ship, which was still laden with passenger belongings. The Odyssey is now headed to Singapore, where it may be auctioned off.

But Mr. Schatz, 67, a former adviser to President Bill Clinton, isn’t ready to call himself a fool. “It was a glorious experience,” he said, “and one that I’m not prepared to end.”

Unlike short-term vacation cruises, Villa Vie was marketed as an affordable “home at sea” for retirees and remote workers with extended port calls for deeper cultural immersion. Passengers were free to hop on and off at different ports, or to stay on board for months or years on end. The cruise offered several residency programs, including suite ownership for the life of the ship, ranging from about $120,000 to $440,000, plus fixed monthly fees of $3,500 to $11,000; a five-year ownership plan starting at about $50,000 along with monthly fees; and short-term flexible rentals.

When Mr. Schatz bought two cabins for himself and his mother, and invested even more money to become a “founder” — meaning he had also purchased equity in the company — he knew the risks of backing a start-up. But he was drawn to the slow pace of travel and the opportunity to explore countries over several days or weeks. He chose not to consult a financial adviser, fully expecting to be warned against the investment. In recent years, several residential cruise ventures have collapsed, undone by high maintenance costs and fees that failed to cover operating expenses.

Before starting Villa Vie Residences, its executive chairman, Mikael Petterson, had backed a residential cruise called Life at Sea from Miray Cruises. That program collapsed before the voyage began, mainly because it was not able to finalize the purchase of a ship. For his next venture, Mr. Petterson made sure to secure a ship. After months of delays and millions of dollars in repairs, the Odyssey finally set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, with 125 passengers.

Beyond the easy pace of the voyage, passengers were united by a shared love for travel and a quiet determination to avoid isolation in retirement. Through self-organized excursions, entertainment and late-night gatherings, the residents built a community on the water.

“It was like a traveling village of really interesting, quirky people,” Mr. Schatz said. “I used to call us the Odd-at-Sea.”

In interviews, many residents described life on the Odyssey as something that could never be replicated on land, and that was worth doing almost anything to save — even lending millions of dollars of their own money to keep the ship afloat when things began to unravel.

This account of what happened in the months leading up to the collapse of Villa Vie Residences and the seizure of its ship is based on interviews with nine founders and 16 other passengers, along with dozens of text messages and internal communications shared between passengers and the ship’s executives and reviewed by The New York Times.

When the voyage was suspended last week, Villa Vie blamed “extraordinary increases in fuel costs” caused by the war with Iran and said it was working to restructure financially. Mr. Petterson told The Times in a phone interview that before the war, sales had been strong, with the company poised to become profitable in early 2026.

In interviews, several residents with founder status painted a different picture. They said Mr. Petterson and the company’s chief executive, Kathy Villalba, called a meeting in November 2025 and announced that they were two weeks away from running out of money. Ms. Villalba did not respond to phone calls or emails.

“Founders knew surprisingly little about the state of the finances,” Mr. Schatz said. “Few, if any, understood that all the money from cabin sales was spent immediately to keep the ship afloat.” (Mr. Petterson disputes this and says he shared financial information with founders every few months.)

Shortly after the meeting in November, Mr. Petterson pitched founders of the Odyssey on a luxury sister brand called Avora Residences, with its own ship, that would operate in parallel to Villa Vie; residents of the two ships would be able to share privileges. In interviews, several founders said they agreed to invest money in the new company but declined to offer exact amounts. They hoped that Avora’s higher prices would generate enough profit to offset the Odyssey’s financial losses.

But in January, Avora debuted as a separate company, creating a competing brand with a separate ownership structure but with Mr. Petterson and Ms. Villalba still at the helm, Mr. Schatz said.

Most of the ship’s other residents were unaware of the extent of the financial troubles, as the founders had signed nondisclosure agreements and were not allowed to share any information discussed in meetings with Villa Vie executives. Once Avora was announced publicly, the messaging to Odyssey passengers from management was optimistic, with talk of improving the Odyssey’s pool and building a casino in the main dining hall. (Neither was done.)

Dana Teton, a 71-year-old retired medical equipment salesman, spent months at a time on the ship. He said that passengers suspected there were issues with the ship based on last-minute changes to itineraries, but they didn’t know how bad things were until the summer, around when the ship reached Singapore.

“For a long time the stress level on the ship was essentially zero because everything was taken care of,” he added. “No airports, no security lines, no immigration, no customs, no packing or unpacking. It was a dream.”

Within months of the Avora pitch, the Odyssey was back in crisis mode. The war with Iran was underway, and fuel costs were skyrocketing. Mr. Petterson once again asked the founders for immediate loans but was turned away. So in April, he sent a message to the rest of the passengers, seeking a $3 million emergency loan for fuel costs with the promise of 12 to 24 percent annual interest rates, according to documents shared on Circle, the ship’s internal communications app, and viewed by The Times.

Sharon Myers, a 62-year-old retired Canadian paralegal, was on a rent-to-own plan for her cabin on the Odyssey. As a solo traveler who wanted to avoid the tedium of packing, unpacking and moving between hotels, she found the continuous travel routine with like-minded people to be a seamless fit. So when the company asked passengers for help, she was tempted. But when she asked for the loan agreement, she discovered that the funds were being directed not to Villa Vie but to an umbrella company called Residential Cruise Holdings.

Ms. Myers said it felt like a scam. “There was a real divide between realistic people who could see what was coming and people who could not face reality,” she said. Several passengers who participated in the loan program said they had yet to receive any repayments.

Mr. Petterson told The Times that Residential Cruise Holdings was intended to become the future parent company of Villa Vie and Avora. Legal restrictions prevented Villa Vie from taking out additional loans, he said. Instead, the loan was made through Residential Cruise Holdings and was intended to cover fuel expenses for the Odyssey, he added. He declined to comment on the status of repayments.

In late July, while the ship was docked in Singapore, the company told the ship’s residents that it had run out of money. Mr. Petterson again asked for loans to cover fuel and operational costs and to prevent the ship from being impounded, according to messages on Circle reviewed by The Times. To save the ship, the company started the Villa Incentive Program, offering guests the chance to buy empty cabins at discounted rates.

“The residents raised almost $2 million to buy time,” Mr. Schatz said, adding that he contributed to the fund so he wouldn’t be stranded with his mother, who had turned 100 just days earlier.

One group cobbled together $400,000 and used one passenger’s personal account to send the funds directly to a fuel supplier, according to messages in a private WhatsApp group. The ship was cleared to leave Singapore and set sail on Aug. 7, but the problems weren’t over.

By this point, Whitney Olson, 47, a onetime owner of a Montana car dealership and a Villa Vie founder, had spent more than $1.5 million on her two cabins, equity and payments to keep the vessel operational. She said she had also considered lending Mr. Petterson $2 million in April, contingent on a financial audit and assurances in the event of bankruptcy. Mr. Petterson refused to provide the information, Ms. Olson said. “He was more interested in taking the money from the residents at these exorbitant interest rates than giving me what any investor would ask for,” she said.

Mr. Petterson told The Times that he could not provide the information that Ms. Olson had requested because the company’s finances had not been audited at that time.

As the ship left Singapore, Ms. Olson devised a plan to take control of the Odyssey. Along with two other passengers, she started a resident-backed investment company. They sought to pool money from residents and pay off the vessel’s debt holders to establish a self-sustaining co-op similar to the one used by the World, the only successful residential cruise in service.

Many residents had criticized Villa Vie’s business model, saying the monthly fees set in 2023 were too low to keep up with inflation. Under the new company, they proposed adjusting fees to cover real-time fuel charges, port fees and crew wages without relying on external loans.

The buyout effort collapsed last week after investors said they had uncovered far more debt than expected and failed to reach a deal with the ship’s primary lender, NRP Maritime Asset Management AS, a Norwegian maritime fund manager. Taking over the voyage would have exposed the residents to significant legal liabilities and high costs for debt repayment and legal bills, estimated at $3 million for just the first two months, the investors said, while operating costs were too high to keep monthly fees affordable.

Staying in hotels and short-term accommodations in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, the Odyssey’s former residents have spent the past two weeks planning what might come next. Some said they would keep traveling in Asia, while others decided to stay in Cambodia while they awaited news about the ship’s future.

Ms. Olson said she planned to cross the land border to Vietnam, where she would put her belongings in storage before taking a previously booked trip to India to see the Taj Mahal and Bengal tigers with her family. But she still had her mind on the cruise.

“I’m still going to watch to see what happens with the Odyssey at auction, and see if there is a way to pick it up for cheap,” she said. “It was so special. I’m not ready to be done.”

Sun Narin contributed reporting from Sihanoukville, Cambodia.

Ceylan Yeğinsu is a travel reporter for The Times who frequently writes about the cruise industry and Europe, where she is based.

Republicans’ Losses in New York Were Bad. Then Came Their Freakout.

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The party’s losses in New York mirrored those across the nation, but leading Republicans in the state quickly blamed each other for the results.

By Dana Rubinstein

When Mike Lawler, a Republican congressman from New York, conceded his race on Tuesday to his Democratic challenger, Cait Conley, he said it was important to be “gracious in defeat.”

If Mr. Lawler was trying to model decorum, some of his Republican colleagues in the state seemed to have missed the message.

In the days following the brutal, 19-point loss sustained by the Nassau County executive, Bruce Blakeman, to the Democratic incumbent, Gov. Kathy Hochul, the state Republican Party has descended into a vicious, backbiting brawl.

An incoming Republican congressman called for the state party chair to be fired. The Republican he’s replacing, Representative Elise Stefanik, criticized Mr. Blakeman for running a “low-energy” campaign — the same insult Mr. Trump lobbed at Jeb Bush, the former governor of Florida, during the 2016 Republican presidential primary.

Marc Molinaro, a former Republican congressman and incoming state assemblyman, suggested a different sort of cleaning: The state party, he wrote on X, “needs an enema.”

Circular firing squads are a common post-defeat phenomenon among politicians, but Tuesday’s loss for the Republicans, both nationwide and locally, was particularly crushing.

Not only did Ms. Hochul outperform the polls to trounce Mr. Blakeman, but Democrats flipped a pivotal congressional seat held by Mr. Lawler in the Hudson Valley. They also retook significant territory in southern Brooklyn; flipped the town supervisor’s seat in Hempstead, the base of the Nassau County Republican Party, for only the second time in more than a century; and even took power in Pelham Manor, a small village in Westchester County, for the first time in decades.

If the results were ugly for Republicans, so was their post-election fracas.

Mr. Blakeman responded to Ms. Stefanik’s slight with a wholesale attack on her character.

“Elise Stefanik is a selfish, do nothing politician that didn’t lift a finger to help Republican candidates in New York this year,” he said on social media.

In an interview with The New York Times on Friday, he also disputed the contention that he had run a low-energy campaign.

“I took two days off in 11 months,” he said. “I think that’s pretty remarkable.”

And he kept up the anti-Stefanik drumbeat.

“She has no right to criticize anybody, because as a so-called leader of the party in this state, she did nothing,” he said.

Ms. Stefanik declined to comment further beyond her posts on social media, where she pointedly acknowledged that feelings were “raw in the aftermath of Tuesday’s result,” an experience she said she was not herself familiar with, since she had “never lost any of my seven elections.”

“I know that this is a tough loss in NY and I imagine it takes time to process,” she wrote on X. “I’m going to give some Upstate grace whether deserved or not.”

The performance by Democrats was, of course, buoyed by a surge that returned both the House and Senate to Democratic control and routed Republicans in Texas, South Carolina and Maine. Mr. Blakeman pointed to those losses in his interview with The Times.

“This was nationwide,” he said. “It was in every state.”

But some Republicans argued that there was plenty of blame to go around locally, too.

Inna Vernikov, a Republican New York City councilwoman, accused Mr. Blakeman of misleading potential donors by suggesting the race was closer than it was, likening it to a “grift.”

“When a campaign runs and publishes polling that is not an accurate reflection of what credible external polls show, while everyone knows the political reality is different, but then uses those polls to attract donors to gain financially on the race without a shot of winning, that is a grift,” Ms. Vernikov said in an interview.

Mr. Blakeman dismissed Ms. Vernikov.

“I don’t think about her,” he said in an interview on Friday. “She’s inconsequential in politics in this state.”

The disputes had some New York conservatives lamenting the standing of the state Republican Party.

“Infighting within the party betrays the faith of us regular schmucks who actually believe in candidates and try to help them,” wrote Bob Lonsberry, a conservative talk radio host in upstate New York.

Ken Girardin, a former Republican operative, suggested that the state party should have done a deep dive into why Lee Zeldin, its former standard-bearer, narrowly lost the governorship to Ms. Hochul in 2022.

“A lot of Republicans want to take the patient into surgery before they’ve looked at the X-ray,” Mr. Girardin said, noting the party’s lack of introspection into why Mr. Zeldin underperformed in the party’s purported stronghold of upstate New York, including Onondaga, Saratoga and Monroe Counties.

Mr. Girardin also lamented the lack of Republican Party infrastructure, an issue that also bedeviled the Democratic Party in 2022, and that Ms. Hochul has spent the ensuing years trying to fix.

“The state party has three things: access to R. N. C. data, U. S. P. S. mailing privileges, which allow the State Committee to mail at a cheaper rate, and Nelson Rockefeller’s brownstone on State Street,” Mr. Girardin said. “Beyond that, it’s not like the State Committee has a core of volunteers the way that county parties do.”

Anthony Constantino, one of the few Republicans in New York to win a heavily contested race on Tuesday, did not disagree, and on Wednesday urged the party to fire its leader, Ed Cox. (Mr. Constantino did not have his party’s backing during the primary in June.)

“In NYS, the Republican Party is mostly a Con Job that helps Democrats win,” Mr. Constantino wrote on social media. “Even Bruce Blakeman was in on the con. He just wandered around like a headless chicken going from stupid dinner, to stupid dinner and charming the ‘party’ while ignoring the people. I am with the people and insist we rebuild the Party. Fire Ed Cox!”

Asked if he agreed with the notion that Mr. Cox should go, Mr. Blakeman was circumspect.

“I think it’s very healthy to have that discussion,” he said. “I think in a lot of cases new blood can be very helpful.”

Mr. Cox did not respond to a request for comment. But in a statement issued Friday afternoon, the Republican chairman called for unity.

“This is not the time for accusations or a circular firing squad,” Mr. Cox said. “It’s a time for Republicans to regroup, come together and develop a strategy for moving forward, building upon the foundation of the six House seats that Republicans continue to hold.”

Dana Rubinstein covers New York City politics and government for The Times.

Jason Reding Quiñones joins what is expected to be a succession of departures at the Justice Department after the midterm elections, including that of the leader of the national security division.

By Devlin BarrettGlenn Thrush and Alan Feuer

Devlin Barrett and Glenn Thrush reported from Washington, and Alan Feuer from New York.

The U. S. attorney who had overseen a centerpiece of President Trump’s retribution campaign, the so-called grand conspiracy inquiry of Obama-era officials, has resigned amid growing dissatisfaction with his performance, people familiar with the situation said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the departure of the prosecutor, Jason A. Reding Quiñones of the Southern District of Florida, on social media. He joins a succession of departures at the Justice Department after the midterm elections on Tuesday, including those of John Eisenberg, the head of the national security division, and Harmeet Dhillon, the chief of the civil rights division.

Mr. Blanche, in making the announcement, did not mention Mr. Reding Quiñones’s work on the grand conspiracy case, but instead cited his efforts on violent crime, drugs and the indictment of the former Cuban president Raúl Castro.

Mr. Reding Quiñones, a close ally of the influential right-wing lawyer Mike Davis, had long been viewed as ineffective and had largely been marginalized. Many of the office’s most sensitive investigations were already being overseen by a top Blanche deputy, Aakash Singh, according to three people with knowledge of the situation who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.

Officials were frustrated not only with Mr. Reding Quiñones’s inability to demonstrate progress on the grand conspiracy cases but also with his troubled stewardship of a marquee U. S. attorney’s office responsible for major drug and gang investigations.

Mr. Reding Quiñones did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he thanked Mr. Trump on social media. “I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” he wrote.

Mr. Reding Quiñones presided over an office in deep crisis. The Southern District had more than 200 lawyers when he arrived, but by the fall it fell by about half, after a spate of firings and resignations.

So many career prosecutors have fled that Mr. Reding Quiñones, an Army reservist, was forced to bring in military lawyers to fill the ranks.

Mr. Reding Quiñones is at least the third U. S. attorney in the Trump administration to step down after being assigned to investigate all or part of the “grand conspiracy.” Trump loyalists have used the catchall term to describe the effort to file criminal charges against former Obama administration officials, intelligence veterans and Democratic operatives for purportedly misusing their positions to harm Mr. Trump.

Two U. S. attorneys in Virginia were forced out of their jobs last year, having displeased senior Trump administration officials by concluding that criminal charges were not warranted against figures such as the former F. B. I. director James B. Comey.

Mr. Eisenberg, who stepped down on Friday, has overseen a series of investigations into leaks to the news media, some of which have been sharply criticized by federal judges. As assistant attorney general of the national security division, he also supervised prosecutions of terrorism and espionage cases, and charges against John R. Bolton, the former national security adviser, over his retention of classified material after he left the White House. Mr. Bolton pleaded guilty and is set to be sentenced next month.

In Mr. Reding Quiñones, the Justice Department found a compliant prosecutor who was eager to pursue the grand conspiracy inquiry, with the help of a judge who had proved herself amenable to Mr. Trump’s legal arguments: Judge Aileen M. Cannon in Fort Pierce, Fla.

But the investigation appears to have mostly floundered. A career prosecutor in Miami who oversaw the case concluded that there was not sufficient evidence to support criminal charges against John O. Brennan, the former C. I. A. director, and was subsequently removed from the investigation.

The administration called a longtime ally, Joseph diGenova, out of retirement to lead the case. He proceeded to slowly retrace the previous investigations. Senior administration officials clashed with Mr. diGenova, and he left under pressure in September.

Another Trump loyalist assigned to the case, Kurt Olsen, left weeks later.

Ever since, the grand conspiracy investigation has largely been led by Justice Department officials in Washington — chiefly Mr. Singh — who have been guiding the prosecutors in Florida, according to people familiar with the case.

It remains unclear who might succeed Mr. Reding Quiñones, but for now the office in Miami and its satellite outposts across South Florida will most likely be run by his chief deputy, Yara Klukas.

As part of the broader investigation, the Justice Department filed new charges against Mr. Comey in Washington in October, without securing a grand jury indictment or obtaining a judge’s signature. Prosecutors have accused him of directing a leak of classified information to a New York Times reporter in 2016. Mr. Comey has denied the accusation and is seeking to have the case dismissed.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

After Governor Abbott’s Defeat, Houston’s Mayor Changes Course on ICE

The New York Times November 06, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Mayor John Whitmire has instructed Houston police to stop notifying immigration agents when they encounter someone without legal status during routine street stops.

By J. David Goodman

Reporting from Houston

The stunning wave of Republican defeats is already having an effect in Texas.

Mayor John Whitmire of Houston said he was directing city police officers on Friday to limit their cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement during traffic stops, bucking a policy imposed on Texas’s largest city by Gov. Greg Abbott.

Under an executive order from the mayor, Houston police officers will no longer alert ICE agents when they encounter an unauthorized migrant during routine traffic stops or in connection with other low level infractions.

Instead, officers will only alert ICE in cases where a person has been arrested and is being brought to, or has already arrived at, a county jail.

“If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse,” Mr. Whitmire said in an interview with The New York Times. “We just are not going to deal with the nonviolent contacts.”

The change in how Houston officers interact with immigration agents was a direct result of Tuesday’s election, Mr. Whitmire said. Mr. Abbott lost his bid for re-election to what would have been a record fourth term as governor.

“The governor was requiring us to contact ICE,” Mr. Whitmire said. “It created a lot of anxiety” among Houston residents.

He added that the shift was “certainly consistent with the new leadership in Austin,” referring to the slate of Democrats elected to every major statewide position in Texas on Tuesday.

“We won’t have new leadership until January,” Mr. Whitmire said. “But I’m willing to make a responsible decision that in the next two months we’re going to go to a more effective policy.”

A spokesman for Mr. Abbott’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The change comes as prosecutors in Harris County are pursuing a criminal case against an ICE agent who struck a Mexican construction worker in October with a vehicle in Houston, injuring him. A grand jury indicted the agent, Mario Alberto Morales, late last month.

The county’s prosecutors were also investigating the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo who was killed during an encounter in July with ICE agents in Houston.

The Houston police chief, J. Noe Diaz, said he supported the mayor’s order. For his officers, he said, “it’s about treating the people that they come in contact with with dignity and not diminishing their vulnerability because they’re immigrants in our community.”

The mayor’s order described its intent, declaring that “law enforcement resources are finite” and are best used by “investigating and deterring violent crime.” The decision was made to maintain “the trust and cooperation of all residents” of the city, the order said.

“The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE,” according to the order, reviewed by The Times. “If a person is not otherwise going to jail on new charges or other warrants, Department personnel shall not contact ICE regarding that person.”

In April, Mr. Abbott’s office threatened to pull $110 million in public-safety funding to Houston, including money for its police department, unless the mayor promised to stop enforcing a city ordinance and took steps to repeal it.

The ordinance directed city officers to hold people wanted by ICE no longer than necessary to complete a traffic stop or other brief street encounter.

City Council members who spearheaded the passage of the ordinance said at the time that the directive from Mr. Abbott’s office violated the Constitution by requiring officers to detain people beyond the time necessary for a police stop.

Though the ordinance had not been Mr. Whitmire’s idea, he voted for it. But after Mr. Abbott threatened the funding, he urged the council to adopt new language to comply with the governor’s demands, saying the city needed the state funding for its police and fire departments. The council ultimately complied with the governor.

Mr. Abbott lost his race to Gina Hinojosa, a state representative who will be the first Latina governor. Mr. Whitmire said that he had not discussed his decision directly with Ms. Hinojosa but had spoken with other newly elected Democratic leaders.

As mayor, Mr. Whitmire, a moderate Democrat and former longtime member of the state senate, has argued in the past that confrontations with the Trump administration over immigration enforcement were “counterproductive.” He has also pointed to his relationships with top Republicans in the State Capitol as an asset for the city.

“I had a good relationship with Abbott and the lieutenant governor,” he said in the interview, referring to Dan Patrick, a conservative Republican who also lost on Tuesday. “But I have even better relationships with the Democrats.”

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

New York Is Set to Take On Amazon Over Drivers, if Its Leaders Can Agree

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Mayor Zohran Mamdani backs a bill to stop Amazon from outsourcing its deliveries, which would be a blow to the company. The City Council speaker, Julie Menin, and business leaders have concerns.

By Sally Goldenberg and Emma G. Fitzsimmons

None of the drivers who zip around New York City in cargo vans and box trucks emblazoned with the ubiquitous Amazon logo are actually employed by the company, instead working for an assortment of third-party delivery companies that have contracts with the e-commerce behemoth.

Now, in a move that could deal a blow to Amazon, the largest company in America, Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants to ban the use of such contractors and require the company to hire the drivers directly. The proposed ban, included in a broader licensing bill, would be the first outright prohibition in the country on the use of so-called delivery service partners.

Standing between Mr. Mamdani and the corporate titan is Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council, who finds herself in a tough spot.

Ms. Menin, a centrist Democrat who is keen on building her public profile, has staked out a business-friendly position in a city run by a democratic socialist mayor who is skeptical of corporate excess. She says she is concerned that the bill might cost the city jobs and lead Amazon to jack up prices.

In recent days, as her team reviews and amends the bill, she has indicated that she is considering paring it down to focus only on licensing the warehouses that work with the third-party delivery companies and regulating their operations, according to two people familiar with her thinking. That version of the bill would not require Amazon to directly hire the drivers.

But Ms. Menin must contend with a groundswell of support for the legislation after an emotional Council hearing in April that featured testimony from drivers describing unsafe working conditions, including car crashes. She is still open to a ban, and has asked her staff to research its implications, according to a person familiar with the negotiations.

“New York City regulates everything from nail salons to barbershops, yet major online retailers like Amazon have gone unregulated for far too long,” she said in a statement. “It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections and more responsible delivery practices that don’t leave vehicles idling on our streets for hours.”

She said the measure “can and must” protect workers without costing any jobs.

The bill already has more than enough sponsors to pass in the Council if Ms. Menin schedules a vote.

Supporters believe it would lead to safer conditions for drivers, higher pay and fewer barriers to unionizing.

“This is the most important labor and worker protection bill at the municipal level in the country right now, hands down, and it is against one of the most powerful companies in the world,” Tiffany Cabán, the legislation’s main sponsor and a democratic socialist, said in an interview.

Amazon says that if the bill is approved as is, it might sue the city. Opponents of the measure have engaged in a multimillion-dollar lobbying effort, running digital ads warning that it would “break Amazon’s same-day and two-day delivery” and raise “your costs even higher.”

Ty Barnes, the owner of NorthStar Logistics, a company that delivers Amazon packages in the Bronx, said he employs about 100 workers who deliver more than 100,000 packages each week. He said he often hires people who are struggling to find work, and that the bill would force his business to close.

“My business would be absolutely destroyed,” he said. “I don’t think the mayor and the Council members realize who I am and what exactly I do.”

The bill would bar companies like Amazon from contracting with third parties for warehousing or delivering packages, with a grace period that includes certain extensions, and would mandate that the companies directly employ anyone providing a “core delivery service.” If a contractor goes out of business as a result of the legislation and terminates its drivers, those workers would have to be rehired by Amazon.

Amazon’s global success relies heavily on third-party delivery firms. In New York City, it contracts with more than 40 partner companies that collectively employ more than 5,000 people, according to a company spokesman, Steve Kelly.

Asked if Amazon would comply with the bill’s rehiring requirement, Mr. Kelly said Amazon would consider “relocating operations and delivery facilities outside of New York City.”

Mr. Mamdani has seized on the issue — which offers him a chance to take on a conglomerate whose founder, Jeff Bezos, is one of the world’s richest people — as he tries to burnish his credentials as a pro-worker politician.

“When a driver wears an Amazon vest, drives an Amazon van, follows a route Amazon sets and Amazon insists that driver does not work for them, what is that if not exploitation?” he said at a rally with Ms. Cabán and supporters of the bill last month.

But as the mayor was promoting the legislation, his administration’s lawyers were expressing reservations to the City Council, Ms. Menin told reporters during a news conference last month.

Nicholas Paolucci, a spokesman for the Law Department, and Cassio Mendoza, a spokesman for the mayor, would not provide any detail about those concerns. Two people familiar with talks between the teams of Mr. Mamdani and Ms. Menin said city lawyers were exploring whether the bill was pre-empted by federal law. Mr. Paolucci said he was confident that the final bill would pass legal muster.

The Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act bars states and municipalities from enforcing laws related to motor carriers. The New York bill, as written, would void contracts between carriers and contractors, in potential violation of a constitutional contract clause, and would potentially affect interstate commerce, Brendan McGuire, a lawyer at the firm WilmerHale, wrote in a memo that was provided to The New York Times.

He was retained by the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a pro-business group funded by Amazon that has spent over $8 million lobbying against the legislation.

Amazon has also donated to the National Urban League, a civil rights group focused on economic inequality. Its president, Marc Morial, recently held a call with reporters to warn that the bill would shut down Black-owned small businesses at a moment when his organization is trying to address a racial wealth gap.

“If you put them out of business, are they due reparations?” Mr. Morial said, adding, “We’re up against interests that might have some good motivations, but they have not considered the consequences.”

Kelly Nantel, a spokeswoman for Amazon, said in a statement that the bill “would directly undermine” the company’s commitment to “creating good jobs” and working with small business owners, like those employing the third-party delivery workers.

If Amazon were to relocate its delivery operations, she said, “this would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery, deteriorating the experience for millions of customers in New York City.”

The bill has drawn support from across the political spectrum: The president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Sean O’Brien, who has supported Republicans, and the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America are united behind it.

It follows a report last year from Brad Lander, then the city comptroller, that detailed some of the dangers of the delivery industry. The report said the business model used by Amazon and other companies had led to a large increase in traffic crashes near warehouses, known as last-mile facilities, and a high rate of worker injuries.

Many delivery workers say that their jobs are difficult, and they should be able to afford life in the city, especially when Amazon is so profitable.

Jerome Sloss, 33, a musician from Indiana, has been delivering Amazon packages in Queens for two years and is a member of the Teamsters union. He said that his working conditions were often unsafe — driving vans without proper equipment and having to double-park in perilous locations — and the wages were too low at $24.75 per hour.

“If I was back in Indiana, that would be pretty decent money,” he said. “For New York, it’s just enough to pay your rent and a few bills, and you’re living paycheck to paycheck.”

Sally Goldenberg is a Times reporter covering New York City politics and government.

Emma G. Fitzsimmons is a public policy correspondent for The Times, covering New York City.

U. S. Global Health Strategy Jeopardizes Prevention of Pandemics, Experts Warn

The New York Times November 06, 2026

U. S. Health Policy

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration has been negotiating agreements with dozens of individual countries. Public health experts say a global agreement would be far more effective.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Country by country, the Trump administration has been negotiating secretive agreements with nations across Africa to provide health aid under strict conditions. The agreements, structured to benefit the United States, are undermining efforts to prepare the world for the next pandemic, putting even Americans at risk, public health experts warn.

In one striking example, under an agreement signed in February that was never made public, the United States is set to stop funding health care workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of the year. Congo has been struggling to contain an Ebola outbreak that has topped 10,000 cases and has spread to two other regions of Africa.

The plan, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, provides Congo with $900 million over the next five years, and was signed before the Ebola outbreak was detected.

Still, several public health experts said it was an example of the Trump administration’s focus on near-term benefits for the United States over the long-term partnerships needed to weather international crises.

“They have shown incredibly poor foresight proposing further cuts right where workers are needed to fight infectious threats that we all know are coming,” said Peter Maybarduk, the director of access to medicines for the advocacy group Public Citizen.

In response to questions from The New York Times, the State Department said it would work with Congolese officials to ensure they can pay government health workers, but did not say whether it would grant an extension on the Dec. 31 deadline.

The administration has signed 36 such agreements so far, but has not released them publicly. Some agreements, including most recently for Botswana, Cameroon, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Congo and Lesotho, were obtained by Public Citizen through a freedom of information request and made available to The Times.

The State Department has said it intends to eventually sign agreements with about 70 countries across the developing world.

“One deal at a time risks building 50 slow systems instead of one fast one,” said Dr. Raj Panjabi, who served as the White House’s senior director for global health security and biodefense during the Biden administration. “The only way to see that new biological threat fast is a global system where every country is expected to share, and where the U. S. is at the table helping write those rules.”

The next grave health threat could come from a country that has not signed a deal with the United States, he said, or it could be an accidental or deliberate release, perhaps of a pathogen engineered to be more deadly.

The State Department said partnerships with individual countries and regions deliver faster results, and are more accountable, than multilateral agreements.

Dr. Panjabi helped write the newest version of the International Health Regulations, a legally binding set of rules for countries to detect and disclose outbreaks that could breach borders. Member nations of the World Health Organization began following those rules last year. (The rules have since prompted disclosure of the hantavirus outbreak in May and the accidental death of a lab worker in Serbia last month.)

But the Trump administration, which withdrew the United States from the W. H. O. in January 2025, rejected the regulations, inaccurately saying they “would give the W. H. O. the ability to order global lockdowns, travel restrictions, or any other measures it sees fit” during a public health emergency.

The United States, along with Israel and Argentina, also rejected an agreement last month by member countries of the United Nations that pledged collaboration and solidarity in responding to pandemics.

“The United States just seems really determined to increase our vulnerabilities by sitting out of the most important conversations,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, a co-developer of the Global Health Security Index, which assesses pandemic preparedness in countries.

Since the Covid-19 pandemic, in which low-income nations lagged richer ones by more than a year in gaining access to vaccines, members of the W. H. O. have been trying to hammer out a global treaty that would allow for faster, more equitable access to diagnostic tests, vaccines and treatments the next time. They have until May to finalize the terms.

But the path to consensus has been rocky. In negotiations, including this week in Geneva, low-income nations, including a coalition of African countries, are holding out for guarantees of early and affordable access to medical tools in return for sharing information. Higher-income nations are trying to shield intellectual property rights.

The United States was involved in the global discussions until President Trump withdrew the nation from the W. H. O. on his first day back in the White House. The administration also cut much of the foreign aid the country disbursed to low-income nations, instead pursuing bilateral deals with countries as part of its “America First Global Health Strategy.”

At least 11 of the new agreements, including the one with Congo, include requirements to share information from outbreaks in exchange for foreign aid.

They require countries to share specimens and related data from an outbreak within five days of receiving a request from the United States. Under the terms, the United States then can share that information with other entities — pharmaceutical companies, for example — that can develop tests and medical countermeasures.

But the agreements do not guarantee early or equitable access to the new tests, treatments or other tools that might result. Many give the United States direct access to national health databases, but without privacy protections or oversight from civil society organizations.

The agreements instead say the United States would “prioritize” providing the country with medical tools “behind the U. S. government’s domestic need” and at costs “equal to or below those paid by” the United States.

By contrast, the global agreement, once finalized, would provide affordable medical tools to all low-income nations, not just the one that provides information.

Some experts worried that by setting up a parallel process, the American agreements would undermine the already contentious global negotiations.

“The bilateral approach will weaken the effort we are doing to bring the continent together,” said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Dr. Kaseya said he advised African ministers to agree to the bilateral deals only if they were satisfied with the terms, and helped some countries like South Sudan negotiate more “respectful” language. But ultimately, he said, “we need to respect sovereignty of our countries.”

A few countries, including Zimbabwe and Namibia, rejected the Trump administration’s demands, saying the terms violated their sovereignty or their laws. The United States withdrew all health aid from Zimbabwe as of Sept. 30, and announced that it would stop funding H. I. V. programs in Namibia after 2027.

Other countries successfully pushed for more favorable terms than their contracts initially proposed. Zambia’s agreement, signed after 10 months of negotiation, is no longer contingent on the Trump administration’s access to Zambia’s minerals, and does not require the country to share information on pathogens for 25 years.

But many countries that rely on aid from the United States are not in a position to fight back and forgo aid, Mr. Maybarduk noted.

“This is the take-it-or-leave-it deal that the United States has put in front of them in order to restart some of the health funding that was taken away,” he said. “These are the offers you can’t refuse.”

Dr. Samu Bijou Pekwa, chief of staff in Congo’s health ministry, said her country welcomed the agreement with the United States because it would give local officials more control over the funds. American aid was previously carried out by organizations that gave the Congolese government little say over how the money was spent, she said. The organizations were “not even involving us,” she added.

According to the memorandum of understanding with Congo, the United States plans to stop paying health care workers “by the end of 2026, costing $12,025,689,” transitioning that responsibility to the Congolese government.

Dr. Pekwa said Congo and other international partners can take over the payments but the government must ensure the workers exist and then confirm their credentials. That process will take at least six months, she said.

The State Department noted that the United States is the largest donor to the current Ebola response, contributing more than $1.2 billion in health and humanitarian assistance. But experts have said that the loss of logistical and scientific support, once provided by the U. S. Agency for International Development and the U. S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has hindered efforts to contain the outbreak.

Yet some public health experts saw reasons for optimism.

Some money for logistics, including transport and testing of patient samples, has come from the Pandemic Fund, set up in 2022 to move money quickly in outbreak situations. The fund now has a portfolio of $11.5 billion of investment across 128 countries, according to Priya Basu, its director.

She added that new sources, including private companies and countries that have not traditionally been large donors, now seem poised to invest in the fund.

Other experts noted that low- and middle-income countries were learning to collaborate — pooling their resources, expertise and purchasing power — rather than rely on richer nations.

“I think it was just laid bare during Covid that they were on their own,” said Rachel Cohen, a senior adviser for the Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative.

“There is such an incredible amount of work that’s happening at the national level, at the regional level, at the continental level,” she said. “Nobody is waiting around for the U. S. to lead anymore in the same way as before.”

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.
