John D. Rockefeller IV, West Virginia Governor and Senator, Dies at 89

The New York Times November 06, 2026

John D. Rockefeller IV (1937-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

The rare Democrat in a fabled family of wealthy Republicans, he served 30 years as senator and helped bring health insurance to millions of low-income children.

By Robert D. McFadden

John D. Rockefeller IV, who as a social worker with inherited millions and a fabled name went to live with coal miners in Appalachia in the mid-1960s, then became a two-term governor of West Virginia and five-term United States senator, making the expansion of health insurance central to his political legacy, died on Friday at his home in Washington. He was 89.

A family representative, Shelley Rodgers, confirmed the death.

Mr. Rockefeller’s pedigree — as the great-grandson and namesake of the founder of Standard Oil — assured him a national profile even while he was serving as his state’s governor from 1977 to 1985. In the Senate for the next 30 years, he amassed a voting record that was generally liberal while also championing national security and veterans’ rights.

He and Senator Edward M. Kennedy, the Massachusetts Democrat, were the principal Senate supporters of President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton’s 1993 plan for comprehensive health care for Americans. It died under massive opposition from the health insurance industry.

Four years later, Mr. Rockefeller went on to coauthor legislation that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which covers millions of children in low-income families who otherwise would have been uninsured. He also wrote laws to provide extended care services for veterans, including home health care, and voted for the 2010 universal health care mandate known as Obamacare.

Mr. Rockefeller said his championing of health care was directly linked to his exposure as a young man to the plight of children without access to even basic preventive care. “It doesn’t make me liberal,” he told The New York Times of expanding health care options during the Obamacare debate. “I care.”

Widely known as Jay, Mr. Rockefeller was the great-grandson of the businessman and philanthropist John D. Rockefeller, who built an oil-based empire that made him the nation’s first billionaire. His descendants became bankers, corporate titans, philanthropists, governors and a vice president; Jay was the rare Democrat among them.

Like many of his forebears, Mr. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, collected fine art and found that opportunities came easily. Yearning for extraordinary experiences, he studied language and culture in Japan, living on $50 a month, then joined the Peace Corps as an aide to its director, R. Sargent Shriver. He took a State Department job but was given nothing to do. He was drifting.

At 27, at a friend’s suggestion, he joined Volunteers in Service to America, a federally funded antipoverty program (now known as AmeriCorps VISTA), and went to Emmons, W. Va. It was four miles from the nearest paved road. Steep hills loomed all around. School buses could not get through in winter. Coal mines were closed or had skeleton crews. Most of the 60 families were on welfare and illiterate.

The town was suspicious of do-gooders, especially a 6-foot-6 out-of-stater with the surname Rockefeller. “The people thought I was either a Republican organizer, a federal agent looking for moonshine stills or a state official checking on welfare recipients,” he told The Associated Press in 1965.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

It took six months just to organize a community meeting.

Mr. Rockefeller achieved modest results: a Little League team, a community association, a meeting hall, the start of a library and reliable school bus service to Charleston, 15 miles away. But for Mr. Rockefeller, it was life-changing.

“Emmons made everything begin to fall into place for me,” he told The Times. “I came to love these people and realize I really could make a difference in people’s lives.”

In 1966, he moved to Charleston, capital of the then heavily Democratic state, and became a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Legislature’s House of Delegates. “I now realize that helping the poor to help themselves cannot be done in just one community,” he said. “You have got to make changes at the top.”

Like a Kennedy, his name had the power to shape his life. At a time when his uncle Nelson was governor of New York (and later served as vice president); his uncle Winthrop was running successfully to be governor of Arkansas; and his uncle David was president of the Chase Manhattan bank, a Jay Rockefeller campaign in West Virginia, even for a modest office, was irresistible to the national press corps.

He breezed to victory and, in the Legislature, backed tax reforms and an environmental bill to control coal strip mining, which scars surface landscapes and causes erosion, unlike the costly and dangerous business of digging deep mine shafts.

Some pundits were already talking about a future run for president. Mr. Rockefeller seemed in no hurry. After the 1968 assassination of Senator Robert F. Kennedy of New York, Governor Nelson Rockefeller held the appointment power and thought of his nephew. “I got a call from Uncle Nelson offering me Bobby Kennedy’s seat, and I said no immediately, ” he recalled to The Times in 1991.

Instead, Mr. Rockefeller won the largely ceremonial, four-year post of West Virginia secretary of state, which became his launchpad for the 1972 governor’s race.

His opponent that year, the incumbent Republican, Arch A. Moore Jr., who was backed by mining interests, called Mr. Rockefeller a carpetbagger and said his legislative opposition to coal strip mining was really an attack on coal mining itself and a threat to thousands of jobs in the state.

The issue proved decisive. Mr. Rockefeller lost to Mr. Moore by 73,000 votes. Vowing to run for governor again in four years, he accepted an appointment as president of West Virginia Wesleyan College, located in Buckhannon and with a student population of 1,625.

In 1976, no longer a strip mining abolitionist, he won the governorship handily with mining industry support. He claimed that land reclamation practices had changed enough to make strip mining acceptable, a flip-flop that critics called political expediency.

He was re-elected in 1980, but in his second term, a national recession hit West Virginia hard. Unemployment rose to 21 percent, the highest in the nation. Residents tightened their belts, and the Rockefeller administration made steep budget cuts.

In 1984, Mr. Rockefeller ran for Senate, edging out a Republican political novice, John Raese, by 52 to 48 percent, despite outspending him 12 to 1. Critics accused him of buying elections; he used $11 million of his own money in his 1980 campaign for governor and even more in his first race for the Senate.

He made no apologies for his campaign spending and acknowledged that he was one of the Senate’s richest members. He lived like a Rockefeller: Besides a palatial home in Charleston, he had a 3,000-acre estate in Pocahontas County in West Virginia, a mansion near Rock Creek Park in Washington and a ranch in Grand Teton National Park at Jackson Hole, Wyo.

Mr. Rockefeller, who variously chaired the Senate committees on commerce, intelligence and veterans affairs, was overwhelmingly re-elected in 1990, 1996, 2002 and 2008.

After the 2001 terrorist attacks, he initially supported the U. S.-led invasion of Iraq, based on Bush administration claims that President Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction. But while chairing the Intelligence Committee in 2008, Mr. Rockefeller oversaw a report that said the president and his top officials “led the nation to war on false premises,” noting the false link between Saddam to the Sept. 11 attacks and the terror group Al Qaeda.

With the death of his colleague, Senator Robert C. Byrd, in 2010, Mr. Rockefeller became West Virginia’s senior senator. He did not run for a sixth term and, at 78, retired from the Senate in January 2015.

When born in Manhattan on June 18, 1937, the only son among four children of John Davison Rockefeller III and Blanchette Ferry (Hooker) Rockefeller, he was named simply John Rockefeller, without the traditional middle name and Roman numeral in his family lineage. His parents and sisters, Sandra, Hope and Alida, called him by his nickname, Jay, and it became his Everyman tag for life.

“As a boy,” he told Life magazine in 1966, “I was told I should make up my own mind whether I wanted to carry on the full name, which I think stands for public service, a sense of responsibility and a high standard of demand on oneself. When I was 21, I wrote a letter to my father saying I wanted the name and the responsibility.”

His father was a philanthropist, instrumental in creating Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts. After John III died in a car crash in 1978, his lifetime giving, before bequests, was estimated at $94 million. Jay recalled his father teaching him about money by giving him a weekly allowance of 15 cents and instructing him to divide it evenly, so that a nickel each was used for spending, saving and charity.

Jay grew up in Manhattan and Westchester County, graduated in 1954 from Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire. He graduated from Harvard in 1961 with a degree in Far Eastern languages and history. In graduate school at Yale University, he studied Asian history and Chinese language.

In 1967, he married Sharon Percy, the daughter of Senator Charles H. Percy of Illinois; the marriage made the cover of Life magazine. She became chief executive of WETA, the public television and radio station in Washington. In addition to his wife, he is survived by four children, John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; two sisters, Hope Aldrich and Alida Messinger; and nine grandchildren.

In 2010, an underground explosion at the Upper Big Branch coal mine in West Virginia killed 29 miners in the nation’s worst coal mine disaster in 40 years. Mr. Rockefeller, long a critic of mine safety violations, called for new criminal penalties, but they stalled because of Republican and industry opposition.

In 2014, before leaving the Senate, he hailed the indictment of Donald L. Blankenship, former chief executive of the mine’s operator. “As he goes to trial,” the senator said, “he will be treated far fairer and with more dignity than he ever treated the miners he employed.” Mr. Blankenship was convicted of a mine safety misdemeanor and served a year in prison.

In recognition of Mr. Rockefeller’s half-century of public service to the citizens of West Virginia, West Virginia University in 2014 named its School of Policy and Politics after him and designated its library as a permanent home for his Senate archives.

Adam Bernstein contributed reporting.

Robert D. McFadden was a Times reporter for 63 years. In the last decade before his retirement in 2024 he wrote advance obituaries, which are prepared for notable people so they can be published quickly upon their deaths.

She Commands the Sunken Titanic, From 1,000 Miles Away

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A Virginia judge, empowered by quirks in maritime law, has overseen the salvage of the remote shipwreck for decades. Now her rule is being challenged.

By Marc Davis

Marc Davis, a writer in Washington, has been following the fate of the Titanic wreckage since 1996.

From her seat in the old Art Deco federal courthouse in Norfolk, Va., Judge Rebecca Beach Smith presides over perhaps the most intriguing case in maritime law: the salvaging of the Titanic.

Since 1987, the company R. M. S. Titanic Inc. has raised about 5,500 artifacts from the ship with the court-sanctioned understanding that it can never sell the objects. But it can put them on display. So the company has permanent exhibitions in Las Vegas and Orlando plus traveling shows that have been seen by 35 million people.

In March, though, the company argued it was broke — so broke, it said in court papers, that it needed to auction hundreds of the artifacts so it can take good care of the rest and pay off its debts.

Judge Smith was skeptical. Years ago, as a younger judge, she sometimes raised her voice and stared down lawyers whom she questioned. But at a Titanic hearing in August, she spoke in a conversational tone as she questioned the depth of the company’s financial straits, her authority firmly established by four decades on the bench.

“There seems to have been misrepresentations to the court in this regard,” she said icily.

Two weeks later, she extended a temporary ban on any sale.

For decades, Judge Smith, 77, has controlled all matters involving the Titanic. She decides what can be salvaged and how, what can or cannot be touched and what must be done with the brittle artifacts after they are raised.

The Titanic’s original owner, the White Star Line, is defunct. The insurers who paid out after the 1912 disaster are long out of the picture. So Judge Smith comes as close to operating as the wreck’s owner as anyone alive.

“She has a real passion for using maritime law to protect the Titanic and keep the artifact collection together,” said Ole Varmer, a maritime lawyer and co-author of “Titanic Law and Policy.”

But how did Judge Smith come to oversee the remains of a ship that was built in Belfast, sailed from England, was heading to New York City and sank off the coast of Canada in international waters more than 1,000 miles from Norfolk?

A quick answer might be that Norfolk is a hub for shipping and for the practice of maritime law. The real answer is that the laws of salvage are arcane and can seem even nonsensical to the uninitiated.

Judge Smith’s authority, as it turns out, stems from a ruling by her predecessor who found that bringing a single wine decanter recovered from the Titanic into the Norfolk court was enough to give him jurisdiction over the entire shipwreck.

Decades have passed since that ruling, which has not been successfully challenged. But the legal seas began to roil this summer when lawyers for the salvage company whose auction plan she put on hold, argued that, actually, Judge Smith does not control everything about the world’s most famous shipwreck.

In the United States, maritime law is as old as the Constitution itself. Article III, Section 2 gives federal judges jurisdiction over all admiralty cases. So legal matters involving shipwrecks in U. S. waters typically end up in the nearest federal court.

But what if, like the Titanic, the wreck is in international waters? What if it’s 400 miles off the coast of Newfoundland, resting on the ocean floor, improbably upright, in two pieces, two and a half miles under the ocean surface?

Here is where things can get complicated.

International waters have no sovereign; no single nation can claim the oceans. But courts around the world can oversee a salvage operation on the high seas if a claim is brought and the nation has applicable law.

For decades, U. S. judges have recognized claims on individual items salvaged within their territorial jurisdiction. But their authority expanded in the 1970s and 1980s when judges began to create a mechanism to manage the salvaging of shipwrecks found deep in international waters.

One key ruling came in 1990 after a 19th-century side-wheeler, full of bounty from the California gold rush, was found in international waters off the coast of South Carolina.

The American group that found the wreck, led by Tommy Thompson, an Ohio inventor, now had to figure out how to defend their claim. They couldn’t raise the ship or fence it off. It rested more than a mile under the ocean’s surface.

Thompson’s lawyer told him to grab something from the wreck and take it to court to register his claim for exclusive salvage rights. He snatched a chunk of coal and hustled it off to the Norfolk courthouse, where Judge Richard B. Kellam wrote an oft-cited legal opinion. He reasoned that if the coal was physically within the court’s jurisdiction, it could be viewed as representing jurisdiction over the entire wreck and its cargo. Kellam ordered the so-called “arrest” of the coal, which established the court’s jurisdiction over the wreck and the salvors. He then awarded Thompson’s group exclusive salvage rights.

It was a bit of legal fiction. Maritime lawyers call it “constructive in rem jurisdiction” — the notion that a court can assume jurisdiction over a wreck in international waters if part of the wreck is brought into court.

And it worked. Soon, many other famous shipwreck cases came to the courthouse in Norfolk.

The heralded invincibility of the Titanic as an ocean liner rapidly dissolved in the North Atlantic in 1912 when, on its maiden voyage, it hit an iceberg and sank, sending roughly 1,500 passengers and crew members to their deaths.

It would be 73 years before the wreck was discovered and another two until a Connecticut company called Titanic Ventures joined forces with a French oceanographic institute to begin salvaging the wreck.

Their joint expedition raised approximately 1,800 artifacts from the ocean floor in 1987, including some iconic items like a bronze cherub statue from Titanic’s grand staircase and a bell from the ship’s crow’s nest.

The company brought the artifacts to France where a court granted them title to the objects, but not exclusive salvage rights. A few years later, the company — now reconstituted into a new company called R. M. S. Titanic Inc. — faced challenges from a competitor that was also interested in recovering items from the ship.

Lawyers for R. M. S. Titanic quickly brought the crystal wine decanter, bearing the White Star logo, to Norfolk. It was their chunk of coal, and they asked Judge J. Calvitt Clarke Jr. to use the “constructive in rem” approach to grant the company exclusive salvage rights.

He did in 1994, after the company promised not to sell any salvaged items. It also agreed to keep the artifact collection together, and to make money only through public exhibitions.

For a while, the company thrived and continued financing expeditions, including a gala journey in 1996. Two cruise ships with 1,700 passengers accompanied a salvage vessel to the wreck site. Three Titanic survivors joined the actress Loni Anderson and the astronaut Buzz Aldrin in mingling with the guests. The Discovery Channel paid $3 million to film it all. The company raised 400 artifacts.

Two years later, R. M. S. Titanic raised a 15-ton section of the ship’s hull, nicknamed the Big Piece, that was lying, dislodged, on the ocean floor. It is the centerpiece of the company’s exhibition in Las Vegas that includes recreations of the opulent Grand Staircase and what the company describes as “a chillingly lifelike Promenade Deck set to the temperature of that fateful night.”

With his bushy white eyebrows and gravelly voice, Judge Clarke was a commanding presence with the power, at any time, to yank R. M. S. Titanic’s status as the ship’s exclusive salvor.

“We all work for him,” the company president George Tulloch said in a 2000 interview. “ He says, ‘Jump!’ and we say, ‘How high?’”

Relations between the company and the judge weren’t always rosy.

In 2000, R. M. S. Titanic proposed making “surgical incisions” into the wreck to search for marketable treasures. “We want the first-class mail,” said the company’s largest stockholder. “We want the first-class baggage. We want the safes and the purser’s bags. We know exactly where everything is. We can hit it like a target.”

Such talk alarmed Judge Clarke and disturbed historians. The court was flooded with letters of protest and the judge ordered the company to drop any plans to cut into the wreck, detach anything or sell anything.

“A judicial voice has spoken, and history rejoices,” John P. Eaton, a Titanic historian, wrote at the time.

When the judge’s eyesight started failing around that time, he asked Judge Smith to work with him on the case, to learn its complex history and to eventually take over.

She did in 2004, when Judge Clarke died at the age of 83. At that point, Judge Smith — a high school valedictorian, law school star and the first woman appointed to the federal bench in Virginia history — had been a judge for 15 years and had earned a reputation as a no-nonsense jurist.

“Judge Smith has no tolerance for idiots or being unprepared,” David N. Ventker, a Norfolk maritime lawyer, said. “If you argue with her, well, that’s just not very smart. And if your briefs are snarky or disrespectful, that doesn’t play well, either.”

Known as someone who guards her privacy, Judge Smith declined to be interviewed, but she is well known in Virginia legal circles, where she has handled many high-profile cases. In one, she sentenced a man to life in prison for killing a female courier, recommended he never be paroled and spoke of her duty to protect society from his “dark side.”

“When will it erupt?” she asked. “Whose mother? Whose daughter? Whose sister? You’ve got a daughter. Would you want your daughter meeting up with someone like you?’‘

Maritime lawyers say the judge has similarly shielded the Titanic, an attitude evident in what she told lawyers during a hearing almost two decades ago.

“I am concerned,” she told lawyers in the case in 2008, “that the Titanic is not only a national treasure, but in its own way an international treasure, and it needs protection and it needs to be monitored.”

Since the spring, the salvage company has been pushing to auction 361 items recovered in the first expedition. The company owns those objects by order of the French court.

The effort has put Judge Smith and the company on a collision course.

Their relationship has not always been adversarial. In the early years, she and Judge Clarke had mostly supported R. M. S. Titanic’s salvage rights against competing claims. More recently, though, the judges had interceded when they felt the company was overstepping its bounds.

In 2017, Judge Smith resisted when R. M. S. Titanic asked her to remove a federal agency, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, from overseeing the company. Years earlier the company had agreed to let the agency oversee its operations as a condition of Judge Smith giving the company title to the artifacts it had raised since 1993.

Judge Smith bristled at the company’s request and expressed frustration that the court was “having to constantly be in a combative relationship with R. M. S. T.”

“The reason that NOAA is here is because of all the machinations and happenings through the years with the court,” she said at a hearing.

She refused the company’s request that she name a different overseer.

“I am not going to let, to use a colloquialism, the fox guard the hen house,” Judge Smith said. “That is basically what occurs when R. M. S. T. is guarding the artifacts.”

The federal government has argued against any auction of the artifacts, suggesting any sale would breach the covenants that R. M. S. Titanic made in 2011.

At a hearing in August, Judge Smith, challenged the depth of the company’s financial straits. The company, in turn, challenged the judge’s jurisdiction over the items in question.

R. M. S. Titanic said Judge Smith has no authority over the 1,800 artifacts recovered in 1987 because the company’s title to them was conveyed by the French court.

The French government, however, has also objected to an auction, noting that the artifacts were conveyed to R. M. S. Titanic “subject to assurances made by the company that the collection would neither be sold nor dispersed.”

So far, Judge Smith has yet to budge on her ban on any auction. On Aug. 24, she ordered the company to produce an exhaustive inventory of all its artifacts so as to register their whereabouts and condition. She ruled that it had agreed to keep the artifacts together as a single collection, no matter when they were salvaged, when they received title to them from her in 2011.

“After decades of proceedings and in the context of R. M. S. T.’s mounting legal challenges, recent staff reductions, and the worsened financial situation,” she wrote, the company’s legal filings “do not assure the court that the collection is intact and will remain so after R. M. S. T.’s planned auction.”

The company has appealed.

It now says it is so broke, it could run out of money in six to 12 months, a prospect that would place all of the Titanic artifacts in some risk.

“Without revenue from the sale of items from the French Collection or an alternative source of funding,” the company wrote in court papers in October, “R. M. S. T. may not survive long enough to take advantage of any appellate decision.”

A Cornell Fraternity Was Supposed to Have an Adviser on Hand. It Didn’t.

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

University rules required Chi Phi to have a live-in adviser on the premises the night a woman said she was raped at the fraternity house. The organization had not hired one.

By Debra Kamin

It was Hawaiian Night at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, and students flowed in and out. The woman now known as Jane Doe arrived at about 11 p. m., having already had several drinks, and headed upstairs.

But one person was missing from the sprawling Tudor house on Edgemoor Lane: a live-in adviser.

University rules required the fraternity to have a responsible adult living in and watching over the house at all times during the school year.

But on the night in 2024 that Jane Doe said she was sexually assaulted there by seven of the fraternity’s members, no such person was on hand — or even employed by the fraternity, according to interviews and records obtained by The New York Times.

The failure to hire a live-in adviser was an apparent violation of rules adopted in the wake of earlier scandals involving fraternities at Cornell. But it also seemed to be emblematic of a larger breakdown in oversight, by the fraternity, its members and the university itself, on the night of the alleged assault.

The former student said in a lawsuit filed in September that she had been drinking on Oct. 19, 2024, before meeting up with Chi Phi members at a party at the house, where she was plied with ketamine and sexually assaulted over several hours. All the men she accused have denied any wrongdoing. None have been charged with a crime.

Cornell’s Chi Phi chapter was suspended soon after the woman reported being raped to university investigators. An email obtained by The Times sent to a group of fraternity alumni on Feb. 9, 2025, said that the lack of a live-in adviser resulted in “one more major violation and vulnerability to the chapter.”

Such advisers had been required since 2021 as part of reforms enacted by the university’s former president, Martha Pollack, after a hazing scandal involving the Sigma Nu fraternity.

“The stakes are high, and leaders of student organizations must come to understand their responsibility to promote the health and safety of our campus community,” Ms. Pollack said in announcing the reforms.

The rules required fraternities and sororities or a related organization to hire the advisers, and records suggest that Chi Phi had complied with the requirements in years past. Traditionally, the fraternity gave the job to an alumnus or graduate student, tax records and interviews show.

In 2024, the university’s rules required the adviser to have moved in at the start of the academic year, which began on Aug. 26.

In an email, Rebecca Valli, a spokeswoman for Cornell, said that the university confirmed in writing with Chi Phi fraternity members in mid-September 2024 that a recent graduate would live in the chapter house as its adviser.

A lawyer for the recent graduate, Blake Haberstock, said his client signed licensing paperwork with Cornell to serve in the position, but never accepted the job because it was never officially offered to him by the fraternity.

“While he was in discussions for the position, it never materialized,” said the lawyer, Adam Ford.

He said his client was not even in Ithaca the night of the Chi Phi party.

Mr. Ford, who represents several other former Chi Phi members, added that many of his clients, including Mr. Haberstock, became victims of online harassment after their names were listed in social media posts that falsely accused them of being active members of the fraternity on the night of the party.

Gillian Fisher, a lawyer for Chi Phi, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Valli, the Cornell spokeswoman, said that the university requires a fraternity’s national organization or local housing corporation to notify Cornell of any changes to their live-in adviser arrangement. She said that Chi Phi had not notified the school of any such changes, and added that Cornell does not take steps to independently verify the status of live-in advisers on campus.

Students active in other fraternities at Cornell said in interviews that live-in advisers have duties like stocking cleaning supplies and toilet paper and ensuring the house stays clean. Some fraternities require them also to be present for social events at the house, including weekend and late-night parties.

Calls to more than a dozen former Chi Phi students, including previous live-in advisers, to ask about the traditional role of their live-in adviser, went unanswered.

During the period when the Chi Phi house at Cornell was apparently without a live-in adviser, the fraternity members were partying hard, the records and interviews show.

Ketamine appeared to be easily accessible and less than 24 hours before Jane Doe arrived for the party, the campus police made a drug-related arrest there.

Debra Kamin is an investigative reporter for The Times who covers wealth and power in New York.

Are the School Culture Wars Over in Texas?

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

In Texas, teaching on race and gender was restricted, Christianity was encouraged and private school vouchers expanded. It may be hard for Democrats to reverse those policies.

By Vimal Patel and Dana Goldstein

Texas was ground zero for a yearslong Republican effort to transform education.

The state restricted teaching around race and gender, and made Western culture more of a focus in history and English lessons. It wove teachings from the Bible throughout the public school curriculum. It launched a private school voucher program.

Other Republican-run states, like Ohio and Iowa, borrowed from a similar playbook. But in recent years, few were quite as ambitious as Texas.

All of that would seem to be over now, after Democrats on Tuesday took the Texas governorship, state assembly and possibly its school board.

But is it?

It is not clear how much the state’s new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, can do to repeal Republican policies.

Texas Republicans still hold the State Senate. And the governor-elect has sidestepped culture war issues, avoiding debates about transgender children, said Jon Taylor, the political science chair at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

“She ignored it,” he said. “And I think you’re going to continue to see that as we go forward.”

Ms. Hinojosa, whose campaign did not respond to a request for comment for this article, has avoided talking about issues like D. E. I. or how teachers discuss gender.

“In the past we have evaluated politics as right versus left — I just don’t think those labels apply at this moment in history,” she said in an interview with The New York Times last month. She added, “I just don’t think that the culture wars are the fight of 2026.”

Culture war issues were Gov. Greg Abbott’s priority, not hers, she has said. In one ad, she introduced herself with the catch phrase, “I’m Gina Hinojosa. My pronouns are ‘mom,’ ‘Texan’ and ‘soon-to-be governor.’”

Other Democrats who flipped governor’s seats were also circumspect when it came to topics like D. E. I. or conservative book bans. Successful governor candidates in Iowa, Ohio and Wisconsin emphasized issues like universal preschool and school funding. They criticized the private school voucher programs that have swept the country during the Trump era.

But like Ms. Hinojosa, several also face a divided government. Those governor-elects did not promise to repeal voucher programs, instead saying they would seek to limit eligibility to low-income families or provide more accountability and transparency on how the money is spent.

Jorge Elorza, chief executive of Democrats for Education Reform, a group that supports school choice, praised the approach.

“Our goal is to spur and catalyze a more expansive K-12 conversation on the left,” he said.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, praised Ms. Hinojosa’s strong anti-voucher messaging but said she also expected that among the new crop of Democratic governors, “you will see people take on issues that are considered traditionally Republican.”

Those issues include improving early reading instruction, protecting children from harm online and partnering with employers to better prepare young adults for the work force.

Conservatives are still worried. Daniel Buck, a Wisconsin-based research fellow with the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think tank, said Democratic governors could easily chip away at access to school choice programs without ending them.

“I see education reform as largely dead in the water,” he said. He added that some on the right were learning a valuable lesson: Their schools agenda might have been more durable with at least some centrist Democratic support, as was the case in previous political eras, such as under President George W. Bush.

“You have to shake hands across the aisle if you want to get anything meaningful done,” he said. “It’s a humbling thing to say.”

In Florida, where Gov. Ron DeSantis led the way on anti-D. E. I. and pro-school choice policies, little is expected to change, since a Trump-aligned Republican, Byron Donalds, won the governor’s race, and Republicans also kept control of the Legislature — one of the party’s few bright spots.

Mr. Donalds has indicated he would advance Mr. DeSantis’s education policies. But he has also named other goals that are more likely to be bipartisan, such as creating individualized annual “success plans” for each child, and workplace apprenticeships for high school and college students.

In Texas, simply having a Democrat as governor comforted many educators, even if it remains unclear what Ms. Hinojosa will prioritize.

“These have been very dark times on campus,” said Pauline Strong, an anthropology professor who has taught at the University of Texas at Austin starting in 1993. That was during the administration of Ann Richards, the last Democrat to lead Texas. “It’s a new dawn and we’re going to see much better days ahead.”

In interviews, professors across Texas hoped for the return of programs that had been eliminated for ideological reasons, like women’s and gender studies. Some professors hoped Ms. Hinojosa would issue directives about how to interpret laws and policies, effectively defanging some of the higher education legislation.

But Ms. Hinojosa, a University of Texas at Austin graduate, did not talk much about higher education on her campaign. She preferred talking about local public schools.

Ms. Hinojosa said she was inspired to get into politics when her son’s elementary school was threatened with closure because of budget problems. She ran for Austin’s school board in 2012 and served for several years. During the campaign for governor, she opposed Mr. Abbott’s state takeover of struggling school districts, vowed to roll back standardized testing and said A. I. did not belong in elementary schools.

She highlighted endorsements she received from public school superintendents and coaches, and critiqued, again and again, the new private school voucher program Mr. Abbott signed into law last year.

Ms. Hinojosa also has promised to fire the state’s education commissioner on her first day in office, partly over the voucher program.

The vouchers, known as Texas Education Freedom Accounts, provide about $10,000 per student to help low-income and middle-class parents pay for private school tuition or home-schooling. Ms. Hinojosa has referred to the program as a “scam,” arguing it reduces funding to traditional public schools and gives a handout to families whose children were already enrolled in private school.

Even so, when asked directly if she would repeal the program, Ms. Hinojosa said she would, theoretically, but emphasized, “I don’t see that as a reality, frankly,” citing Republicans in the Legislature who support vouchers.

Ms. Hinojosa may have more power to reshape the state’s public universities, because she will be able to appoint regents, the ultimate governing authorities of higher education institutions. A series of Republican governors who have waded deeper and deeper into culture war politics — George W. Bush, Rick Perry, Greg Abbott — have ensured Republican domination of university governance for decades.

Even here Ms. Hinojosa may face obstacles. The Texas Senate must confirm her regent picks.

María C. González, an English professor at the University of Houston, said she spoke to Ms. Hinojosa months ago and urged her to be as aggressive as Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, a Democrat who moved quickly to reshape university governing boards after she took office.

She said Ms. Hinojosa liked the idea but was noncommittal.

Despite the applause on the left, Sherry Sylvester, a fellow with the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank, downplayed the idea that Ms. Hinojosa’s victory was a repudiation of the state’s approach to education.

“I don’t believe the people of Texas have made this political change to bring gender studies back to Texas A&M,” she said.

Alan Blinder contributed reporting.

Vimal Patel writes about higher education for The Times with a focus on speech and campus culture.

Dana Goldstein covers education for The Times.

Connections Coach

As Microsoft pours billions into artificial intelligence, the company has offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees. The work force was already on edge.

Credit... Tara Anand

Supported by

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Within an hour of Microsoft’s announcement of buyouts last week, employees rushed to an internal site to see whether they had been offered one. So many people were checking at once that employees speculated on the company’s internal social network that the site had buckled under the traffic.

The offer, extended to about 60,000 employees, or more than a quarter of Microsoft’s work force, was the largest in the company’s history. It was also the company’s second buyout this year, and another shock to a work force grappling with big changes brought on by artificial intelligence.

For years, Microsoft occupied a distinct position among the tech industry’s biggest companies. While its pay packages often lagged behind Silicon Valley rivals like Google and Meta, employees said, the company countered with strong benefits and a reputation for stability. As recently as September, Forbes ranked Microsoft the world’s best employer for the third straight year.

But the tech industry’s A. I. race is upending many workplaces, Microsoft included. The buyout offer, said six Microsoft employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity, landed on workers strained by mounting expectations to use A. I., stagnant pay and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure.

Though Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, it is clearly shifting its spending priorities. Two days after the buyouts were announced, the Redmond, Wash., company reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year.

The fear among many workers now is what comes next, and some have begun organizing. Before the buyout offer, a group of current and former employees circulated an open letter among colleagues accusing the company of pursuing A. I. with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos. It called on Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how A. I. is built and used, and to stop tying A. I. use to rewards or reprimands.

Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, said the buyouts were meant to give employees who might be ready for something new “choice and agency.” She said the buyouts were not related to how A. I. was changing work. (A Microsoft spokeswoman said “maintenance timing,” rather than a traffic surge, had briefly delayed the release of some buyout offers on the internal site.)

Ms. Coleman also did not rule out future layoffs.

Employees offered a buyout have until Dec. 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on Dec. 31. They will receive a minimum of eight weeks of base pay, and the size of the payment varies by job level and tenure.

The offer followed a string of cuts that had already shaken employees. Microsoft laid off 10,000 workers in 2023, and more than 15,000 in 2025. This spring, about 8,600 U. S. employees were offered a retirement-age buyout, and about 30 percent accepted it. This summer, the company cut about 4,800 more jobs. Microsoft’s head count in June was 223,000, down 5,000 from a year earlier.

This time, Microsoft said it expected less than 5 percent of the 60,000 employees offered a buyout to take it.

Some employees have already signed the offer, including one who has been at Microsoft for nearly a decade. She was her family’s main earner and worried about the job market, she said. But years of pressure to use unreliable A. I. tools, the constant threat of layoffs and what she saw as a widening gap between the company’s stated values and its actions made staying feel worse. Colleagues urged her to stay, she said, because they would have to absorb her work.

Others are staying, at least for now, some by choice and some because they feel they have none. A senior software engineer who has worked at Microsoft for more than five years said he wanted to stay to try to improve the company. He said a recent squeeze on pay, the push to use A. I. and now the buyouts had left far more of his colleagues feeling expendable.

Several employees said that merit raises this year had been unusually small, in some cases less than 1 percent, and that managers had described rewards budgets as tight. At a company town hall last month, a question about how executives balanced spending more than $100 billion a year on A. I. against flat rewards for the workers carrying out that strategy drew more than 80 reactions, roughly twice as many as most other questions seen by The New York Times.

Ms. Coleman said Microsoft was trying to stay competitive on pay while it remained “a company that has to think about our operating expense and our capital expense.”

The tension had begun to show up in pay in other ways, too, employees said. Gretchen Thomas, 57, a design leader, left Microsoft in September after five years because the pressure grew steadily heavier, she said, including shifting priorities and faster deadlines.

“I just can’t believe how grim it’s gotten just in the last three years,” she said.

This year, Ms. Thomas’s raise and bonus were in line with those of her colleagues. But her manager had reduced her stock award, typically the most valuable part of a Microsoft employee’s pay, because, according to a memo seen by The Times, she did “not consistently” show speed, urgency and willingness to experiment, including with A. I.

Ms. Coleman declined to discuss individual pay decisions, but said the company encouraged employees to experiment and use its tools. “Of course some of that includes A. I.,” she said.

For those who stay, employees said, the bigger worry is the work left behind. All of the employees said that they did not expect departing colleagues to be replaced, and that the remaining staff would absorb their work. Ms. Coleman said Microsoft had thousands of jobs open but acknowledged the company needed to make “some shifts in the work force.”

(The Times has sued Microsoft and OpenAI, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)

The day after the buyout announcement, a group of teams in one of Microsoft’s software organizations gathered at a Dave & Buster’s for an event to raise morale that had been planned for a month.

Before the food came out, a five-year engineer who was at the event recalled, a manager stood on a chair, acknowledged that all the attendees were refreshing their email and weighing the buyout offer, and urged them to set it aside and celebrate the work they had done.

At his table, the engineer said, no one talked about anything else.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve spoken with engineers, designers and researchers at Microsoft. Many joined because the company felt like the stable choice in tech. It no longer does, they told me. When buyouts were announced, the real question for many wasn’t whether to take the money — it was what would happen to the people who stayed.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

A Democrat Will Govern Texas. Republicans Won’t Make It Easy.

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

After a sweeping Democratic victory, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa will try to reshape a state molded by decades of conservative policymaking, with Republicans still in control of the State Senate.

By Lauren McGaughy

Reporting from Austin, Texas.

For the first time in a generation, Texas Democrats will have a real chance to govern. Republicans may not make it easy.

On Tuesday, Democrats won races up and down the ballot, from U. S. Senate to agriculture commissioner, and took control of the Texas House after Republican domination since 2003. The new leaders take office in January, just ahead of the next legislative session.

The Democratic victory was thorough and stunning — and left big questions about what comes next for the country’s second most populous state.

How aggressively will Democrats seek to remake the political landscape in what until Tuesday was the incubator of American conservatism? What promises will become legislative priorities? And how much can Democrats get done with Republicans still in control of the State Senate?

The newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, is a longtime state representative who knows the inner workings of the Texas government. But she’s never served in statewide office, and on the trail, she and the Democrats made big promises.

Ms. Hinojosa pledged to abolish the state’s billion-dollar school voucher program, which districts say drains resources from public education. She has said she will regulate data centers. She has promised to tackle affordability, proposing an end to corporate tax subsidies, a ban on private equity firms buying houses and a one-time $1,500 refund check from the state’s rainy day fund for every household.

The governor-elect has said she will oust her predecessor’s picks to lead state agencies and root out corruption. As a lawmaker, Ms. Hinojosa opposed the state’s abortion ban and restrictions on L. G. B. T. Q. rights. She helped organize a walkout against conservative voting bills.

Ms. Hinojosa ran for governor as a populist, pledging that she and her party would not shut out conservative voices.

“We will have a bipartisan transition, and we will have a bipartisan administration,” Ms. Hinojosa said at her first post-election news conference in Austin on Thursday.

Nevertheless, some in the far-right old guard, including prominent conservative activists, are pressuring the Republicans left in power to block, obstruct or otherwise undermine Democrats.

Tom Oliverson, a lawmaker from Cypress who chairs the House Republican Caucus, said he wants to protect three decades’ worth of conservative lawmaking.

His job is “to keep the Republicans together and preserve what we have already achieved,” Mr. Oliverson said. “We’re going to make the best of it.”

One institution in particular — the State Senate — remains firmly in Republican hands. If it so chooses, the conservative majority could stymie the state’s newly elected leaders. Some senators appear ready.

“Texas stands as long as the Texas Senate Republican caucus holds the line,” Charles Schwertner, a Republican senator, posted on X on Tuesday. “We will.”

State Senator Bryan Hughes, who wrote the abortion ban, promised on social media that Republicans would work with Democrats — with one caveat. “Make no mistake: We will be the firewall against bad and destructive policy.”

Under Dan Patrick, the hard-line Republican lieutenant governor, lawmakers outlawed abortion, loosened gun restrictions and injected Christianity into public schools.

Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden attorney general, was a national standard-bearer for conservative policies.

Greg Abbott, the outgoing governor, issued orders and rules backing Donald Trump’s border policies and targeting L. G. B. T. Q. rights. He installed friends and donors in every state institution, targeting diversity and inclusion programs and instituting policies that could take Democrats years to unravel.

Mr. Abbott, Mr. Paxton and Mr. Patrick all lost their jobs Tuesday night.

Ms. Hinojosa is expected to reverse many of Mr. Abbott’s executive orders and choose new leaders for dozens of agencies, commissions and public universities — which means thousands of hires. She has promised on her first day to fire Mike Morath, the head of the Texas Education Agency, an architect of some of the most conservative school policies.

Finding thousands of talented people who can implement Ms. Hinojosa’s vision will be difficult, said Gene Wu, the chairman of the Texas House Democratic Caucus. The transition team will be looking for people to step away from private sector roles, he said, to “replace Abbott’s cronies and sycophants.”

Installing Ms. Hinojosa’s picks in top jobs could be difficult. The State Senate has the power to reject many appointees. Its Republican members could also hold up or block House bills to exert leverage.

Conservative senators could cause gridlock in the State Capitol, said John Colyandro, a former senior adviser to Mr. Abbott.

“It is going to be really tough for her to get people confirmed if she doesn’t compromise on policy,” Mr. Colyandro said.

Senate Republicans also could try to gut the power of the lieutenant governor, who presides as the chamber’s president, before the Democrats officially take over next year. Vikki Goodwin, who will step into the role in January, also ran on an affordability platform — and backed legalizing marijuana.

Mr. Oliverson, the Republican representative, said an early priority would be to find a House speaker whom conservatives can support. He would not weigh in on the early front-runner for the job, Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat first elected in 1973. Ms. Thompson would be the first Black speaker and first female speaker.

When asked Thursday about the possibility that Republicans would undermine Democrats before they even take office, Ms. Hinojosa said she looked forward to working with the party’s lawmakers. She said Mr. Abbott had been “gracious” and helpful.

“I would hope that elected leaders from both parties don’t get in the way of the progress we can make together,” she said.

Texas Democrats have not determined what policies they will focus on first. But leaders say they will not put social or cultural fights ahead of pocketbook issues.

“Fun fact about L. G. B. T. people: They pay bills like everyone else,” Kendal Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democratic Party, said in an interview.

Carol Alvarado, the chairwoman of the Texas Democratic Senate Caucus, said Democrats in the Legislature will be looking for an issue on which they can deliver quickly with Republicans, like regulating data centers.

“People don’t want the bickering,” Ms. Alvarado said. “There is so much that we have to do, and we can’t start off on the wrong foot.”

Mr. Wu said Democrats don’t plan to “ram stuff down people’s throats like the Republicans did,” but predicted big changes. He wants government out of bedrooms and doctor’s offices, he said. He wants power shifted back to local communities.

“Texas is a place where people value their freedom,” Mr. Wu said. “We can go back to being Texans today.”

Lauren McGaughy is the Texas politics correspondent for The New York Times, writing about the ways that policymakers in the second largest state are changing lives for their citizens and influencing American politics.

How A. I. Just Blew Up a Key Tenet of Computer Science

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

A longstanding hypothesis held that some problems would always be hard for computers to solve quickly. But OpenAI disproved it — raising the possibility of radical new efficiencies.

By Cade Metz

Cade Metz has written about A. I. for more than 15 years. But he has never solved a 1,000-row Sudoku puzzle.

To understand the latest shocking development in A. I.-generated math, it helps to think about Sudoku.

Solving one of those nine-box number puzzles, especially at the highest difficulty levels, can be fiendishly time-consuming. But once you have a solution, it’s easy to double-check that you got it right: Just scan each row, column and box and confirm that each integer appears exactly once.

It’s an analogy that Russell Impagliazzo, a professor of computer science at the University of California, San Diego, invokes to explain a high-profile math question called “P vs. NP.” For years, Dr. Impagliazzo explains, he and other computer scientists have assumed that math and computer science obey that apparent truth about Sudoku: Solving a problem is much, much harder than checking that a solution is correct.

Sitting at the intersection of mathematics and theoretical computer science, “P vs. NP” is among the million-dollar Millennium Prize problems laid down by the Clay Mathematics Institute 25 years ago. In non-math speak, “P” represents computational problems that can be solved quickly, while “NP” represents problems whose solutions can be checked easily.

Common sense says that checking solutions should be much easier than finding solutions. “If P and NP follow intuition, then they should definitely not be equal,” said Ryan Williams, a professor of engineering and computer science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

On Oct. 26, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, cast doubt on that seemingly obvious argument. While the broader problem of “P vs. NP” remains unsolved, the company announced that its newest artificial intelligence technology had refuted a related conjecture called the exponential time hypothesis, or E. T. H., which Dr. Impagliazzo proposed in 1998 with his colleague Ramamohan Paturi and a Bell Labs researcher named Francis Zane. Similar to the argument that P can’t equal NP, the E. T. H. held that certain problems must always remain hard for computers to solve quickly.

OpenAI’s result indicates that isn’t the case. It hints that machines could in theory solve Sudoku puzzles just as quickly as they could check their solutions — even when the grid spans 1,000 rows or more. The finding also suggests that computers could rapidly design new algorithms and new electrical circuits for new kinds of computers, helping to create their own successors.

“If you have a really fast algorithm for Sudoku solving,” Dr. Impagliazzo said, “you could use it to design optimal circuits.”

Among many other mind-bending scenarios, OpenAI’s proof could point to a future in which computers rapidly crack the encryption that guards the world’s secrets or design new medicines by optimizing the behavior of proteins in the body. All of this is theoretical. But machines are already moving in this direction, with new approaches that could turbocharge chip design, drug discovery and other areas.

OpenAI’s announcement is just one of nearly 400 scientific findings that the company and its A. I. rivals released in recent weeks, claiming to answer important questions in math, physics and computer science that have bedeviled human experts for decades. Just after OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic, its primary rival, said that it too had disproved the E. T. H.

(The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

For decades, computer scientists have wondered whether powerful machines could find hidden shortcuts that allowed them to solve hard problems with surprising speed. As Dr. Impagliazzo puts it: “Are there very impressive shortcuts that can avoid actually enumerating all the possible solutions and just get to the best without going through all the rest?” OpenAI’s disproof of his hypothesis hints that those shortcuts might exist after all — a finding that Dr. Impagliazzo called “very shocking news.”

“It is also a shock,” he added, “that the work was not done by a human being.”

Although OpenAI’s result is enormously unsettling for experts like Dr. Impagliazzo, it has no real effect on today’s technologies: For now, the magic shortcuts are possible only in theory.

“Immediate, practical applications? There aren’t any,” Dr. Williams said.

But he and others believe that OpenAI’s result could point to new applications in the future. This kind of theoretical result often requires years, or even decades, of engineering to realize its potential.

In the mid-1980s, theoretical computer scientists proposed something called an interactive proof. But the idea did not deliver a practical application until the 2010s, when it helped power the blockchain technologies that underpin bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.

The most intriguing potential application could involve artificial intelligence itself: In using A. I. to debunk the exponential time hypothesis, OpenAI and Anthropic raised the possibility that machines could one day have the power to improve themselves in extraordinarily efficient ways. And that is exactly the phenomenon, called recursive self-improvement, that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are now trying to unlock.

“This could lead to better A. I.,” Dr. Impagliazzo said, “in all sorts of ways.”

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

The Blue Wave Has Tech Bros Scrambling for Data Centers in Space

Wired November 04, 2026

A wave of Democratic candidates across the country—and notably in Texas, a national data center hot spot and home to Elon Musk’s SpaceX—won their state and congressional races on Tuesday, including many candidates who voiced opposition to the data center industry. The results have sent some corners of the tech industry looking to the heavens for answers.

In recent hours, data center enthusiasts have proclaimed on social media that they’re still “bullish” on building data centers—just not necessarily in Texas, or even on Earth at all. Instead, they say, it’s time to focus on data centers in space.

Elon Musk—who spent more than $400 million of his fortune supporting Republican candidates who all went on to lose their midterms races—has been among those leading the charge. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours of Wednesday, after it was clear that Democrats had taken the House and Senate.

Jordan Lasker—the man behind the X account "Crémieux,” which is a popular follow in the tech world and is known for posting race-based pseudoscience—also weighed in, saying, “Data centers in space are an incredible idea and anyone who doubted them didn't think enough about tonight's election results.”

Throughout the day, Musk employees, tech investors, AI researchers, venture capitalists, and industry fans joined the chorus of support for space-based data centers. Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the techno-optimist think tank Foundation for American Innovation, argued that ocean-based data centers should also be considered. (In June, China began operating what it claims is the world’s first underwater data center.)

Some companies are already trying to put compute in orbit. Among them are Google, which launched a satellite that it says contains “data center class TPU,” and SpaceX, which says it aims to deploy “thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027.” Blue Origin is also in the mix, having filed for a Federal Communications Commission permit to launch 50,000 satellites that will constitute an “orbital data center system.”

There are also a few startups aiming to build data centers in space, including Starcloud, which claims to have carried "the first Nvidia H100 GPU into orbit" in November 2025.

Despite being technically possible, the realities of in-orbit data centers are difficult. Among other things, space-based data centers are much more expensive than land-based ones, can’t grow to hyperscale size, and are subject to the risks and whims of satellite launches.

When it comes to Texas data centers, the concerns of tech bros aren’t completely unfounded. Experts tell WIRED that the change in leadership could translate to some concrete changes in the industry—albeit with limits.

Although Democrats will have control of the Texas House of Representatives, Republicans still have control over the state’s senate. Robert Paterson, professor of land use and environmental planning at the University of Texas at Austin, tells WIRED that the split means that some immediate attempts at change “will probably be stymied a bit.”

Adrian Shelley, director of nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen’s Texas office, tells WIRED that the legislature would be a likely place to hash out high-impact policies like the reallocation of state agency resources. However, he adds that the governor could effect more immediate changes by issuing executive orders, or requesting the resignation of politically appointed officials in state agencies.

Shelley says that these oversight agencies—such as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission, and the Texas Water Development Board—have the authority to charge fines for breaking state law, or in extreme cases to revoke permits for projects like data centers. But Paterson notes that Texas developers have particularly strong “vested rights,” which protects the terms of their projects from the moment their permits are approved, even if construction hasn’t begun.

Another medium-term route to reshaping Texas’ data center industry could be to give more power to its counties. Paterson noted that nearly half of the state’s data centers exist in unincorporated territory, which puts them outside the jurisdiction of city zoning laws.

Unlike other states, Paterson says, Texas counties have relatively limited enforcement abilities. Under the state's so-called Dillon’s Rule, counties only have powers that are “specifically allotted to it by the state.” So while they have authority over things like access and egress to county roads or construction on floodplains, he says they don't have the zoning authority that would help closely regulate projects like data centers.

Paterson says that the new attorney general could theoretically adjust the terms in the state’s biannual handbook, which establishes the limits of county authority. He also argues that even in a split legislature, especially since anti-data-center sentiment crosses party lines, state lawmakers could propose a viable bill giving counties “limited zoning authority over data centers."

Shelley tells WIRED that since “data centers were a decisive factor in this blue wave,” the upcoming legislative season will be “very interesting.”

“I will say the data center industry hasn't shown a lot of interest in working with state lawmakers or local leaders,” Shelley says, “and I will be interested to see if that changes.”

If not, there’s always low Earth orbit.

‘We Have No Shared Reality’: Two Political Influencers on the Future of Politics Online

Wired November 04, 2026

A voter going to the polls Tuesday night was more likely than not to use information from their favorite influencer than traditional news when casting their vote. According to a recent YouGov survey, nearly 65 percent of 2,000 adults surveyed say they receive their political information from digital creators.

Given that that statistic jumps to 77 percent when you isolate Gen Z, it’s unlikely to change anytime soon. On the heels of a historic Democratic wave capturing the House and Senate Tuesday, Kat Abughazaleh, who ran for an Illinois House seat earlier this year as a Democrat, and Republican strategist CJ Pearson talked about the future of influencers and algorithms at the WIRED World Fair in Miami on Wednesday.

The Trump administration has been particularly aggressive in welcoming right-wing creators into the White House. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt opened formal press briefings to digital creators last year and hosted influencer-specific briefings during her tenure. (Leavitt’s move garnered hefty criticism for favoring softball questions, especially as the administration cracked down on the presence of more traditional media in press briefings.)

Pearson, who previously served on the RNC’s Youth Advisory Council, has been directly involved in these efforts, and points out that multiple federal agencies are now copying the White House’s playbook. He said that it’s simply the cost of getting people’s attention in the digital age.

“It’s a very chronically online administration,” he said. “With how short people’s attention spans are, you have to make [things] interesting.” Not all of the White House’s efforts have been received smoothly on the right: Pearson believes the administration’s decision to distribute portions of the Epstein files to 15 right-wing creators last year was “a misstep.”

For Abughazaleh, a former Media Matters reporter, the administration’s embrace of the internet signals something far more nefarious. Abughazaleh brought up the Department of Education’s recent use of the “Malfoid” meme—a gender-bent Harry Potter fascist figurehead—which, she said, was being promoted for a too-online audience of “incels.” And the White House’s embrace of “AI slop and brutality,” seen in ads about ICE actions, was turning “cruelty into content” rather than informing people, she says.

“They’re trying to ruin your attention span,” she said.

Abughazaleh and Pearson are pretty far apart on the political spectrum. The WIRED forum included some testy exchanges, including whether or not ICE facilities can be called “concentration camps”—a term Abughazaleh, who was arrested for protesting outside an ICE facility last year, used consistently. (The charges were dropped after allegations of misconduct by prosecutors before a grand jury.) They also skirmished over Pearson’s claim that Elon Musk had turned X into a “bastion of free speech.”

But both agreed that reliance on algorithms is increasingly creating echo chambers with young Americans of both parties.

“Algorithms show us what you want to see,” Pearson said, mentioning that his friends on the left will sometimes send him articles on political topics he simply hasn’t seen before. “The deeper question is, is that good for society or for democracy?”

On this, Abughazaleh agrees. “We have no shared reality,” she added.

The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms

Wired November 04, 2026

Leading the Future, the biggest pro-AI super PAC network, is walking away from the midterm elections with just over $20 million still in the bank and a roster of dozens of successful congressional candidates from both sides of the aisle.

At first glance, that looks like a win. The details tell another story, though. The donations went overwhelmingly to safe candidates, and the results in the small handful of riskier races that Leading the Future got involved with indicate that its plans to shape the election fell flat.

When Leading the Future entered the scene in August 2025 vowing to “oppose policies that stifle innovation," it had a war chest of around $100 million thanks to some of Silicon Valley’s biggest tech billionaires—including Andreessen Horowitz, Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman—and was led by major political strategists.

Designed as a “structured ecosystem,” it set a goal of having ”maximum flexibility to engage in the 2026 election cycle and beyond.” The network is made up of 501(c)(4) organizations and federal and state super PACs catering to both sides of the aisle: American Mission largely gives to Republicans, while Think Big largely gives to Democrats. Its structure and overlapping strategists quickly drew comparisons to Fairshake, a massive, well-funded pro-crypto super PAC network that dominated in the 2024 election.

“They came out guns a-blazing, saying, ‘Be afraid, we are going to spend our millions to influence not only how lawmakers legislate us but also against you in your primaries and in your reelection,’” Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, tells WIRED. ”The purpose of that was to bully lawmakers into acquiescence, intimidate them into not sticking their necks out on AI safety or tech industry regulation at all.”

Leading the Future did not respond to requests for comment.

Late last year, Leading the Future took on Democrat Alex Bores, a former Palantir engineer and state lawmaker running in New York’s 12th congressional district on an AI safety platform, spending millions of dollars in attack ads against his primary bid.

“They fully expected to bury him, put his head on a spike, and parade it around as proof that they could,” says Haworth. Instead, Bores’ candidacy became a high-profile proxy war between competing AI philosophies, boosting his profile and platform. The pro-AI safety network Public First, which has significant financial backing from Anthropic, spent $15 million boosting Bores’ candidacy. Though Bores didn’t win, he came second in a crowded primary field to another candidate, Micah Lasher, who campaigned on tech accountability and AI safety.

Leading the Future spent about $26 million in independent expenditures on the primaries alone. But spending tapered off as it headed into the general election, as the network dropped about $10 million in total while overwhelmingly backing candidates in safe races. Its funding also dropped off, with the network reporting zero donations in the second and third quarters.

The strategy seems to have shifted around the same time that stark polling began coming back showing widespread distrust of Big Tech and cronyism in Washington, DC. (An NBC exit poll found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers played a “major” role in their vote.)

Backing safe candidates was, simply put, “an influence play,” says Haworth. ”They're trying to ingratiate themselves with incoming members of Congress.”

The co-founder of Public First Action says that the midterms marked a victory for AI safety. “Voters in both parties delivered the same verdict tonight,” says Brad Carson. “This is a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way.”

Results weren’t great in the riskier races that Leading the Future jumped into.

One of its biggest bets was on Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham and an incumbent running to serve a full term in South Carolina. Graham earned the moniker “Data Center Darline” from her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews due to her enthusiastic support of AI and data center expansion. American Mission donated more than $2 million to Graham, who ultimately lost with 46.5 percent in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1998.

Of the other toss-up House races that Leading the Future weighed in on, almost all were in support of Republican candidates through the American Mission super PAC. The exception was Democratic Florida representative Jared Moskowitz’s reelection campaign, which it funded through Think Big. Moskowitz won by 13,000 votes against challenger Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton.

In North Carolina’s 1st congressional district, Leading the Future through American Mission backed Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel who served as an assistant secretary of defense working on cyber policy under President Donald Trump in 2025, in her primary. Guardrails Alliance, another player in the AI safety network, backed her opponent, Democrat Don Davis, who previously cosponsored a bill that would limit tax giveaways for data center development. Davis won.

Leading the Future also backed Aaron Flint, a retired combat veteran, conservative commentator, and former state director for Republican representative Ryan Zinke, who was running in Montana’s first congressional district. Flint conceded to his Democratic opponent Sam Forstag, a Democratic wildland firefighter who landed endorsements from major progressives including Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez and advocated for strict federal oversight of AI. (The Associated Press has yet to call the race.)

American Mission Florida, a state-level super PAC in the Leading the Future network, got $3 million in support of Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds. While both Donalds and opponent David Jolly took nuanced approaches to the AI safety issue, they diverged strongly on the issue of data center expansion, with Donalds opposing statewide bans or moratoriums on data centers.

After Tuesday night, Silicon Valley will be bracing for what’s expected to be a reckoning over the expansive power and freedom it has enjoyed thus far during Trump’s second term. Democrats have vowed to bring Big Tech bosses to Capitol Hill for hearings. Senator Ron Wyden signaled what's to come in a pithy statement on X. “Subpoenas,” he wrote.

Blade Runner 2099 Shows the ‘Silver Linings’ of a Replicant Takeover

Wired November 04, 2026

Ridley Scott’s 1982 film Blade Runner casts a long shadow. In some ways, literally.

It defined what noir sci-fi would look like for years to come: the rain, the dramatic lighting, the trenchcoats. Denis Villeneuve delivered a worthy sequel in 2017 with Blade Runner 2049, but for some fans nothing will ever touch the original.

Silka Luisa tries not to think about these things. “If I didn’t love Blade Runner this would’ve been way too hard,” the showrunner of Prime Video’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 said Wednesday during the WIRED World Fair event in Miami.

Luisa’s show differs quite a bit from its forebears. It still has the humanoids known as replicants, but in 2099’s future, they’re the ones calling the shots, giving humans the grunt work they used to do. Set 80 years after Blade Runner and 50 years after 2049, it focuses on a replicant Blade Runner, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), on the search for rogue agents. Along the way she gets teamed up with Cora, played by Hunter Schafer, a human pretending to be a replicant to survive. (We’d say more, but the show doesn’t premiere until November 25, and, you know, spoilers.)

If this vision of dystopia sounds too familiar for comfort, Luisa hears you. When asked about how she chose to tackle the franchise, she noted that in the last couple of decades, “the present caught up to the films” as megacorporations and environmental collapse became realities in ways they weren’t in 1982. The point of her Blade Runner is to show what happens in a post-revolution world and “not focus on the fears we’re living with right now.”

That doesn’t mean that Blade Runner 2099 is entirely a dystopian tale. For Luisa, it’s about showing the “silver linings” of a world run by replicants. To do that, she picks up on some of the environmental themes touched on in Villeneuve’s movie, which showed how Earth had been wrecked by human activity. Blade Runner 2099 depicts a world that replicants are trying to bring back from the brink of ecological collapse using the skills they gained when they were working for humans. “They’re able to rehabilitate the planet,” Luisa says.

Blade Runner 2099 also gave Schafer a chance to flex some action-hero muscles—something she’d never done before and something her costar, Yeoh, has been doing for decades. Schafer jumped right in, running and diving across the screen from the pilot onward. For the fight scenes, though, she got some help from Yeoh.

“It was really physically demanding,” Schafer said during WIRED’s conference. “I felt so lucky to have Michelle Yeoh, who is the fucking master, as a scene partner.”

But back to that shadow cast by Scott’s original adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? In addition to being a sci-fi classic, it also created a whole new template for what dystopian fiction could look like. It broods.

Luisa insists there’s a little more hope in hers—and hopes audiences see that, too. She also wants audiences to know that replicants aren’t the same as the AI bots humans are fixated on in 2026. “They’re more akin to us,” she said. “AI, I just don’t have that same sympathy for.” Hear that, Claude?
